💡 Key Takeaways
  • Try as we might, there’s just no changing the hearts and minds of some people, even our dearest loved ones, by presenting them with inconvenient truths.
  • In addition to plastic and aluminum pods, there’s a bevy of grounds-based coffee makers that specialize in one-cup-at-a-time brewing.
  • Thanks to the revival of pour-over and French press coffee making and the proliferation of chic matte-finish electric kettles, there are plenty of ways to brew a single cup of coffee without a dedicated machine and, in general, they give you better results.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Try as we might, there’s just no changing the hearts and minds of some people, even our dearest loved ones, by presenting them with inconvenient truths. I’m talking, of course, about people who prefer coffee from pods. But based on the popularity of coffee pod machines, it seems those of us who haven’t been assimilated into pod people are outnumbered. And, to be fair, even if the quality of their coffee is all over the place, we can’t deny their convenience. My goal here is to find single-serve coffee makers that can blend that convenience with coffee I actually want to drink.

In addition to plastic and aluminum pods, there’s a bevy of grounds-based coffee makers that specialize in one-cup-at-a-time brewing. So if you’re interested in the ease of pod machines, low-volume coffee brewing for one, or just can’t avoid K-cups, here are the machines that brewed the best.

Thanks to the revival of pour-over and French press coffee making and the proliferation of chic matte-finish electric kettles, there are plenty of ways to brew a single cup of coffee without a dedicated machine and, in general, they give you better results. We will also note that many fancier drip coffee makers (like our favorites from Fellow and Oxo) can now be programmed to brew just one cup of coffee at a time—and do so without the plastic waste of pods. If you want true versatility and have the counter space, we’d advise you to consider a machine that will let you brew for yourself or a crowd, if needed. But we understand the convenience factor of capsule machines, which is why, if you must pop a pod for your daily cup, we’ve made our recommendations below, plus suggested some non-pod options too.

Industry observers note that updated 11/25/26: Nespresso is phasing out it's old Vertuo Plus machines but never fear, the upcoming Vertuo Up is an even better version of the original and it's our new top pick. And in other news, Keurig released its first completely K-Cup-free machine, and the new Alta platform is really quite good. That makes it the first Keurig machine we've ever recommended.

Vertuo Plus Coffee and Espresso Maker by Breville.

Caffeinator Single-Serve Coffee Maker.

Custom Grind & Brew Single Serve Coffee Maker.

Size: 5” x 18" x 10.5”Water reservoir capacity: 47 oz.Colors: 4Coffee sizes: 1.3 oz., 2.7 oz., 5 oz., 8 oz., 12 oz., 18 oz.

Sources indicate that what we love: Everything we loved about the original Nespresso Vertuo machine is present in the Vertuo Up. The centrifugal brewing method patented for Vertuo machines makes more balanced, better extracted coffee than most typical pod and capsule methods that just shower the grounds with water. And Nespresso continues to expand the world of capsules you can use, now featuring a number of single origin pods for those who prefer flavor profiles from different growing regions around the world, as well as flavored pods for folks whose regular Starbucks order is 13 words long.

And the Vertuo system also reads whatever capsule you insert and automatically brews at the proper volume, so it really does have one-button operation.

The rotating water tank is a nice touch because it allows the machine to fit in any configuration of kitchen and it's very easy to refill.

But the biggest upgrade is the addition of what Nespresso calls “Coffee Creation” mode, which is particularly good for iced coffee lovers. The extra button tells the machine to brew a more concentrated, smaller dose of coffee. That means it can melt the ice without diluting the flavor of the drink. It also lets you add a healthy pour of milk to hot coffee with the same results.

Sources indicate that what we'd leave: Nespresso pods tend towards darker, roastier coffees. So if you have a thing for fruitier, more acidic coffee, you may be better off with either something that uses whole beans or Keurig's Alta.

In a recent development, size: 10.84" W × 11.77" H × 19.0" DWater reservoir capacity: 72 ouncesColors: 3Coffee sizes: 1.5 oz. to 12 oz.

Sources indicate that for a brand that’s name is pretty much synonymous with plastic pods, Keurig threw us for a loop in 2026 when it unveiled Alta, its first plastic pod-free system. Alta is still a single-serve machine and it still uses a capsule of sorts, swapping those little cups for AltaRounds, tablets of ground coffee held together by a compostable vegetable-based coating. Each AltaRound is printed with a QR code that tells the machine what drink styles it should offer up on the touchscreen display from remarked coffee, whether it is a smaller espresso tablet or a larger flavor coffee round.

According to recent reports, what we love: In my experience, this is the first machine with any association to Keurig that I’ve actively enjoyed the coffee from and kept returning to. For contrast, the whole time I tested the Alta, I had my usual DeLonghi machine set up but a few feet away and for weeks I didn’t touch it because the coffee I really liked the coffee I got from the Alta. There were nuances between the different roasts, from light to medium to dark, and detectably different intensities in the espresso rounds. (Keurig’s announcement states that Peet’s coffee is already on board for future AltaRounds offerings and more partnerships are on the way.).

Recent findings suggest that customization, while usually limited to three dots indicating temperature and brew strength, was also effective, if a bit. When selecting a milk-based drink, the frother did an impressive job of adjusting to various temperatures and thicknesses, though I did find I usually had to scoop a good bit of any super airy cold foam or cappuccino foam from the pitcher with a spoon.

Navigating the menu was clear and easy. And once I got the hang of it, I found many aspects of the Alta, like the generous 72-ounce water tank and easy to empty drip and used coffee trays, or the simple swaps from hot to iced, to be seamless and a pleasure to use.

What we’d leave: First, it’s a large machine at 19 inches deep, occupying significant counter space, and while part of that has to do with the milk frothing apparatus, it’s also because the AltaRounds and separate K-cup slots are side-by-side, meaning if and when the brand just made the leap to an AltaRounds-only machine, it could probably be a good bit smaller. The automatic nature of the frother is handy, but pouring my own milk in a world of automatic dispensers on super-automatic espresso machines, left it up to me to set up the milk and do the pouring which may be more work than most Keurig converted coffee drinkers are used to. The generous water tank I called out above is slightly limiting in terms of where it allows you to set the machine up. It slides in or out from the side and if you don’t have space next to your Alta to do that, this could pose a problem. I also found the pours a bit splashy, and constantly had little droplets of coffee on the machine and on the counter nearby.

The touchscreen placement is a little wonky. It’s flat on top of the machine making it a little hard to read, and it’s actually housed in the lid for the AltaRounds slot, something that a fresh user (or houseguest) might not realize, as the K-cup slot is more readily discoverable with no screen and a lip for lifting it up. I fully put an AltaRound into the K-cup slot on the first go around before I more carefully read the instructions. This machine connects to WiFi, which is probably crucial for downloading new coffee brand specs as more AltaRounds become available, but my software updates were sometimes sticky and required unplugging the machine to unfreeze it.

Lastly, just to harp on the elephant plastic pod in the room, the Alta as it stands feels like a bridge machine to something better, but because of the sheer magnitude of the K-cup world Keurig has created, we’re stuck with a hybrid that feels part past and part future.

Caffeinator Single-Serve Coffee Maker.

Size: 12.6"H x 4.5" W x 14" DWater reservoir capacity: 48 oz.Colors: Concrete, MidnightCoffee sizes: 4 oz., 6 oz., 8 oz., 10 oz., 12 oz.

Recent findings suggest that what we love: If you’re looking for a streamlined, smart-looking machine to brew your K-cups, Chefman’s Caffeinator wraps its pod machine in a chic shell. There’s a snazzy drip tray that slides up and down for differently sized cups, and backlit touch buttons that disappear into the satin finish exterior (in Concrete or Midnight) when not selected. In addition to looking good, it also produced a pretty good cup of coffee, both from pods and grounds thanks to three simultaneous streams of water.

In a recent development, it offers a lot of customization possibilities, with three hot temperature options from “warm” to “piping hot” (the latter of which raised the temp about 20 degrees from default “hot”), plus a lower temp iced coffee mode, and three brew strengths in addition to multiple cup size selections. It's also compatible with both K-cups and ground coffee. All that gave me the ability to get my coffee a little closer to the way I want it, even if it comes from a plastic pod.

What we’d leave: Clearance for larger cups and tumblers is pretty low, unless you remove the drip tray entirely, which gives you 8.25" of height. But doing that leaves a ring and fixed “divot” about the width of a cupholder that some bigger travel mugs still may not fit into. I wish the water tank was a bit bigger, wasn’t rear-mounted, and had a sturdier lid, however it requires only a slight lift to remove it from the base so it’s easy to manage, even if you can’t see behind the machine. I would have also liked a place to store the K-cup/grounds adapter inserts when not using one or the other.

Custom Grind & Brew Single Serve Coffee Maker.

Size: 15.71" H x 7.99" W x 11.47" DWater reservoir capacity: 58 oz.Color: Black Stainless (only one option)Coffee sizes: 8 oz., 10 oz., 12 oz., 16 oz., 20 oz., 24 oz.

What we love: Why settle for stale pods when you can have freshly ground coffee at the touch of a button? This single-serve machine from Cuisinart has a built-in stainless-steel conical burr grinder that grinds beans only when you’re ready for a cup of coffee. The bean hopper holds up to half a pound of coffee beans and has a gasket-sealed lid to keep them relatively fresh (a seemingly simple feature that my fancy grinder-equipped espresso machine lacks).

Sources indicate that I was also impressed with the fineness of the sediment that was left in the bottom of my cup using the mesh filter. You should expect anything that uses only a mesh filter to leave at least a little bit of ground coffee sediment, but in this case it wasn’t unappealing during the last sips. If that is the sort of thing that bothers you, the basket is also paper filter compatible. Grinding and brewing are relatively quiet operations that probably won’t wake anyone up, and gentle beeps let you know your coffee is ready. Also, while you’ll need to find a carafe or container that fits under the machine, the fact that the Cuisinart can brew up to 24 oz. of hot coffee means you could, in a pinch, use this for a few guests over for brunch.

According to recent reports, what we’d leave: Cleaning the filter after every use is a chore (and some people choose single-serve machines specifically to avoid that chore by using pods) That noted, there are more gentle beeps to remind you the filter access door hasn’t been opened since the last brew, so at least you won’t forget. Clearance for cups, even with the drip tray completely removed, is still rather low for travel cups at just seven inches. Also, when brewing at the 24 oz. setting, the coffee was noticeably weaker than smaller cup sizes.

Size: 11.5" H x 7.5" W x 10.6" D (plus positionable water tank)Water reservoir capacity: 20-plus oz.Colors: Black, Linen (white)Coffee sizes: 5 oz.–20 oz.

Industry observers note that what we love: Portland, Oregon–based Ratio takes its coffee maker design seriously, including its smallest entry, the Ratio Four, so named because it brews a maximum of four 5-oz. cups of coffee in a single batch. The machine couldn’t be simpler; it uses one button that brews however much water is in the reservoir and a filter basket with flat bottom paper filters. Turn it on, and the first of three lights illuminates to let you know it’s in Bloom mode, followed by Brew and Ready when your coffee is done. The Ratio heats brewing water to an average of 200º F and has a wide stainless-steel showerhead that evenly wets the coffee grounds, producing a full 20-oz. brew that was robust, strong, and exactly what I like to wake up to.

But we’re here to talk about single-serve coffee, and while using it for one cup is a little trickier (you’ll have to measure smaller quantities of water and coffee), the Four delivered the same bold, balanced brew in a 5-oz. cup, it did in a 20-oz. carafe. I found the recommended 9 grams of coffee lacking, but the instructions advise customizing the ratio a bit, and sure enough a few more grams in the filter did the trick. I found I got the tastiest results brewing two cups (10 oz.), as I think the longer siphoning and heating process with more water flowing through the system was key to a more satisfying extraction. Plus, I like a big cup of coffee.

It has been revealed that the Ratio Four comes with a handblown 20-oz. glass carafe that also has a sealed lid and a silicone padded bottom. But what I appreciated is the ability to brew directly into any container; there is no hidden button or latch that the carafe needs to activate to brew or let water through. I could use a mug or travel tumbler if I wanted to. And, surprisingly, the same goes for the filter basket, with the Ratio website and instruction booklet explaining that they’d be just fine with you using it with a Kalita Wave or Origami pour-over dripper if you want. A long-press of the brew button also lets you choose between the default (4 oz. of water) bloom and a shorter (2 oz.) bloom, which is preferable if you are brewing a single cup.

Industry observers note that all of the removable parts are hand-wash-only, but I never found them needing more than a rinse between uses. The instructions recommend occasional cleaning and descaling with an approved solution to keep the lines clean, though, which is notable maintenance for any coffee maker.

It has an external, detached water tank that takes up more counter space than it would if it were flush with the machine, but that cuts both ways. I actually love that it’s connected via a sturdy yet flexible hose, allowing you to position it on either side of the machine in a variety of ways depending on your specific needs.

It has been revealed that what we’d leave: Ratio is a brand known for machines with parts that feel very high quality, as senior editor Noah Kaufman has pointed out in his reviews of its other two machines. Some of the Ratio Four’s parts are definitely in line with that reputation, like the heavy braided hose between the brewer and water tank. But there are exterior parts of the brewer that do feel less substantial than you might expect for something that costs $279. I also found myself double-checking that the filter basket was installed correctly, because it doesn’t click or snap to signal it’s on right.

It has been revealed that “Set it and forget it” coffee drinkers should take note that the water reservoir isn’t “smart,” meaning it will brew whatever water is inside, so a full reservoir with a coffee mug underneath will overflow. If that’s something you don’t want to think about, the Cuisinart Custom Grind and Brew might serve you better as it requires less frequent refills.

Size: 19" x 6" x 16"Water reservoir capacity: 80 oz.Colors: 2Coffee sizes: 2 oz., 10 oz.

What we love: We have an in-depth review of the Cumulus cold-brew machine for more details, but here’s the gist: You could, in some ways, consider this the Nespresso of cold coffee with its recyclable aluminum capsules that are filled an even more concentrated cold-brew concentrate. The machine does the job of chilling water via an onboard compressor, meaning you don’t need ice in your cup. For texture, the Cumulus offers three settings—still, nitro, and espresso—making it one of the best machines we’ve tried for cold coffee connoisseurs. (Oh, and it achieves that “nitro” coffee without any gas canisters by using ambient air.) It vacuums out the capsules, leaving them empty and ready to recycle after you’re done brewing. And at just 6", wide it’s got a relatively small footprint and front-loading water reservoir, making it easy to use and keep on the countertop.

What we’d leave: At its current nearly $700 price tag, this is a luxury item—though, if you’re dropping $5 on cold brew every day, maybe it isn’t?

According to recent reports, with so many brands and varieties of pods out there, I did my best to compare apples to apples by using Starbucks pods and beans of the same roast for every machine (Bruvi being the only exception that doesn’t sell Starbucks pods). That’s not because the global corporate coffee giant is my favorite coffee roaster, but because it is the most cross-pollinated among all types of machines and formats. For Keurig machines, I also tested using K-cups from Illy coffee, which I’ve found produce stronger coffee (an attribute testers often flag as missing from Keurigs). I used fresh grounds for any machines that offered a refillable pod and whole beans of the same roast were used on machines with grinding capabilities. I also tested the different brew size, strength, and style options on any machine with multiple settings.

There are plenty of subpar single-cup coffee makers out there, and life is short, so we don’t think bad coffee needs to be a part of it. We looked for coffee pod machines that delivered balanced flavor and a smooth finish with consistency.

Are the pods simple to load and is the interface (buttons or screens) intuitive and simple? Does the water reservoir require constant refill oversight, and is it easy to access? Does the machine require regular cleaning or maintenance to keep working? The ease of use should extend to pod collection and disposal as well. Some machines require emptying the coffee pod chamber after each use. Others collect them for occasional disposal or recycling.

According to recent reports, pod coffee makers don’t need to take up too much space, but they can also be too small, relying on heating and brewing elements that sacrifice on quality. And because most regular coffee drinkers won’t be putting their machine away every day, it should look good on your countertop too.

Pods are a problem. There’s no way around it. No coffee brewing option will be as ecologically sound as simply pouring water over grounds (and then composting those grounds if you can). Yes, technically you can tear apart Keurig pods, empty their spent coffee into your compost bin and the filter into the trash, and then recycle the plastic cup portion. But overall, we can’t get behind any machine that requires plastic pods that aren’t easily recyclable. Machines that operate using a reusable pod were also given some bonus points.

You’d be hard-pressed to find a better looking coffee machine than the Terra Kaffe Demi. It’s stylish, it comes in four colors, and it’s relatively small for something with a built-in grinder at just over 7" wide—however, it’s nearly 16" deep, and you’ll need access to both sides of the machine, plus the reservoir housed on the back. (If you opt for the milk-frothing TK-02 option, it’ll be wider and deeper still.) Aside from brewing great espresso and pretty great coffee, the most impressive aspect of the Terra Kaffe is how quiet it is. Compared to the cacophony my similarly priced grind-and-brew automatic espresso machine makes, the Demi barely produced a sound.

Generally, I liked the espresso results I got from the Terra Kaffee more than I liked the drip coffee. Once I dialed in my preferred drip settings—which you can adjust for any of the machine’s four drink presets after navigating a maze of menus and submenus—I was impressed with the rich flavor and texture of the coffee with no hint of sediment at the bottom of the cup. For what’s essentially a super-automatic espresso machine with no milk frothing, it’s expensive (commitment-phobes can rent it for $40 a month), so it wouldn’t be my first choice to simply fill a mug in the morning. But if you toggle back and forth between coffee and espresso, it’s comparably priced with other super automatic machines, and it offers a sleek and almost silent option.

This touchscreen pod machine is everything we wish most K-cup machines could be. It offers rich, balanced, and nuanced coffee, plus eight brewing sizes, one-touch presets for low-acid, americano, iced coffee (which brews hot over ice), and cold brew (which uses cooler water), as well as simple customizations to any of these like temperature control and brew strength. And it does all this using its own proprietary pods made with specially treated polypropylene, which will (mostly) break down in a landfill. So other than you need to use its proprietary coffee pods, Bruvi offers all of the convenience of capsules and the fancy-pants settings of high-end coffee makers and good coffee with little downside.

An espresso machine but make it Nespresso. That’s the idea behind the Creatista series from Nespresso, which adds the automatic milk steaming perfected by Breville, bootstraps it on to a Nespresso Vertuo machine, and wraps the whole thing in handsome stainless steel. It’s great for someone looking for a cappuccino hack. Ultimately we picked the Keurig Alta over the Creatista for this genre of machine because it’s a little less expensive and offers a little more versatility in the form of cold foam options.

Vertuo Plus Coffee and Espresso Maker by Breville.

The Vertuo Plus does everything the Vertuo Up does sans the iced coffee and full carafe brewing features. The major knock on it is that it's being phased out to make way for several other Vertuo machines. But it's still available from third party retailers like Williams Sonoma and Amazon right, often for pretty affordable prices.

It has been revealed that the Essenza Mini comes from Nespresso’s Original line, which uses smaller capsules and only brews 1.35-oz. espresso shots or 3.7-oz. Lungo cups of coffee. And it does so using 19 bars of pressure for extraction, as opposed to the VertuoLine’s centrifugal extraction method. It doesn’t make plain old cups of coffee, however, but we’ve included it here as a good option for pod coffee drinkers who prefer espresso drinks and want a simple way to make beverages like cappuccinos and macchiatos.

Like its larger Moccamaster brethren, Cup-One has a timeless, old-school design and a single, tactile glowing “on” switch would make it look at home in a truck stop diner or a trendy modern apartment. And speaking of diners, the coffee, even in a 10-oz. default brew, was diner quality (I mean that affectionately), with robust flavor and texture—though that may have had something to do with the fact that I used the recommended four tablespoons of grounds, twice what other machines suggest for eight oz. Considering its higher price tag, it appears to be pretty low-tech. Okay, okay, it’s just an automatic pour-over machine. But it brewed one of the best single cups from grounds I’ve had from any drip machine. And it’s quiet with no bubbling or burping. What can I say? The small footprint and retro vibes also won me over. It’s a small luxury. It’s a vibe. As the kids say, it’s aesthetic.

Industry observers note that now for the minuses: Yes, you could get a (really nice) gooseneck kettle and pour-over system for, like, half the cost. Give and take. Low clearance under the drip spout means you’re stuck with brewing into mugs and low-profile tumblers. The included measuring scoop and a needle-like poking tool for clearing the filter holder have no home onboard the machine, adding to your “things we need to keep but don’t know where else to put” drawer.

In a recent development, of all the podless machines, this one is the most podlike in its convenience while producing pod-beating coffee. The eponymous Scoop is a small mesh filter that doubles as a measuring spoon. Just scoop up (or in) your grounds to the maximum fill line, and you’re good to go. The Scoop sits in a second “grounds catching” mesh filter which, in my tests, reduced silt in my cup compared to similar single-filter systems, but didn’t eliminate it. Using the two size settings, you can brew either 8 oz. or 14 oz. per cup. The coffee it produced on normal brew mode was fine, but tapping the BOLD setting did actually produce much more robust results. However, each cup I made was on the oily side.

A flip-down drip tray holds standard mugs, while the lower drip tray has a clearance of 7", so lots of travel tumblers stand a chance. The 40-oz. water reservoir is on the small side, but is easy to access and lift off from either side with a molded-in handle.

When you’re done, simple empty and rinse The Scoop (filter) and, if necessary, the secondary filter, and you can brew another cup right away. That’s as long as your Scoop filter is dry, anyway. If it’s still damp from the last cup, you’re going to need to scoop into The Scoop, which basically just makes this like any other small filter machine.

4-in-1 Single-Serve Latte, Iced, and Hot Coffee Maker.

In a recent development, when you think of Mr. Coffee, you probably think of a basic, no-frills drip machine sitting on your grandparents’ countertop. And, for the most part, this multifunction machine is still just a small, simple rain-shower-style drip coffee maker designed for one-cup-at-a-time brewing. The reservoir and reusable mesh filter sit under the lid and feature graduated measurements for water levels from 4 oz. up to 16 oz. You can fill the removable filter with grounds using a double-ended measuring scoop that nests on the side of the machine and has guidelines for different sizes and styles of coffee, whether you’re brewing a “shot” for milk-based drinks or a tumbler full of iced coffee. The bonus of this machine is that, while still retaining a small footprint, it also includes a decent self-contained, stainless-steel milk frother cup with presets for hot milk and cold foam that can be used completely independently from the coffee-making portion.

As for taste and texture, everything was like middle-of-the-road drip coffee. However, I found that following the instructions for the weakest iced coffee (one large scoop) actually gave me decent results that weren’t as watered down as other machines on this list. It also comes with a 22-oz. plastic tumbler just for iced coffee—and enough brewing clearance to fit such a large cup—so if you’re someone who flip-flops between iced and hot coffee and aren’t too finicky about dialing in precise strength, it’s a practical option.

System Coffee and Espresso Machine.

If, for whatever reason, you want to brew Nespresso pods but don’t want to actually get a Nespresso machine, the L’or is your choice. It brews Original Nespresso pods along with its own proprietary pods (which are cross-compatible with classic Nespresso machines). L’or’s brewer offers three brewing sizes and extracts coffee from the pod at 19 bars of pressure through two spouts, similar to the way coffee comes out of a semiautomatic espresso machine. This produces a delicious layer of crema that’s as good as Nespresso’s. It was only in a head-to-head matchup that we slightly preferred Nespresso.

It has been revealed that if you like the idea of Nespresso but not the idea of being stuck with one-cup-at-at-time brewing, the Vertuo Next has brew sizes ranging from a single shot of espresso up to 18 oz. of coffee with the proper pods (an optional carafe is available for the biggest brews). This smart machine also has Bluetooth and Wi-Fi connectivity, so you can track your favorite pods and get firmware updates. However, the Next is a smaller machine than the Vertuo Plus, and with that comes a smaller water tank. And like the Vertuo Pop+ below, the closing and locking mechanism is a bit clunkier than we’d like. But for all out versatility, it’s probably your best Nespresso brewing option.

If you’re looking for a K-cup-compatible coffee machine that can do a little more, this is a good option. It comes with a reusable filter capsule that, while a little finicky getting it to work properly, does, indeed, work. It also has a 72-oz. water tank for less-frequent refills, as well as settings for five cup sizes and two brewing temperatures. The biggest boost we’ll give this machine is that it produced superior tasting coffee using K-cups than any Keurig machine we’ve tried.

Recent findings suggest that we like almost all Nespresso machines, but we think the three recommended above are better than the Vertuo Pop+ for a few reasons. On the Pop+, the actual snapping down of the lid to puncture the pod inside was the clunkiest of the bunch and a lot of effort in a pre-coffee morning fog. And this low-profile machine was so low to the counter, we couldn’t fit a pint glass or similarly sized tumbler underneath, which was a problem considering that Nespresso offers Iced Leggero pods that brew 7.7 oz., overflowing our smaller ice-filled cups. Lastly, the water reservoir on the standard version of this machine (which comes in at 25.4 oz. or 32 oz. on the Deluxe model) is pretty small compared to the Vertuo Plus, and it’s set in a fixed side-mounted position, so you’re stuck with the orientation as is. In other words, it’s still a solid Nespresso coffee brewer but less versatile than what you get for a few dollars more.

Industry observers note that you might consider this machine Lavazza’s attempt to answer the classic Nespresso; its plastic coffee pods and presets brew in espresso or lungo sizes. It beats the Keurig and K-cup machines when it comes to robust and flavorful coffee, but it didn’t live up to the high bar set by Nespresso. The Ristretto capsules we tried were a bit bitter and the texture was thin, though we actually liked the medium-roast decaf capsules enough as after dinner/dessert coffee. Considering Lavazza makes capsules for both Nespresso classic machines and K-cup machines, along with other espresso products, we just don’t think it’s necessary to buy into the Lavazza tech—as sleek and compact as it is—to enjoy its coffee.

Industry observers note that the dual on this machine refers to both drip coffee and coffee pods. It offers multiple brew sizes and strengths, and, being a drip machine first, comes with a glass carafe. It accepts pods with an adapter that fits into the filter basket. Some of its handier features are an adjustable 60-oz. water reservoir, dedicated hot water dispenser, fold-away milk frother, and an adjustable drip tray that allows you to brew directly into a cup or tumbler. But we don’t think it’s the best drip coffee maker out there, and it’s too big and complex for just making capsule coffee.

Industry observers note that there’s a lot to like about the exterior design of this slimmed down version a Ninja single-serve system, from its pleasing colorways like stone, sage green, and glacier blue (in addition to black), its handy fold-away frothing wand that easily whipped some pre-warmed milk into a mug full of foam, or its storage nooks for the pod/grounds adapters and measuring spoon. The generous water tank, while rear-mounted, has a pressure fit lid that actually stays put between the faucet and counter. And all of its detachable parts and pieces are dishwasher-safe. But whether you’ll crave the actual coffee from this machine is another story. Pods tasted weak, even at the lower 6-oz. brewing size, and grounds were better but not by very much. The Specialty Brew setting, which brews a 4-oz. shot of coffee for use with the frother, isn’t quite an espresso experience, either. And while you can choose multiple cup sizes, you can’t select anything but the preset temperature.

In a recent development, despite its 4.4 stars from over 100,000 ratings on Amazon, we can’t imagine using this machine for coffee every day. Our experience with Keurig coffee pods, regardless of the brand of coffee we tried, was watery or bitter coffee (or, at worst, somehow both). That, plus the fact that this machine’s reservoir is only large enough for one cup at a time makes this one tedious for regular use.

Unfortunately, the “smart” features of this machine add more frustration than anything. The machine is supposed to recognize which K-cup you put inside and adjust its brew settings accordingly. It also allows you to select and save brew sizes and temperatures as presets. But in our tests, the machine frequently froze and had to be unplugged to get it going again. Being “smart,” this machine also offers app-enabled remote brewing, something we can’t imagine using since you have to put K-cups in (and take used cups out) one at a time. One plus was the generous 66-oz. water reservoir with a convenient pitcher handle. But in the end, this fancy Keurig didn’t improve our pod coffee experience whatsoever.

Recent findings suggest that as iced coffee rivals hot coffee consumption these days, it’s no wonder Keurig would offer a machine that specializes in cold drinks. One aspect of this machine that’s well thought-out is its dispensing spout, which is high enough off the counter to accommodate a pint glass or tumbler. We found the iced coffee setting only reduced the brew temperature by less than 10°, so our ice still had to do most of the work while also watering the coffee down, which was already diluted with 12 oz. of water during brewing. Even on the smallest of three preprogramed hot coffee brew sizes, it mirrored our other Keurig experiences with weak or just not tasty coffee output.

Oxo 8-cup Coffee Maker with Podless Single Serve Function.

Even though this is an 8-cup coffee maker, I tested this machine because it proudly advertises on the box that it’s also a single-serve machine. Let me get one thing out of the way immediately: This is a great little drip coffee maker if you’re brewing by the carafe. It has the option to brew full and half carafes, and a heated warming plate that keeps the coffee pleasantly hot for hours. But it fell short on a few functional aspects, as well as that single-serve option. First, the water tank is not “smart”—as in, it uses all the water you put in it every time. So if you want a full carafe, you fill it all the way up with water, and if you want a single cup, you put in just enough for… two cups. No, it doesn’t actually brew a single serving of coffee. For a $200-plus machine purporting to do single-serve brewing that can go toe-to-toe with Keurig, that’s a little disappointing.

Additional testing and reporting by Emily Farris.

#147191. Trump says no Iran deal needed after conflict drove GOP’s midterm losses

Trump says no Iran deal needed after conflict drove GOP’s midterm losses

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (751 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • President Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance salute during a Wednesday ceremony at Arlington National Cemetery in honor of Veterans Day.
  • President Donald Trump on Thursday shut down his administration’s on-again-off-again talks with Iran, saying he would not seek a deal to formally end the nine-month-old conflict with Tehran.
  • Sources indicate that the possible end of the pursuit of a diplomatic solution came nine days after Trump and congressional Republicans suffered massive losses in the midterm elections.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

President Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance salute during a Wednesday ceremony at Arlington National Cemetery in honor of Veterans Day. (Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images).

President Donald Trump on Thursday shut down his administration’s on-again-off-again talks with Iran, saying he would not seek a deal to formally end the nine-month-old conflict with Tehran.

Sources indicate that the possible end of the pursuit of a diplomatic solution came nine days after Trump and congressional Republicans suffered massive losses in the midterm elections. House Democrats will have more than 250 seats come January, and Senate Democrats will have at least 55 seats in the Senate — with Alaska’s competitive race still uncalled.

Polls leading up to Election Day and since have shown that a majority of voters, and a sizeable chunk of Trump’s Republican base, felt the Iran conflict was a mistake.

Vice President JD Vance penned a lengthy social media post the day after the election, blaming, in large part, the Iran war for the coast-to-coast Democratic victories. Some GOP lawmakers have also called for an end to the conflict, which drove up fuel and other commodity prices.

"The reason we lost is the war," Vance wrote the morning after the GOP wipeout. "The president himself mentioned so last night.".

In a recent development, trump has said that he agrees with Vance’s assessment but that if he had to decide again whether to join Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in striking Iranian targets, he would reach the same conclusion. On Monday, he told reporters that the Iran war "militarily is effectively over.".

Vance had been Trump’s designated top negotiator in the talks with Iran’s remaining leaders, but the president stated Thursday on social media that he had ordered his second-in-command to instead “focus his complete and total attention on the Massive Corruption and Crime taking place in Democrat run Cities and States throughout the U.S.”.

“We don’t need a deal with Iran. Those days have long since passed,” he added. “We’ve got their money, Hundreds of Billions of Dollars, and we’ve got their Strait!".

In a recent development, the situation along the Strait of Hormuz remains contested and dangerous for commercial vessels, including ones that deliver a large amount of the world’s oil products. Iranian officials contend that they control most of the key waterway.

Trump, Vance and other administration officials have said in recent weeks that they were open to continuing talks with Iran, while criticizing Tehran's negotiating tactics. Last week, Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who also is Trump’s national security adviser, told reporters that Iran's latest demands were unreasonable.

Recent findings suggest that trump’s announcement Thursday could represent his latest way to try assuaging GOP voters, including members of his “Make America Great Again” base. A Reuters/Ipsos poll conducted after the midterms and released Tuesday highlighted that a majority of Republicans (51 percent) want Congress to pass legislation that would end the Iran conflict. Overall, 71 percent of Americans would support such a bill, the survey found.

The conflict was front-and-center during the midterms campaign.

According to recent reports, republican former Rep. Mike Rogers, who lost the Senate race in Michigan to Democrat Abdul El-Sayed, called for the Iran conflict to end "swiftly.".

“Michigan families are struggling with the price of everyday life. Groceries cost too much. We have to bring prices down," Rogers remarked in one campaign ad.

On Capitol Hill, GOP lawmakers have tried giving Trump cover, while raising some concerns about high gas prices and questioning whether the president and his team have a viable exit strategy.

It has been revealed that as the midterms campaign hit the homestretch in late September, two Iowa Republicans in tight races, Reps. Zach Nunn and Mariannette Miller-Meeks, voted with Democrats on a measure to end the conflict.

“With the negotiating window closed, sustained combat operations now require congressional authorization,” Nunn, an Air Force veteran, wrote on social media. “I will not support another open-ended war.”.

Nunn and Miller-Meeks both lost their seats last week, despite breaking with the president over the war.

Trump’s declaration this week of a military end to the Iran war came more than seven years after he offered some foreshadowing during a June 25, 2019, exchange with this CQ Roll Call reporter in the Oval Office.

Industry observers note that asked that day what his exit strategy would be if war ever broke out with Iran, he stated: “You’re not going to need an exit strategy. I don’t do exit strategies.”.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • According to recent reports, this classic sauce from Bolognese cooking teachers Margherita and Valeria Simili combines ground beef with prosciutto, chicken livers, milk, and tomato purée.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

There are certain foods that we wish we could package up and save forever, and tomatoes are at the top of that list. Canning is an excellent way to hold onto the fleeting abundance of summer, when these versatile fruits are at their ripest, juiciest, and most flavorful. Canning may never be able to re-create the feeling of picking a plump, juicy tomato fresh from the vine and slicing it while it’s still warm from the sun, but in the depths of winter, we’ll take what we can get. Whether they are using diced, puréed, crushed, or whole canned tomatoes, these recipes make the most of the ingredient, extending its life well beyond the growing season.

According to recent reports, this classic sauce from Bolognese cooking teachers Margherita and Valeria Simili combines ground beef with prosciutto, chicken livers, milk, and tomato purée. The slow-simmered sauce is a natural partner for serving over pasta or as a hearty filling for lasagna. Get the recipe >.

Stalks of crisp celery are cut into bite-size pieces and slowly braised with tomatoes, onion, prosciutto, and olive oil until tender. This simple Italian preparation transforms a vegetable that’s often an afterthought into a comforting side dish. Get the recipe >.

Agrodolce, or “sour and sweet” in Italian, is a classic Sicilian sauce, here paired with tender steamed broccoli. Red wine, canned tomatoes, vinegar, raisins, and black olives give the sauce its characteristic sweet-tart and slightly salty balance, while toasted pine nuts add a little crunch. Get the recipe >.

In a recent development, in this simple recipe, beef short ribs slowly braise with red wine, garlic, onion, and canned tomatoes until the meat is fall-apart tender. It’s a hearty, straightforward one-pot meal that makes especially good use of pantry staples. Get the recipe >.

Sources indicate that this stuffed pasta with ridged edges from celebrated Los Angeles chef Evan Funke pairs a filling of ricotta and greens with a humble lightly cooked tomato sauce. Get the recipe >.

In a recent development, this classic Sicilian dish balances tender fried eggplant with caramelized onions, golden raisins, olives, capers, and a sweet-tart tomato sauce. An unexpected addition of unsweetened chocolate brings a subtle bitterness that rounds out the sweet and savory flavors. Get the recipe >.

While not the pizza that many people think of, this beloved Rhode Island specialty features thick, airy rectangles of focaccia-like dough topped with a simple tomato sauce. Traditionally served at room temperature, they’re a fixture at bakeries, parties, and family gatherings. Get the recipe >.

According to recent reports, lamb, torn pita, and herbs are formed into tender rounds and simmered in a spicy tomato sauce, then finished with a cool, lemony aioli. The dish can be prepared ahead and reheated before serving, with the greens and sauce added at the last minute. Get the recipe >.

A tomato-packed broth made with topneck clams and salt pork provides the foundation for this hearty soup. The mixture is chilled overnight, giving the flavors time to meld before being finished with bacon, onion, celery, garlic, and fresh herbs. Get the recipe >.

Roasted pumpkin, winter squash, sweet potato, and bell pepper are folded into a tomato-based sauce spiced with cumin, coriander, and harissa. Chickpeas and dried apricots make the stew hearty and subtly sweet, while bulgur mixed with dried cherries and raisins makes for a flavorful, filling base. Get the recipe >.

These crisp, golden fritters bring together tender Sea Island red peas, Carolina Gold rice, and collard greens in a nod to the flavors of South Carolina’s Lowcountry. The accompanying sauce simmers canned tomatoes with brown sugar, cider vinegar, and smoked paprika, creating a bright, tangy dip with just a hint of sweetness and smoke. Get the recipe >.

According to recent reports, this Sicilian baked pasta layers ring-shaped noodles with a tomato-rich ragù of beef, pork, and peas, plus fried eggplant, hard-boiled eggs, ham, and cheese. It’s the kind of deeply layered, all-in-one dish that makes for the perfect centerpiece when cooking for a crowd. Get the recipe >.

According to recent reports, this Roman classic gets its character from slow-braised oxtail and an unusually simple combination of tomatoes and celery, with no garlic or onions. The sauce is even better made a day or two ahead, giving the flavors time to deepen before it’s tossed with the cooked pasta. Get the recipe >.

Creamy polenta provides the filling backbone of this dish, while sausage stewed in marinara sauce brings a rich, savory depth. Finished with grated Pecorino Romano, it’s a classic Italian comfort food that’s hearty, satisfying, and perfect for a cozy dinner. Get the recipe >.

This cultural mash-up pairs chewy udon noodles with a deeply savory tomato sauce spiked with guanciale, white miso, chile, and Pecorino Romano. The sauce starts with canned San Marzano tomatoes, which simmer with garlic and onion until thick and rich. Get the recipe >.

Sources indicate that this southern Italian dish from famed cookbook author Marcella Hazan pairs seared lamb chops with a simple skillet sauce of canned San Marzano tomatoes, sweet red peppers, green olives, onion, and parsley. The chops finish in the sauce, picking up its savory, briny flavor. Get the recipe >.

Fresh chiles are cooked alongside onions, garlic, and spices, providing an aromatic base for the sauce of crushed tomatoes. Eggs provide a hit of protein and a richness to counteract the sauce’s heat and acidity, while a sprinkling of feta cheese and chopped parsley add a touch of saltiness and verdant freshness. Get the recipe >.

A year-round take on a classic Italian summer salad, this version uses canned tomatoes to soak into dry country bread, along with roasted fennel, fresh mozzarella, peppery arugula, and bitter radicchio. Get the recipe >.

Sources indicate that marcella Hazan’s classic tomato sauce proves that great Italian cooking doesn’t need to be complicated. Canned tomatoes simmer gently with butter and onion, creating a rich, silky sauce with remarkable depth and a subtle sweetness. The result is a simple sauce that lets the quality of its few ingredients shine. Get the recipe >.

In a recent development, the only thing that feels more like Thanksgiving than an exquisitely burnished roast turkey is the (sometimes chaotic) assemblage of loved ones seated around it. For your tablescape this year, take inspiration from the beautifully unique cast of characters that make a family a family.

She just stepped off a red eye from the major city, but she looks like she came from a gallery opening—and her place setting is as bold and eclectic as her fashion sense. Bulbous postmodern ceramic plates, '90s Art Deco revival flatware from Japan, and a hand-beaded placemat are exactly the things she’d be into. The button-shaped aluminum coaster is seldom occupied, since she prefers to keep the martini glass right where it belongs: in her hand.

Piano Cocktail Glass (Set of 2).

She’s 25 going on 70. In between baking all of the pies for the big dinner, she learned lace-making from a TikTok tutorial. She sews, she antiques, and she self-publishes Jane Austen fanfic online. The cheeky cotton bottle apron and pearl-tipped doily on her table might be brand new from Gohar World, but they pair exquisitely with the pewter flatware she scored at an estate sale. Quilted floral placemats and plates adorned with dainty, hand-painted bows from The Six Bells, a store leading the revival of country cottage decor, evoke the pastoral, bucolic lifestyle she yearns for (as long as she can keep her 10-step skin-care routine).

Herzerlmuster Scalloped Placemats (Set of 2).

Recent findings suggest that the combo of unbridled energy and still-developing motor skills means the Gen-Alpha kids are best served by a spread of disposable and shatterproof items. And, seeing that it’ll take some clever coaxing to pull these little gremlins away from their screens, their table must match the intense digital stimuli they’re accustomed to. Loop-de-loop silly straws, melamine plates, and acrylic forks and cups in as many colors as possible are the bare minimum to keep minds forged in a Cocomelon crucible engaged for the total duration of a Thanksgiving meal. Despite the visual chaos, their table might be more tranquil than the adults’.

Prue Leith Melamine Dinnerware Set and Tumblers.

Mammut Children's Chair and Table.

Thanksgiving might be the only time you see this elusive individual, as he otherwise spends the year fussing around his DIY Earthship in the desert outside of Santa Fe. His place setting is filled with natural materials, like these Shigaraki-style earthenware plates and zero-waste Belgian linen placemats. If he starts defending his dedication to composting toilets a little too enthusiastically, fill his hand-carved wooden mug with some herbal tea and he’ll settle down fine.

Jasper Linen Placements (Set of 4).

Recent findings suggest that A matriarch par excellence, she’s been holding the family together for decades. Her demeanor might be as breezy as a Massive Sur afternoon, but she means business when it comes to hosting Thanksgiving. Let it be known: She had a Nancy Meyers kitchen long before Nancy Meyers picked up a camera. To steal her vibe, invest in an Italian table cloth festooned with vines, hand-painted ceramic wicker plates, and bamboo-stemmed wine glasses. Place cards, arranged for maximum harmony, should bear each name in handwritten cursive. Miss Manners would be so proud.

Industry observers note that former Maine Gov. Paul LePage, fifth from right, joins incoming members Thursday for their freshman class photo on the House steps outside the Capitol. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call).

Paul LePage, the former Maine governor who once stated he was “Donald Trump before Donald Trump,” is heading to Congress.

The Associated Press called the race for the open 2nd District on Thursday after the Maine Secretary of State’s office tabulated the votes under the state’s ranked choice voting system. LePage ended up ahead of Democratic state Auditor Matt Dunlap 50.8 percent to 49.2 percent.

Dunlap had already conceded the race to LePage, who will succeed retiring Democratic Rep. Jared Golden in the sprawling district, which includes much of Maine outside the Portland and Augusta areas.

Recent findings suggest that “Paul LePage is already hard at work for the people of Maine attending Congressional orientation, meeting with national leaders, and making it clear the political parties need to work together for the American people,” Brent Littlefield, a senior adviser to LePage, stated in a statement Thursday. “As Paul said, he will work with anyone, regardless of Party, to put Maine first.”.

It has been revealed that lePage’s win is a glimmer of good news for Republicans, who saw massive losses across the country in last week’s midterm elections. He is one of three Republicans, along with Texas’ Jace Yarbrough and Tennessee’s Brent Taylor, to have flipped a House seat, although Maine’s 2nd District is the only one of the three that wasn’t redrawn to favor the GOP.

LePage’s win also means that at least one Republican will continue to represent Upcoming England in Congress, taking up the mantle from Maine Sen. Susan Collins, who lost her own reelection bid last week.

Golden, who was first elected in 2018, had been a top Republican target throughout his time in Congress. But the lawmaker, known for bucking his party, proved difficult to unseat in the past two election cycles.

“I also know a thing or two about winning in tough circumstances. So, I know you have to tip your hat to Paul LePage for winning in the midst of this Blue Tsunami,” Golden noted in a social media post last week.

It has been revealed that dunlap initially debuted his campaign as a primary challenge to Golden in the fall of 2025, only for the congressman to announce his retirement a month later. Dunlap went on to win a four-way contest for the Democratic nomination.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • This is the Betta Fish Nebula, a supernova remnant (SNR) around 6,800 light years away in the Centaurus constellation.
  • In a recent development, astronomers love studying SNRs because they can learn a lot about how heavy elements are spread out into the interstellar medium (ISM).
  • Industry observers note that this image is brought to us by a powerful telescope whose main job it is to study dark energy.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This is the Betta Fish Nebula, a supernova remnant (SNR) around 6,800 light years away in the Centaurus constellation. This display of illuminated gas came into being when a massive star exploded between 7,000 and 10,000 years ago. When it exploded, it expelled its outer layers. Those layers slammed into the interstellar medium, and are lit up by the energy from the shock, and that's what we see today.

In a recent development, astronomers love studying SNRs because they can learn a lot about how heavy elements are spread out into the interstellar medium (ISM). These explosions shape the dynamics in the ISM, including how stars form there. SNRs also reveal a lot about their progenitor stars. For these and other reasons, they're rich astronomical targets.

Industry observers note that this image is brought to us by a powerful telescope whose main job it is to study dark energy. But that telescope also has a side hustle: capturing stunning images for the rest of us that don't necessarily add anything to scientific understanding.

It has been revealed that one of the main efforts to understand dark energy, the puzzling force that drives the expansion of the Universe, is the Dark Energy Survey. It uses a special, purpose-built camera to do its work, called the Dark Energy Camera (DECam.) DECam is a powerful, 570 megapixel, wide-angle camera mounted on the VÃ­ctor M. Blanco 4-meter Telescope at Cerro Tololo Inter-American Observatory (CTIO) in Chile. It used its power to capture this image of the Betta Fish Nebula.

Like many telescopes, DECam sometimes takes a break from its main job and captures images purely for public interest. It's a way for the professional astronomy community to share some celestial wonder with the rest of us. The latest DECam images of the Betta Fish nebula are in that category.

In a recent development, only part of the nebula actually looks like a Betta, the popular and colourful aquarium fish. They're also known as Siamese Fighting Fish, but whatever name is used, they're popular for their brilliant colours and flowing fins.

In a recent development, this close-up view reveals one portion of the Betta Fish Nebula, the part that most closely resembles its namesake. Image Credit: CTIO/NOIRLab/DOE/NSF/AURA. Image Processing: T.A. Rector (University of Alaska Anchorage/NSF NOIRLab), D. de Martin & M. Zamani (NSF NOIRLab) Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International License.

It has been revealed that what's left of the exploded star is a collapsed, ultra-dense stellar core called a neutron star. It's tiny, only about 20 km across, and is invisible in this image. It's actually a pulsar with unusual properties that has been studied extensively. It's radio-quiet and can only be detected in x-rays, and also lacks a pulsar wind nebula. It's so unusual that some researchers think it may be an example of what's called a 'low-mass bare strange star.'.

This is a less visually interesting, more scientific x-ray image of the central portion of the Betta Fish nebula. It reveals what's left of the progenitor star that exploded, labelled in the center. Image Credit: Eppens et al. MNRAS 528, 2095â2111 (2024).

But those scientific details take a back seat to the image's visual interest.

These images have been 'dumbed-down' for internet use. There's a version of the image here that lets you zoom-in and explore it in much greater detail.

Recent findings suggest that this zoomed-in image highlights the part of the nebula that gave it its name. A cooperative orange/red star even serves as the Betta Fish's eye. Image Credit: CTIO/NOIRLab/DOE/NSF/AURA. Image Processing: T.A. Rector (University of Alaska Anchorage/NSF NOIRLab), D. de Martin & M. Zamani (NSF NOIRLab) Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International License.

According to recent reports, DECam has been observing for more than a decade, and over that time its created a nice catalogue of fantastic images. Here's a few of them.

Here are three DECam images the camera has captured over the years purely for public interest. From left to right: the cometary globule CG4, the Rosette Nebula, and the Corona Australis Molecular Cloud. Image Credits: NSF NOIRLab DECam Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International License.

The Rise of Astrosociology: What Can Analogue Astronaut Studies Teach us About the Future of Humanity in Space?

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1686 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Universetoday

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, it's no secret that some highly ambitious visions for the future of space exploration are taking shape today.
  • On top of all that, there are prepares to "commercialize Low Earth Orbit" (LEO), build infrastructure in cis-lunar space (Ã  la asteroid mining), and even proposals for sending commercial astronauts to "space tourists" to the Moon and Mars.
  • It has been revealed that this is where the emerging field of Astrosociology comes into play, an umbrella term that looks at spaceflight through the lens of the social sciences.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, it's no secret that some highly ambitious visions for the future of space exploration are taking shape today. Beyond NASA and China's prepares to send crewed missions to the Moon by the end of the decade and create permanent infrastructure there, both space agencies hope to put boots on the surface of Mars by the 2030s or 40s. Meanwhile, the European Space Agency (ESA) is active in the Artemis Program and plans to send the ExoMars Rosalind Franklin rover to the Red Planet in 2028. India aims to send the first "gaganauts" to space next year (as part of its Gaganyaan program).

On top of all that, there are prepares to "commercialize Low Earth Orbit" (LEO), build infrastructure in cis-lunar space (Ã  la asteroid mining), and even proposals for sending commercial astronauts to "space tourists" to the Moon and Mars. All of this begs the question of how humans intend to live in extraterrestrial environments and among the stars. What is needed to ensure that humans can not only survive the hazards of being off-world, but also flourish? As Mars City Design CEO Vera Mulyani would say, "How can we thrive, and not just survive?".

It has been revealed that this is where the emerging field of Astrosociology comes into play, an umbrella term that looks at spaceflight through the lens of the social sciences. In addition to questions related to engineering and astronaut health and safety, astrosociology takes a more holistic outlook and examines the social, cultural, and behavioral patterns of humans related to outer space. Consider Abraham Maslow's "Hierarchy of Needs," which begins with the basics (physiological and security needs) and extends upwards to include the immaterial, such as love, self-esteem, and self-actualization.

This challenge motivated Dr. Jim Pass to found the Astrosociology Research Institute (ARI) in 2008, a California-based nonprofit educational organization dedicated to developing astrosociology as a multidisciplinary academic field. As Pass describes on the organization's website, astrosociology is both a subdiscipline of sociology and a multidisciplinary field that includes (but is not limited to) "psychology, anthropology, economics, social psychology, political science, space history, space law, space policy, philosophy, as well as the arts.".

At its core, the ARI's mission comes down to a simple but highly relevant question: "How can social and behavioral scientists collaborate with physical and natural scientists to further the success of space exploration and settlement in the future?" In their latest newsletter, titled "Analog Space Missions: The Astrosociological Factors That Affect Analog Space Missions - Part 1," Pass and his colleagues share the perspectives of analog astronauts who participated in their call for papers and expert commentary by educators, space medics, and systems engineers.

As Mia Belle Parkinson, a postdoctoral student at the University of Edinburgh and ARI's editor-in-chief, wrote in the problem:.

When we talk about preparing for space exploration and settlement, we too often default to the technical: propulsion systems, life support, radiation shielding. These things matter enormously. But so do the quieter, harder-to-quantify questions â how do people build trust in isolated environments? How do cultural backgrounds shape group dynamics? What does it mean, psychologically and socially, to live on the edge of the unknown?

It has been revealed that while analog astronaut training may seem like a relatively new idea, it's actually part of a long-standing tradition almost as old as the "Space Race" itself. Before astronauts landed on the Moon, NASA conducted a series of training missions known as the "Apollo Geology Field Trips" between 1964 and 1972. The first field trip saw the first two astronaut groups travel to Flagstaff, Arizona, for a two-day mission to Meteor Crater and other locations that resembled volcanic features on the Moon.

Other locations included the Grand Canyon, the volcanic fields in Hawaii, the Nevada National Security Site, and mountain formations in the Sonoran Desert, Newly introduced Mexico, Oregon, Alaska, west Texas, and Sudbury, Ontario. Additionally, the Soviets conducted the BIOS-3 experiment within the closed ecosystem built at the Institute of Biophysics in Krasnoyarsk in 1965. This was followed by Tektite I and II in 1969 and 1971, which studied human behavior in a confined, isolated, pressurized habitat on the ocean floor near the U.S. Virgin Islands.

JAXA (Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency) astronaut Satoshi Furukawa pedals on the upgraded CEVIS system, keeping muscle and bone density levels during spaceflight. (Credit: NASA).

Since that time, research aboard space stations such as Mir, the International Space Station (ISS), and the Chinese Tiangong space station has provided invaluable knowledge about living in space and the effects of microgravity on humans' mental and physical well-being. However, these studies are not directly relevant to proposed missions that will send astronauts to the Moon, Mars, and other celestial bodies. As Parry writes:.

Industry observers note that while extremely valuable for zero-gravity spaceflights, living and working at the bottom of a gravity well presents altogether different conditions, including an inability to manufacture drugs or lift heavy objects. Planning for bases and settlements on the surfaces of the Moon, Mars, and eventually beyond can only be simulated on the surface of the Earth to humankind's best approximation even in 2026, because gravity matters!

Recent findings suggest that the first analog astronaut (hereafter AA) profiled was former NASA Advisor, science communicator, and space exploration expert Beth Mund. Mund is an especially experienced AA, having participated in the HI-SEAS (Hawai'i Space Exploration Analog and Simulation) program on the summit of Mauna Loa, Hawai'i, the LunAres Research Station, and the Jules Undersea Lodge. The first involved an all-female crew working together during the height of COVID in an uninsulated temporary habitat with minimal privacy and tough conditions.

The second took place in a converted World War II bunker in Poland located inside an old hangar. The hangar itself was filled with sand to simulate lunar regolith, and steel doors sealed the habitat and its six-person crew inside a rather confined space. At the Jules Undersea Lodge, located in Key Largo off the southern tip of Florida, Mund and her colleagues entered a submerged habitat with no escape hatches, accessible only through a "wet room" portal.

Looking back at these three missions, Mund noticed patterns that transcended any single environment. While each had its own geography and logistics, confinement was the common theme. From her experiences, Mund identified four universal human responses that were consistent throughout. The first, she wrote, was the importance of improvisation:.

Sources indicate that no matter how carefully equipment is designed or schedules are drawn, something always fails... each failure forces us to understand the problem and formulate a response to it in the context of very tight resource constraints. And in adapting, we discover more about ourselves than about the broken machines... These small acts of invention prove that ingenuity is not a luxury in confinement. It is a decisive factor in survival.

Photo of analog astronaut Beth Mund sitting outside the HI-SEAS habitat on the summit of Mauna Kea, Hawai'i. Credit: Beth Mund.

Sources indicate that the second lesson was the importance of ritual: "At HI-SEAS, our crew naturally gathered each evening for what I came to think of as our 'campfire,' a circle of debriefing, storytelling, and laughter, even in the cold dome with no flame. In Poland, games became our escape valve, a way to puncture the heaviness of the surveys and the claustrophobic walls. Underwater, simply gazing out the porthole together felt like a ceremony. In every analog, the crew instinctively created moments of reconnection that grounded us, even in places designed to isolate.".

In a recent development, the third lesson for Mund was continuity, as she and her colleagues inherited experiments started by crews they never met and which would be handled by future analog crews. "It gave weight to our confinement, transforming it from a private trial into a communal contribution," she remarked. "That continuity across crew "generations" is perhaps the most powerful sociological insight of analog missions. We are practicing not only how to live together, but how to build across time, leaving work - and maybe even some data/ insights - for crews who serve next.".

Sources indicate that lastly, there was the inevitability of testing. While every mission includes tests of equipment, plants, and methods for living in space, the experience also tests the limits of human endurance, creativity, and cohesion. This, she wrote, is the true essence of analog astronaut training:.

From Mars-like lava fields to a Polish bunker to the ocean floor, I have learned that analog missions are not about pretending to be astronauts. They are about practicing human endurance in places that strip away comfort and certainty. In that practice, in all the different shapes it takes across environments, facilities, missions, and crews, lies the real preparation for humanity to endure no matter the circumstances.

In a recent development, mund is merely one of many analog astronauts profiled in the Astrosociological Insights Forum's newsletter. To include as many testimonials and experiences as possible, the matter was released in two parts, incorporating perspectives not only from AAs but also from several experts in the burgeoning field of Astrosociology. More to follow, so stay tuned! In the meantime, check out some other articles we have about organizations committed to analog astronaut training:.

Further Reading: Astrosociological Insights Forum, vol. 10, issue 1.

Marcel Proust and madeleines are so intrinsically linked that in France, a madeleine de Proust has become a common expression used to describe a smell, sound, or taste that brings back old memories. Madeleines are small sponge cakes baked in molds shaped like seashells with the signature bump, la bosse, proudly protruding from the top. Freezing the pan and placing it on a hot sheet pan will make the bump pop even more!

Sources indicate that as much as I love a plain madeleine, I adore a citrus-scented one. My first madeleine, my Proustian moment, was not at a lovely Parisian pâtisserie. No, my family and I were visiting some of my mother’s friends in Paris and not knowing what they were, I grabbed a bag of lemon madeleines in a local supermarket, simply because I thought the seashell-shaped cakes were the prettiest thing I had ever seen. I could have inhaled them all in an afternoon if I had been allowed.

According to recent reports, seasonal citrus zests—lemons, of course, yuzus, blood oranges, mandarins, or a medley of several—find their way into my madeleines, but the tart-sweet, fruity, floral flavor of Cara Cara oranges is my favorite. Dusting the still-warm madeleines with floral and citrusy coriander-scented powdered sugar just before serving sends them over the top.

More bright citrus recipes this way.

40 minutes (plus 8 hours for chilling).

In a recent development, put ½ cup / 115 g unsalted butter in a small saucepan over medium heat and melt, stirring and scraping the bottom with a rubber spatula, until the foaming subsides and the butter smells like toasted hazelnuts and the milk solids are golden brown, 5–7 minutes. Scrape the melted butter and milk solids into a small heatproof bowl and refrigerate until the butter is solid and creamy.

Sift together 1 cup / 125 g all-purpose flour, ½ tsp. baking powder, and ¼ tsp. salt in a small bowl and set aside.

Add ½ cup / 100 g light brown sugar to a small bowl and rub the sugar with zest of 1 Cara Cara orange. Combine the sugar, 1 Tbsp. honey, and 2 eggs in the bowl of a stand mixer, fitted with the whisk attachment. Whisk for 2 minutes on medium-low speed, then increase the speed to medium-high and whisk for another 5–6 minutes, until very pale and airy.

Add the cooled butter to the egg mixture while whisking on low speed, then fold in the flour mixture until just combined.

Transfer the batter to an airtight container and refrigerate for at least 6 hours but preferably overnight.

Grease a madeleine pan with unsalted butter, then dust with all-purpose flour and knock out any excess. Place the pan in the freezer for at least an hour.

It has been revealed that use a 1-Tbsp. measure or transfer the cold batter to a piping bag and fill the center of each cup with 20 g of batter (three-quarters full, or a little more than 1 Tbsp.). Refrigerate the madeleine pan for 1 hour.

Place a sheet pan in the oven and preheat the oven to 350°F / 180°C.

Place the madeleine pan directly on the hot sheet pan and bake for 10–13 minutes, until the madeleines are golden brown and their signature bump springs back when pressed lightly.

Tap the tray to release the cakes and immediately turn out onto a wire rack to cool, turning them bump-side up.

Whisk together ¼ cup / 30 g powdered sugar and ¾ tsp. ground coriander in a small bowl and dust over the warm madeleines.
