Breaking: America’s Data Centers Have a Hidden Death Toll, MIT Researchers Warn

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1010 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scitechdaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • An MIT analysis estimates that powering America’s data centers contributed to hundreds of premature deaths in a single year, with rural populations facing greater risks than city dwellers.
  • Industry observers note that as artificial intelligence drives the rapid construction of data centers across the United States, concerns about their environmental impact are taking on a latest dimension.
  • Researchers at MIT estimate that air pollution associated with data center electricity consumption contributed to approximately 650 premature deaths in the United States in 2023 alone.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

An MIT analysis estimates that powering America’s data centers contributed to hundreds of premature deaths in a single year, with rural populations facing greater risks than city dwellers.

Industry observers note that as artificial intelligence drives the rapid construction of data centers across the United States, concerns about their environmental impact are taking on a latest dimension. The electricity needed to keep these facilities running around the clock can increase air pollution in communities far from where the data centers themselves are built, potentially putting the health of people who live nowhere near them at risk.

Researchers at MIT estimate that air pollution associated with data center electricity consumption contributed to approximately 650 premature deaths in the United States in 2023 alone. Iowa, Nevada, South Dakota, and Kansas had the highest estimated rates of premature deaths per capita, even though much of the electricity demand was concentrated in northern Virginia and Texas. Rates in Virginia and Texas were only about half those in most Midwestern states.

“When people think about the negative impacts of data centers, they usually focus on the neighbors. But our study indicates that the air quality impacts of data centers are very widespread across a large region. Even if you don’t think you are affected because there is not a data center near you, think again,” says Noelle Selin, senior author of the study, a professor in the MIT Institute for Data, Systems, and Society (IDSS) and the Department of Earth, Atmospheric and Planetary Sciences (EAPS), and director of the Center for Sustainability Science and Strategy.

Recent findings suggest that lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory estimated that data centers’ electricity needs accounted for about 4 percent of total U.S. energy demand in 2023 and approximately 4.4 percent of the nation’s overall emissions. Those proportions have likely grown as more facilities have been built.

Sources indicate that determining who bears the health consequences of that growing demand is complicated by the interconnected nature of the nation’s power grid. A data center in Virginia, for example, may increase electricity production at power plants in the Ohio Valley, where a greater proportion of older coal and natural gas plants produce higher levels of emissions.

“Different regions have different mixes of power. If you turn on a major new demand source, by plugging a data center into the grid, you might have to fire up your really dirty power plant to meet that new demand,” Selin indicates.

The pollution can then travel into neighboring states, where local atmospheric conditions can make matters worse. In agricultural regions such as Iowa and Nebraska, ammonia released from fertilizer promotes the formation of fine particulate matter (PM2.5), microscopic airborne particles that can cause heart attacks, strokes, and lung disease.

Recent findings suggest that the estimated health consequences also extend to Kansas, South Dakota, Missouri, and Arkansas. Overall, the researchers found that rural populations face a significantly higher estimated mortality risk from data center electricity demand than urban populations.

Industry observers note that to understand how these risks are distributed, the team developed a model that tracks electricity production and transmission between regions on an hourly basis. While many previous studies relied on average power grid emissions, the researchers assumed that data centers operated around the clock and identified which individual generators would respond to their additional electricity needs.

“Generators that respond to additional electricity demand are often natural gas plants, although the response varies by place and hour,” says Yuang (Albert) Chen, an MIT graduate student and co-author of the study.

It has been revealed that “It was a challenge to gather all the data,” Chen says. “There are more than 10,000 generators in the U.S. grid, and we needed to make sure the data provided for each generator is valid and validated across other data sources.”.

Recent findings suggest that the researchers calculated emissions of nitrogen oxides and sulfur dioxide from individual generators. Both pollutants contribute to the formation of fine particulate matter, while nitrogen oxides also help produce ground-level ozone, commonly associated with smog.

Industry observers note that using a separate atmospheric model, the team simulated how these pollutants formed and traveled across regions. They then drew on epidemiological research linking air pollution to premature death to estimate the resulting health impacts.

Of the approximately 650 premature deaths estimated for 2023, 513 were attributed to fine particulate matter and 137 to smog. Together, they represented about 5.3 percent of all estimated electricity-related premature deaths nationwide.

“While it is not surprising that any additional source of air pollution will result in mortalities, with data centers, when and where these deaths are occurring are different than you might expect,” Selin states.

As companies continue to expand their computing infrastructure, the findings suggest that decisions about where to build data centers and how to power them need to account for public health well beyond the immediate surroundings.

“When people are thinking about data center siting and operations, it is important to consider more than just things like land and energy prices. They should also take air quality considerations into the equation,” Chen says. “This is a good baseline to think about where we should build data centers and how we should supply those data centers with electricity.”.

The researchers hope to investigate the air quality consequences of a growing industry trend in which data centers incorporate their own on-site power plants. They could also examine whether adjusting when these facilities consume electricity could reduce their impact on air quality.

Industry observers note that reference: “Spatially distributed air quality and health impacts of data center electricity demand in the United States” by Yuang Chen, Shen Wang, Juan Ramon L Senga, Andrew Scott White, Anthony YH Wong, Lyssa M Freese, Michelle L Bell and Noelle E Selin, 19 November 2026, Environmental Research Letters. DOI: 10.1088/1748-9326/aebbd4.

This research was funded, in part, by the MIT Energy Initiative Society of Energy Scholars and the MIT Martin Family Society of Fellows for Sustainability.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, quasars are the cosmos' most luminous objects, generated by supermassive black holes (SMBH) that are accreting enormous amounts of matter. Astronomers keep finding these massive objects further and further back in time. The ESA's Euclid just found the newest record holder: the telescope observed it 40 million years sooner than the previous record-holder, and it was found at redshift z=8.13, corresponding to about 630 million years after the Big Bang. That's firmly in the Epoch of Reionization.

It has been revealed that the quasar's technical name is J1504+6252, but it's been given the more recognizable name DÃºn Aonghasa. DÃºn Aonghasa is an ancient stone fort on top of a cliff in Ireland, where it looks out over the Atlantic Ocean.

The discovery is in research published in Astronomy and Astrophysics titled "Euclid: Discovery of a quasar at z = 8.13 hosting a 360-million-solar-mass black hole." The lead author is Julien Wolf, who was a postdoc at the Max Planck Institute for Astronomy when the research was done.

According to recent reports, one of the hallmarks of modern astronomy is the discovery of massive objects in the Universe that formed much sooner than astronomers thought they could. The JWST is driving much of this.

"Quasars powered by rapid accretion onto supermassive black holes (SMBHs) have been uncovered deep into the first gigayear of cosmic history," the authors write.

Now the Euclid Space Telescope is contributing to that trend. Euclid was launched to study dark energy and the expansion of the Universe. A big part of that job is measuring galaxies at different redshifts in its Euclid Wide Survey, to see how their morphologies are different over time. That will reveal how dark energy has changed over time.

This is what DÃºn Aonghasa, the fresh quasar, looks like in the actual Euclid image. It's the red dot in the center. Image Credit: ESA/Euclid/Euclid Consortium/J. Wolf et al.

Euclid found DÃºn Aonghasa in its Euclid Wide Survey imaging, but didn't confirm it. Follow-up observations by Keck, the Hubble, the Large Binocular Telescope, and especially the JWST provided the confirmation. JWST spectroscopy let the researchers measure "a systemic redshift of zsysâ=â8.129âÂ±â0.005, corresponding to only 630âMyr after the Big Bang and shifting the quasar redshift frontier by â39âMyr," the authors write. 39 million years is about 6% of the age of the Universe at that epoch. The quasar is now the first quasar observed at z > 8.

DÃºn Aonghasa's luminosity is what lets astronomers observe it at such a great distance. Its luminosity helped researchers measure its mass and its accretion rate, and DÃºn Aonghasa contains 360 million solar masses.

According to recent reports, this figure shows absolute UV magnitude as a function of redshift for high-redshift quasars, galaxies, LRDs, LBDs, and other JWST-selected AGN up to zâ=â11. Orange squares show recently identified Euclid quasars, and the green star shows DÃºn Aonghasa, which is more UV-luminous than the LRDs, other JWST-selected AGN, and Lyman-break galaxies at comparable redshifts. JWST-selected AGN are shown as circles and colour-coded according to their phenomenological classification: LRDs in red, LBDs in blue, and other AGN in black. Previously known quasars are shown as grey circles. Open purple diamonds are Lyman-break galaxies. Image Credit: J. Wolf et al. A&A Volume 715, November 2026 A356.

DÃºn Aonghasa and its high redshift brethren pose the same familiar question: how did they get so large so rapidly?

"Assembling a black hole of several hundred million solar masses within the first few hundred million years, despite its right now sub-Eddington accretion rate, requires either a massive seed or sustained, highly efficient early growth," the authors write.

While an actual answer to their growth is elusive, finding them helps constrain an eventual answer.

âFinding quasars at ever-increasing distances, at the edge of the observable universe, teaches us something about how the black holes in their centres grew,â said lead author Wolf in a press release. âThe closer to the Big Bang we find them, the faster their black holes must have grown or the more massive they must have been at birth â or both.â.

Recent findings suggest that aside from their puzzling masses, these quasars also open different windows or probes into aspects of the early Universe. They give astronomers long sightlines into the intergalactic medium, letting them study its opacity during reionization, and its metal enrichment.

It has been revealed that the quasars also serve as probes of how matter was distributed. "Quasars further mark rare, highly biased peaks in the underlying matter distribution and therefore trace the densest regions of the early large-scale structure," the researchers write.

On galactic scales, these high-redshift quasars are probes of how SMBH masses and the masses of their host galaxies co-evolved. Both masses tend to correlate, but there's no obvious reason why. AGN feedback could play a role, so could mergers, or a shared source of fuel for growth. But there's no certainty, so finding more high-redshift quasars may lead to an answer.

These things are all related, but the main result of finding these quasars is facing the questions posed by their high masses.

In a recent development, finding these quasars and supermassive black holes is forcing astronomers to consider different explanations for how they grew so massive so promptly. One explanation is super-Eddington accretion, but DÃºn Aonghasa isn't accreting matter that rapidly. Another is massive seeds, but current formation models struggle to accommodate those. Another explanation is that quasars experienced super-Eddington accretion very early in the Universe, under very different conditions.

According to recent reports, heavy seeds could explain these quasars, but what could they be? Astrophysicists don't know, but some candidates are Direct-Collapse Black Holes, or maybe sequential runaway stellar collisions in extremely dense star clusters.

According to recent reports, another, more exotic and theoretical possibility for heavy seeds is primordial black holes (PBH). These are theorized to have formed in the very first moments in the Universe, when dense pockets of gas collapsed directly into black holes. With such an early head start, these PBH could've formed into heavy seeds without needing physics-breaking levels of accretion.

Primordial black holes are only hypothetical. If they're real, they could've formed by direct collapse of dense pockets of matter shortly after the Big Bang. They could've acted as seeds for the very early, very massive SMBH found in the Epoch of Reionization. Image Credit: ESA/Hubble, N. Bartmann., CC BY-SA.

It has been revealed that luminous quasars like DÃºn Aonghasa are rare in the Epoch of Reionization. So far, there are only seven of them. The only path to an explanation for their masses is through more observations that find more of these ancient quasars, and hopefully ones even more distant.

âAnd this may happen sooner than we think,â said co-author Silvia Belladitta a scientist at the Max Planck Institute for Astronomy. âThis highlights how promptly Euclid is expanding our census of the most distant quasars. Each new discovery brings us closer to understanding how supermassive black holes formed and grew in the early universe.â.

"DÃºn Aonghasa establishes a latest quasar redshift frontier as the first confirmed quasar at zâ>â8, providing a powerful new benchmark for early SMBH growth," the researchers write in their paper's conclusion. Its large mass indicates that it must have grown a lot before it was observed, but its bolometric luminosity contradicts that. So the mystery of massive early SMBH and their quasars is still a puzzle.

Researchers predicted that Euclid will find between 8â23 quasars at zâ>â8, so hopefully, more are on their way.

âIt is unclear how far back in time these supermassive black holes powering luminous quasars exist, but Euclid has a good chance of finding out what that limit is,â said MPIA scientist and co-author Eduardo BaÃ±ados.

Recent findings suggest that it might seem like researchers are chasing a receding horizon, almost like a dog chasing its tail. They build better telescopes in hopes of finding answers to difficult questions. Then their telescopes uncover some answers, but also uncover more questions. It's probably true that there's no end to knowledge and we'll never know everything. But that also means there's no end to learning, no end to Nature, and no end to wonder.

Earth’s Lakes Are Changing in Unison – and Scientists Are Worried

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (648 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scitechdaily

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Lakes play an notable role in regulating Earth’s carbon cycle, and scientists warn that environmental changes occurring across many lakes at once could amplify global climate risks.
  • Lakes around the world are increasingly changing in step, a trend that could weaken a natural buffer against environmental disruption.
  • In a recent development, the characteristics of a lake’s watershed, the land that drains into it, have historically helped buffer its ecosystem against broader environmental changes.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Lakes play an notable role in regulating Earth’s carbon cycle, and scientists warn that environmental changes occurring across many lakes at once could amplify global climate risks.

Lakes around the world are increasingly changing in step, a trend that could weaken a natural buffer against environmental disruption. A newly introduced study found that this synchronization has accelerated markedly since 2000.

In a recent development, the characteristics of a lake’s watershed, the land that drains into it, have historically helped buffer its ecosystem against broader environmental changes. Lakes fluctuated independently, a pattern known as “spatial asynchrony” that spread ecological disturbances across time and space.

Sources indicate that A team led by Prof. Ke Zhang of the Nanjing Institute of Geography and Limnology of the Chinese Academy of Sciences (NIGLAS) combined century-scale sediment records with continuous satellite observations from approximately 2,000 lakes. Alongside growing synchrony, the researchers found a significant decline in network modularity, meaning the lake network was becoming less divided into groups with distinct patterns of change.

The researchers used water clarity and phytoplankton biomass, the mass of microscopic organisms that use sunlight to make food, as proxies for lake metabolic activity. These indicators provide an indirect view of how lake ecosystems process energy and nutrients. Their growing synchrony suggests that the underlying carbon, nutrient, and biodiversity dynamics they reflect may also be becoming more synchronized.

Sources indicate that the study attributes this shift to environmental telecoupling, connections through which climate extremes such as heatwaves and socioeconomic pressures link changes across distant regions. The authors describe this increasingly linked response to large-scale environmental change as a new hallmark of the Anthropocene, a term used to describe a world profoundly shaped by human activity.

Although lakes cover less than 2% of Earth’s surface, they help regulate global carbon and nutrient cycles and biodiversity. Losing the differences in how they respond to environmental pressures could therefore have consequences well beyond individual watersheds.

In a recent development, “This loss of buffering capacity transforms lakes from passive, regionally distinct systems into active amplifiers of global environmental risks. Synchronized lakes can concentrate biophysical fluxes, potentially triggering high-amplitude global pulses, such as simultaneous greenhouse gas emissions or widespread aquatic hypoxia, thereby exacerbating the triple planetary crisis,” Zhang said.

Recent findings suggest that aquatic hypoxia means a shortage of oxygen in the water. The “triple planetary crisis” refers to climate change, biodiversity loss, and pollution.

Recent findings suggest that water management has traditionally treated lakes as isolated local resources, creating what the researchers describe as a “scale mismatch” between governance and the processes shaping these ecosystems. Zhang and his co-authors propose treating interconnected lake networks as a dynamically coupled “Planetary Commons.” Their objective is to protect the local ecological processes that maintain variation across landscapes, without seeking to eliminate synchrony.

In a recent development, to put that idea into practice, the team introduced a framework called Strategic Planetary Lake Areas (SPLAs). By tracking large-scale measures of synchrony and modularity, policymakers could identify priority regions, including regional groups of lakes whose behavior is rapidly converging. These areas could become candidates for targeted polycentric governance, an approach involving multiple centers of decision-making.

“This research not only redefines the critical importance of inland waters in global change studies but also introduces a macroscale dimension to international sustainable development agendas,” Zhang noted. “The work emphasizes that preserving the diversity of ecological responses is essential for maintaining long-term Earth-system stability in an increasingly interconnected world.”.

Recent findings suggest that reference: “Global lake synchrony signals rising planetary-scale ecological coupling” by Ke Zhang, Yaoyao Han, Lindsey Gillson, Xiaoling Zhang, Suzanne McGowan, Michael E. Meadows, Yuan Jin, Luki Subehi, John A. Dearing, David P. Hamilton, Yan Zhao, Lian Pin Koh and David Taylor, 16 November 2026, Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences. DOI: 10.1073/pnas.2611874123.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that well, it's time to talk about everyone's favourite topic these days: artificial intelligence. Specifically, what's our overall policy about it here at Universe Today?

We won't be using AI to generate content on the site. We won't write stories with AI, or make pictures, we won't make background music, and we won't generate video clips using AI.

I blueprint to pay humans to create Universe Today content until the robots make this career untenable.

Sources indicate that is that something you'd like to support? Join our https://patreon.com/universetoday and join the others who are keeping Universe Today independent and ad-free.

Join our Patreon. Support our work. Credit: Anton Podznyakov.

It has been revealed that first, a preamble. My background is in computer science, and the tech nerd in me has been watching with fascination and excitement at the growing capabilities of the technology. I've built an incredible set of personal tools that help me manage the Universe Today website, organize our podcast catalog, transcribe interviews, and so much more. I'm starting to run out of ideas for things to build, which has never happened to me before.

As a person who shares a planet with other humans, I'm concerned about a growing divide between those with access to technology and those without. I'm saddened by the training of LLMs on the work of artists without any compensation to mass produce competing work. I'm working overtime to patch up and harden computers that are getting shredded by automated hacking tools. I'm deeply concerned about our inability to control all this, and a seeming unwillingness to even bother by the people making this technology.

Industry observers note that if you're building a machine that can destroy humanity... DON'T BUILD THE MACHINE. Seriously.

As a person who likes to watch stuff, play games, and read interesting stories, the Internet is starting to feel like a minefield. I'll start to watch a YouTube video and hear the telltale "it's not X it's Y," and realize that I'm just listening to an AI script. Creators I've been following for a decade have suddenly replaced their real, authentic presence with a script from Claude.

Recent findings suggest that it's heartbreaking, but it's understandable. The pressure growing to produce more content, faster, faster. And when everyone else is using AI, you'd have to be an idiot not to do the same.

In a recent development, I recently did a poll on my YouTube channel asking my audience how they feel about AI-generated videos. What would they do if they knew an excellent video was generated by AI? About 75% of you would stop watching, and about 25% would keep going. Humanity's collective response seems to be ambivalence.

The result of our user poll. We asked you if you'd stop watching a video if you knew it was written by AI. Credit: Universe Today/YouTube.

Sources indicate that the main problem right now (apart from the society-wrenching chaos of summoning the machine god), is that we don't know when something was written by AI and when it was done by a human. I know your AI detection skills are top notch and you'd never be fooled by an AI script, but I promise you... you have. And it's just going to get worse.

I don't hate AI, sometimes, I love it. I especially miss the Will Smith Eats Spaghetti era when AI videos were like a cyberpunk fever dream. But I hate being lied to. I hate being deceived by someone who is presenting a video, or writing an essay, or sharing a heartfelt post on Reddit, implying that this is their actual opinion. But it's not, they outsourced it to an AI. I could just skip the middleman and ask the AI directly. "Dear Claude, please write me an essay about who would win in a fight, Batman or Wolverine. Now turn it into a video.".

Here's a video I recently did about how I feel about watching videos and discovering they're made with AI.

The answer is disclosure. Just say what you did, so I don't have to check your work with Pangram and discover that 100% of your video script was written by AI.

And if you do disclose, then I and the other potential consumers of your content can decide for ourselves if we want to watch it, or read it, or listen to it. 25% will stick around, apparently.

You're probably wondering at this point why the publisher of Universe Today is giving you his personal take on AI content. Why not just explain my policies, put it in the footer or something?

Because I'm human, I'm grieving, but I'm in a position to do something about it.

It has been revealed that universe Today is a space news website, written by humans, for humans. This means that humans chose our topics and story ideas, and humans did the reporting and writing to bring you the articles on the website. We don't use generative AI to produce articles, images, music or video clips on the website, in our podcasts or videos.

One caveat on images/videos. These are often provided by the original researchers or press office (et tu NASA?), and are sometimes made with a blend of AI and human artwork. We don't always spot it, but we replace the visuals when we do, or clearly identify them. If you think we got it wrong, [let us know].

Our words were written by humans, but quotes from researchers, or captions supplied by news sources might be written by AI. That's on them, we're not their Dad.

According to recent reports, we may use AI coding assistance for internal development projects. We may also use AI tools for literature search, translation, transcription, grammar and spelling. We'll use AI to assist in researching a topic to better understand it, but it's only there to help a human make something better.

If we get something wrong, we'll fix it in the article and let you know what changed.

And we'll keep doing this until we go out of business, due to a lack of patrons, complete irrelevance, or the end of the world.

Join our https://patreon.com/universetoday to help make this a viable strategy for us.

The day we decided to remove all the advertising from Universe Today and be supported 100% by our patrons.

Recent findings suggest that one of the most prominent features on the Moon is one we canât regularly see, at least not completely. The South Pole-Aitken (SPA) basin is one of the largest, oldest, and deepest impact craters on the Moon, and until recently weâve only been able to observe it from afar - and even then only when we sent orbiters around to the far side, which is never in direct line of sight with the Earth. Recently China has been busily sending landers and rovers to the site, and a new paper, published in Science Advances, details the actual samples returned to Earth by the Changâe-6 mission and combines them with the in-situ data from the Changâe-4 mission and rover. Those details combine to form a complete geological history of the major impacts that formed the basin, and some insight into the age of other impact craters scattered throughout the solar system.

In a recent development, A sense of scale and time helps in understanding the SPA. Itâs roughly 2,200 kilometers across, making it similar in length to the north-south axis of mainland China. And it runs up to 10 kilometers deep, much deeper than any comparable land-based feature on Earth. For a long time, astronomers and planetary scientists have been debating how old it is, with dates ranging from 4.35 billion years ago to around 4.2 billion. That discrepancy is part of what the new paper hopes to solve, but thereâs another larger discrepancy it hopes to solve as well.

Sources indicate that the two halves of the Moon - the one that faces us and the one facing away - appear very different in terms of their features. The nearside is covered in smooth, dark plains called âmariaâ, whereas the far side has many more craters, with almost no volcanic plains and a thick layer of crust sitting on top. This difference, known as the âlunar dichotomy,â has stumped scientists for years. To solve it, many have turned to the SPA.

Fraser talks about collecting the Chang'e-6 moon rocks.

Recent findings suggest that SPA was formed during a gigantic ancient collision that broke through the crust on the far side and exposed underground rock that had been buried since the Moonâs formation. But the main crater isnât the only one in the area. Various smaller craters have formed overlapping the main one, including the Von KÃ¡rmÃ¡n crater (where Changâe-4 landed with its Yutu-2 rover) and the 490-kilometer-wide Apollo basin, where Changâe-6 landed and that was created by a separate impact.

Crucially, those impacts created different types of magnesium-rich igneous rocks. One type, found by Changâe-4 in the Von KÃ¡rmÃ¡n crater, is known as moderately magnesium-rich norite. It crystallized directly from the vast sea of molten rock generated when the SPA-forming asteroid slammed into the Moon. Over millions of years, the lava lake this created cooled, and the minerals separated out into layers. Later impacts then pushed the solid rocks up to the peaks of newly formed craters, and eventually another impact known as the Finsen impact blasted pieces of that cooled lava lake into Von KÃ¡rmÃ¡n crater for Changâe-4 to find.

Another type of rock held even higher levels of magnesium. It was created via a process called magnesium-suite magmatism. When the SPA impact broke the Moonâs crust, the magma from its then liquid interior broke into the crust, cooling underneath its top layer. Later, the impact that created the Apollo basin pushed those now cooled materials up into its western peak ring, and then another impact that created whatâs now known as the Chaffee S crater blasted pieces of rock directly into the path of plains where Changâe-6 collected them billions of years later.

Fraser talks about the Chang'e-6 mission collecting lunar samples.

Combining the data from Changâe-4âs rover with data from around a gram of the 2kg returned by the Changâe-6 mission, while adding a sprinkle of computer simulations, the research team reconstructed a timeline of the early bombardment history of the Moon. The main feature was when SPA was created around 4.34 billion years ago, only a few hundred million years after the solar system itself formed.

It has been revealed that the Apollo basin seemed to have been formed around 4.2 billion years ago, definitively answering why previous estimates of the SPA itself ranged from 4.35 billion years to 4.2 billion or so. Even later, around 3.87 billion years ago, another massive collision created what is now known as the Orientale basin, and after it came smaller impacts like Finsen and Chaffee S, which showered the entire region with debris that mixed the crust rocks in with the soil that formed on the Moon over hundreds of millions of years.

While itâs great to know the Moonâs impact history, this research also has implications for other craters on other worlds. By counting them and using radiometry to estimate their ages, researchers can estimate when there were major swarms of asteroids impacting the inner solar system. But weâre not done with the lunar landscape yet. The SPA is a prime target for future crewed missions, and as more rovers, landers, and, potentially, people start to traverse the wilds of the lunar surface, theyâll occasionally come across fragments of the ancient crust created by massive impacts beyond anything our species has ever witnessed in the solar system. Itâs kind of cool to think that those fragments have been waiting billions of years for us to find and study them.

Losing Weight but Getting Less Healthy? Study Reveals a Dark Side of Keto

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (744 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scitechdaily

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Mice that lost weight on a very low-protein keto diet also developed fatty liver and lost muscle, highlighting the limitations of weight as a measure of health.
  • Recent findings suggest that ketogenic diets have become a popular approach to weight loss, despite conflicting research on their metabolic benefits.
  • Sources indicate that the research, published in Cell Metabolism, began when first author Zhaoyue Zhang, a postdoctoral fellow in the Friedman lab, noticed considerable variation in the protein content of ketogenic diets.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Mice that lost weight on a very low-protein keto diet also developed fatty liver and lost muscle, highlighting the limitations of weight as a measure of health.

Recent findings suggest that ketogenic diets have become a popular approach to weight loss, despite conflicting research on their metabolic benefits. A new study in mice suggests that two often overlooked factors may help explain these inconsistencies: the amount of protein in the diet and the genetic makeup of the animals eating it. The findings also raise questions about whether losing weight on a keto diet necessarily means becoming healthier.

Sources indicate that the research, published in Cell Metabolism, began when first author Zhaoyue Zhang, a postdoctoral fellow in the Friedman lab, noticed considerable variation in the protein content of ketogenic diets. Although these diets are generally high in fat and extremely low in carbohydrates, their protein content could be contributing to differences in metabolic outcomes.

Recent findings suggest that zhang and her colleagues systematically tested diets containing different proportions of fat and protein. After four weeks on a ketogenic diet containing just 5% protein, mice belonging to C57Bl/6J, the most commonly used laboratory mouse strain, reduced their food intake by approximately 40% and lost weight. Mice fed an otherwise similar diet containing 10% protein ate more and gained weight. Both groups produced ketones, molecules generated when the body relies heavily on fat for fuel, suggesting that ketosis alone could not account for the difference.

“The result was so striking,” Zhang notes.

A closer look at the mice that lost weight revealed a more complicated picture. Although their glucose tolerance, or ability to manage changes in blood sugar, improved, they also developed fatty liver. Much of their weight loss was associated with reductions in lean mass, including muscle.

To understand what was suppressing the animals’ appetite, the researchers investigated GDF15, a hormone released in response to cellular stress that can act on the brain to reduce food intake. When they conducted an experiment using genetically modified mice lacking GDF15, even the control mice unexpectedly failed to lose weight on the low-protein diet.

According to recent reports, “At first, I was a bit panicked,” Zhang states. “We had repeated the same experiment many times, and all of a sudden it didn’t work.”.

Retracing her steps, Zhang discovered that the genetically modified mice belonged to a different substrain, C57Bl/6N, which shares approximately 99.9% of its genome with the mice used in the earlier experiments.

“This realization was key, and it became the starting point for the rest of the study,” Zhang says.

Industry observers note that the researchers eventually identified two genes that helped explain the difference: NNT, which protects cells against oxidative stress, and NLRP12, which helps regulate inflammation. The mice susceptible to weight loss, known as B6J, carried mutations in both genes. Feeding them the low-protein ketogenic diet triggered stress and inflammatory responses in the liver, accompanied by rising levels of GDF15 and an inflammation-associated protein called LCN2. Both proteins can influence appetite through their effects on the brain.

Restoring NNT function in B6J mice caused them to eat more and lose less weight. Conversely, disabling both genes in the genetically similar B6NJ mice, which normally carry functioning versions of both genes, caused them to eat less and lose weight. Treatment with N-acetylcysteine, an antioxidant with anti-inflammatory properties, also lowered circulating levels of GDF15 and LCN2, increased food intake, and reduced weight loss.

Sources indicate that zhang cautions that the findings cannot be directly applied to humans, particularly because the 5% protein diet contained substantially less protein than most ketogenic diets used in clinical trials. Future trials could benefit from paying closer attention to both dietary protein content and genetic differences among participants, while looking beyond weight loss and blood sugar control when assessing metabolic health.

The researchers now want to investigate whether other genetic factors influence responses to ketogenic diets and whether the changes they observed can be reversed once the diet is discontinued.

Reference: “Macronutrient composition and genetic background determine the response to a ketogenic diet in mice” by Zhaoyue Zhang, Alexandre Moura-Assis, Shanshan Liu, Alon Millet, Jordan Shaked, Divya Rajan, Katelin Chen, Anduena Toci, Chloe Schaefer, Ijeoma Obi, Sebastian Carrasco, Sandra Kelly Atkinson, Francois Marchildon, Hanan Alwaseem, Michael Isay-Del Viscio, Henrik Molina, Paul Cohen, Kivanc Birsoy and Jeffrey Friedman, 18 November 2026, Cell Metabolism. DOI: 10.1016/j.cmet.2026.10.017.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • With stopgap funding set to expire in less than a month, Senate Republican appropriators Thursday unveiled a roughly $5.3 billion draft fiscal 2027 Legislative Branch spending bill that would boost security funding and sidestep contentious debates over a key watchdog.
  • The proposal would provide $965 million for Capitol Police, a nearly $83 million hike from fiscal 2026, but still short of the more than $1 billion the department requested as threats against lawmakers rise.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A group of visitors walks past the Capitol on Sept. 22. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call file photo).

With stopgap funding set to expire in less than a month, Senate Republican appropriators Thursday unveiled a roughly $5.3 billion draft fiscal 2027 Legislative Branch spending bill that would boost security funding and sidestep contentious debates over a key watchdog.

The proposal would provide $965 million for Capitol Police, a nearly $83 million hike from fiscal 2026, but still short of the more than $1 billion the department requested as threats against lawmakers rise.

And it would bump funding for the Government Accountability Office up to $860 million, an increase of nearly 6 percent from fiscal 2026. That stands in contrast to the version of the bill advanced by the House Appropriations Committee in May, which floated slashing the GAO by 25 percent.

According to recent reports, it joins several other draft spending bills released this week by Senate Appropriations Chair Susan Collins, R-Maine, who is trying to kickstart bicameral negotiations as lawmakers stare down a Dec. 11 deadline to fund the government.

In a recent development, her committee ran into a stalemate on topline numbers earlier this year that stopped it from marking up any of the 12 annual bills, but lawmakers nipped the threat of a government shutdown in the bud ahead of the midterm elections by pushing through a continuing resolution. With that funding now set to expire next month, appropriators are hoping they can wrap up at least some of the bills while punting the rest into the next Congress with another stopgap.

It has been revealed that the Legislative Branch bill is the smallest of the 12 appropriations bills and typically among the least controversial. But debates over the GAO have become a sticking point during the Trump administration as the agency accuses the White House of violating budget laws — a move the Office of Management and Budget has pushed back on, arguing the GAO has no authority over the administration since it is part of the legislative branch.

The GAO has been without a permanent head after its longtime leader Gene L. Dodaro retired last year, although Republicans are now making a last-ditch effort to get one confirmed during the lame-duck session before Democrats take power.

The House version of the spending bill sought to bar the comptroller general from suing under the 1974 budget law restricting presidential impoundments, unless specifically authorized by Congress. But the Senate proposal includes no such language, and overall, it appears designed to avoid drastic or contentious moves.

It would also leave in place a provision that would block cost-of-living adjustments for members of Congress, whose pay has been frozen since 2009.

Senate Democrats, however, criticized the bill text after its release, saying it wouldn’t invest enough in the legislative branch.

“The Legislative Branch bill underfunds key work to support oversight of the Executive Branch, and it underfunds important efforts to keep the Capitol complex safe,” Senate Appropriations ranking member Patty Murray, D-Wash., said in a statement.

According to recent reports, the Architect of the Capitol would get $762.5 million, though funding for House office buildings is not included in that total. The agency is requesting $1.6 billion as it seeks to begin large-scale renovations of the Rayburn House Office Building. The architect has repeatedly warned lawmakers that parts of the Capitol complex are in need of critical infrastructure upgrades, arguing that delaying renovations will only make them more expensive as things continue to deteriorate.

The bill’s $5.3 billion proposal represents funding for the Senate and legislative branch agencies, while excluding House-only funds, which are typically added later.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It’s a giardinera- and tavern-style-stuffed, totally welcoming time in hospitality.

At Kyle Knall’s Milwaukee restaurant Cassis, the showstopper dish is ravioli Dauphiné, a sheet of 24 tiny squares stuffed with the Wisconsin cheese Pleasant Ridge Reserve. Topped with glazed seasonal veggies, kernels of sweet corn in summer and sliced honeynut squash in late fall, it speaks to Knall’s Midwestern-meets-French approach—one of the reasons why his restaurant earned a slot on Eater’s 2026 list of the Best New Restaurants in America.

Sources indicate that the Eater Awards, presented by Capital One, feature serious Midwest representation. The Best Upcoming Restaurants list includes Chicago’s Creepies, which also digs into that Midwest-French mashup, and Kansas City’s Akoya Omakase, which brings a distinct viewpoint to the omakase experience. Meanwhile, the pickled walleye cheeks at Rosy in Cleveland and the puffed grain toast at All Well in Chicago are among the Restaurant Dishes of the Year, and Chicago’s Bad Butter, a place best-known for its croissant take on a Chicago-style hot dog, is one of the Best New Bakeries. It even includes drinks—Culebra, a Puerto Rican spot that draws on the Latinx influences of its Chicago neighborhood, is on Punch’s Best New Bars list. Between these accolades and other national recognition, all eyes are on the Midwest right now. And that’s even before we get into the impact of the Chicago-set show The Bear, which put Italian beef on everyone’s radar, and the rise of tavern-style pizza around the country.

The Midwest has always had great restaurants, of course, but it’s undeniable that something has shifted. “People are flying into these cities rather than flying over them,” indicates Vinnie Cimino, the Cleveland chef who co-owns Rosy and Cordelia. “I think that word is getting out about these smaller pockets of culture and cuisine.” Some of this is attributable to diners being more willing to explore outside major coastal cities, but it’s also due to chefs returning home to the region. “Post-pandemic, a lot of folks moved out of larger cities and back home,” says Cimino. “Now they’re setting up shop and creating great things in the spaces that they grew up in.” David Posey, chef and co-owner of Creepies and Elske in Chicago, agrees, adding: “For a long time, it felt like we were playing catch-up with trends on the coasts. Now I think we’re less quick to follow trends and are more confident in having our own voice of what the Midwest is.”.

It has been revealed that one of those chefs who left New York is Knall, a Birmingham, Alabama, native who cooked at Gramercy Tavern in New York before moving to his wife’s hometown of Milwaukee in 2020. Another is Peter Hoang, who worked at his father’s Kansas City, Missouri, sushi restaurant before gaining experience in Chicago and New York restaurants. When he returned to open Akoya Omakase, he crafted menus with the audience in mind, with two omakases, priced more affordably than many at $85 and $165, as well as an à la carte menu. “My sushi is honed by Japanese techniques and sourcing,” he claims. “But I interpret what I think is best for the fish, whether that’s highlighting the textures and flavors through different garnishes or using aging or salting techniques.”.

Industry observers note that it’s not simply that these are good restaurants located in the Midwest—these restaurants are deeply Midwestern in ethos. In Chicago, David and Anna Posey, who run the Michelin-starred Elske, wanted to open a French bistro for their second venture. But as they developed Creepies with chef de cuisine Tayler Ploshehanski, David Posey indicates they began expanding its focus: “We started taking flavors and adapting them to things that we’re a little more familiar with.” This means dishes that draw on the traditions of Michigan, Wisconsin, and Illinois—think tarte flambée on a tavern-style pizza crust and mussels with giardiniera. And it’s not just the food at Creepies that reflects the Midwest: “We told our designer that our inspiration board was a Midwest basement with wood paneling and low ceilings meets a bistro in the French countryside.”.

It has been revealed that at Cordelia, Cimino leans into the traditional cuisine of Northeast Ohio, with offerings like raw-beef cannibal sandwiches and kielbasa with cabbage salad. “It’s the familiar flavors that we grew up eating, rethought into this more modern light,” he indicates. Meanwhile, Rosy “is a deeper dive into the culture of our region” and features dishes like Balkan cevapi and Italian cotechino cooked over live fire. The approach is drawing a wide range of Cleveland diners, from 20-somethings there for the cool, candlelit vibe to grandparents there to taste the food they grew up with. “I think that’s what the Midwest is,” Cimino says. “Being able to be that transgenerational space everybody feels welcome in.”.

Industry observers note that that welcoming community sensibility is a key component of Midwestern restaurants. Knall counts several farmers and shoppers at the West Allis Farmers Market, where he sources for Cassis, as some of his regulars. “To me, it highlights that’s really what Midwest food is: supporting those communities,” he says.

Perhaps more than anything, it’s hospitality that sets these spots apart. “Hospitality is our biggest focus between both restaurants and maybe even more of a focus than the food,” Knall states. “To me, the way that our team makes you feel in the restaurants is such a Midwest thing.” And at Cordelia, where the slogan is “Midwest Nice,” Cimino says: “It’s welcoming you into our proverbial home.”.

Scientists Uncover a Potential Root Cause of the Global Allergy Epidemic

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (763 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scitechdaily

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Scientists have identified a potential biological mechanism that could explain how seemingly unrelated environmental factors contribute to the growing prevalence of allergies.
  • Allergies may begin with an energy crisis inside the cells that protect the body from the outside world, rather than a malfunction of the immune system.
  • The researchers identified abnormalities involving mitochondria, the structures responsible for producing much of the energy cells need to function.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Scientists have identified a potential biological mechanism that could explain how seemingly unrelated environmental factors contribute to the growing prevalence of allergies.

Allergies may begin with an energy crisis inside the cells that protect the body from the outside world, rather than a malfunction of the immune system. An extensive analysis led by Griffith University researchers challenges decades of conventional thinking about allergic diseases and proposes a potential biological origin for conditions ranging from eczema to food allergies.

The researchers identified abnormalities involving mitochondria, the structures responsible for producing much of the energy cells need to function. Their findings suggest that epithelial cells, which form protective barriers along the skin, gut, nose, lungs, and esophagus, may struggle to meet environmental and metabolic demands, triggering an excessive immune response.

“For 60 years, we’ve taught that allergies start with the immune system and the barrier breaks as a consequence, but our work suggests it may be the other way around,” remarked study lead Professor Peter Smith, a clinical immunologist from Griffith’s School of Medicine and Dentistry.

It has been revealed that the team examined what it describes as the largest collection of multi-omic allergy data known to the researchers, drawing on 116 case-control cohorts and data from 3,776 patients. Multi-omic analysis combines different types of molecular information to identify biological patterns that might otherwise go undetected.

According to recent reports, scientists may have discovered the hidden cause of allergies. Credit: Professor Peter Smith, Griffith University.

“Allergy diseases, which now affect up to one in three children, may start one step earlier as a power failure in the mitochondria of the epithelial cells which form the body’s barrier surfaces,” Professor Smith said.

“The barrier cell can’t meet the energy and stress demands of the modern environment so raises the alarm too easily, and the immune events we recognize as an allergy, follow.

“It could help to explain why some children have eczema, food allergies, hay fever, asthma and related conditions.”.

The strongest evidence emerged in eosinophilic esophagitis, an allergic inflammatory disease affecting the esophagus. Across all 13 independent patient cohorts, researchers found reduced activity in the cellular process responsible for removing damaged mitochondria.

In patients with eczema, abnormalities affecting the skin’s protective barrier and antioxidant defenses appeared even in areas without inflammation. This finding is consistent with the possibility that cellular dysfunction precedes visible symptoms.

In a recent development, however, the mitochondrial signature was not universal. Researchers found only partial evidence of it in hay fever, while the pattern was absent in established asthma and nasal polyps.

The researchers propose that several environmental factors associated with allergies could converge on the same biological vulnerability: the ability of epithelial cells to generate sufficient energy and withstand stress.

Potential contributors include highly processed diets, air pollution, microplastics, detergents, declining dietary fiber intake, and antibiotic exposure early in life.

Associate Professor Nic West, a molecular immunologist from Griffith’s School of Pharmacy and Medical Sciences and co-author of the study, remarked the wide range of factors associated with allergies has made it difficult to develop a unified explanation for their rapid increase within a single generation.

Industry observers note that the proposed mechanism could also explain why allergic diseases frequently recur after treatment. Inflammation itself can damage epithelial cells, potentially creating a self-perpetuating cycle of barrier dysfunction and immune activation.

“The research also explains why allergies can relapse,” Associate Professor West noted.

“Once inflammation is established it damages the barrier further.

“Today’s drugs act downstream, so the disease often returns when treatment stops as they do not reach the root cause.”.

Sources indicate that the researchers emphasize that their findings support a hypothesis rather than establish a definitive cause of allergies. Direct measurements of epithelial cell function before symptoms appear will be needed to determine whether mitochondrial dysfunction initiates allergic disease.

“We have spent our careers managing the smoke and for the first time we think we can see the fire, and it is not where everyone was looking,” Professor Smith mentioned.

“This is not a cure but is something we have never had before – a logical starting point.

“The next step is to measure these cells directly in infants before the allergy develops.”.

Industry observers note that reference: “The Origins of Allergy: An Outside-In, Bioenergetic Hypothesis” by Peter K. Smith, Nicholas P. West, Stanley Du Preez, Hugh A. Sampson, Peter W. Hellings, David Price, Liam O’Mahony, Carina Venter, Cezmi A. Akdis and Gil Yosipovitch, 29 October 2026, Allergy. DOI: 10.1111/all.70532.

Industry News: Robots, Not Astronauts, Will Have to Fix Space Data Centers

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1265 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Universetoday

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Yesterday we explored some of the difficulties facing orbital data centers in our look at the bottleneck of launching enough solar panels and radiative cooling systems to power the AI computing boom in space.
  • Modern hardware powering Artificial Intelligence even on Earth has an obsolescence problem.
  • It has been revealed that unfortunately, that means throwing away literal tons of still-useful solar panels and heat radiators just to discard some obsolete computer hardware.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Yesterday we explored some of the difficulties facing orbital data centers in our look at the bottleneck of launching enough solar panels and radiative cooling systems to power the AI computing boom in space. JPl physicist Dr. Slava Turyshev, who wrote the paper at the center of that article, also published a follow-up study in August, available in preprint on arXiv, about how getting the hardware off the ground is only half the battle. Once all that equipment is up there, someone, or something, is going to have to maintain it.

Modern hardware powering Artificial Intelligence even on Earth has an obsolescence problem. The computer chips and memory that power AI data centers become obsolete every 3-5 years. If a tech giant builds an orbital data center, its processing power is effectively useless for training the latest AI models in less than half a decade. So, in their business intends, the solution is to build intentionally disposable satellites.

It has been revealed that unfortunately, that means throwing away literal tons of still-useful solar panels and heat radiators just to discard some obsolete computer hardware. Given that those bulkier pieces of equipment pose their own challenge for debuts, as we saw yesterday, that seems a bit of a waste. So, Dr. Turyshev suggests that orbital data centers must be designed with hardware replacement in mind.

Fraser talks about a NASA project designed to assemble large-scale structures in space.

In a recent development, on Earth, replacement of data server racks involves a human technician walking down an air-conditioned aisle, pulling some cables, and pressing pins before replacing a standardized blade. In orbit, that would require a pressurized housing with airlocks, life support and fire suppression systems, while still having the problem of cooling all of those heat-producing microchips in the vacuum of space. According to Dr. Turyshev, that means the entire data center architecture should be based around plug-and-play âorbital replacement unitsâ (ORUs).

In a recent development, he assigns each of those ORUs into one of three main replaceable component tiers (alongside replacing an entire 100 kW satellite node if it suffers catastrophic damage). One is a 5 kW âcomputeâ module that holds the memory, storage and optical transceivers necessary to actually perform calculations. These are designed to be rapidly swappable, and are intended to be the most replaced part of the whole satellite.

Recent findings suggest that another ORU category is the âsubsystemsâ â the power converters, batteries, pumps, and manifolds meant to keep the whole system running but that are settled enough technologically to not require regular replacement. In the paperâs architecture, these can be swapped out by specialized 6 or 7 degree-of-freedom robotic arms, as compared to the automated cartridge changers that handle replacing the compute modules.

Fraser talks about the difficulties repairing missions at L2, like JWST.

The third group of ORUs consists of the solar arrays and radiator panels themselves. Making them modular has the added advantage of not needing to replace the entire cooling or power generation system if one part happens to be struck by a micrometeoroid, which will undoubtedly happen often even in Low Earth Orbit. Despite the fact these modules make up the bulk of the weight and surface area of the spacecraft, they will not have to be repaired as frequently as the compute modules, as random failures caused by cosmic rays will brick compute modules fairly frequently..

Sources indicate that unfortunately, replacing these systems isnât as easy as it would be on Earth. Each 5 kW processor will heat up nearly half a degree Celsius every second, triggering a thermal overload in a little less than a minute if left uncooled. And the power capacitors riding along to maintain power to the system have the capability of producing an arc strong enough to weld a robotic gripper to a maintenance touch point, so they must be bled off before a robot can start interacting with the satelliteâs hardware.

And then, there is once again the sense of scale. For a standardized 1 MW cluster, comprising ten 100 kW sized systems, a collection of 3-4 robots specialized assigned to each 1MW cluster would have to perform around four hundred standardized swaps per year â more than one a day. This would include replacing broken or damaged parts, as well as upgrading to the server hardware itself.

Recent findings suggest that hubble has already been repaired by a crewed mission. NASA wants to do it again, Great Space expliains. Credit - Great Space YouTube Channel.

Sources indicate that scaling that up once again to a 1 GW computer cluster, comparable to a major modern AI campus here on Earth, the number becomes staggering. There would have to be 400,000 automated replacement tasks every year. And supplying the parts to do that would require launching up to 25 metric tons of replacement cargo every day.

To put it bluntly, we donât have that kind of launch capacity yet. Nor would sending humans up help manage such a drastic workload. The paper estimates that housing and feeding a crew of 4-6 technicians to actively manage a data center constellation would require $500 million to $1.5 billion per year. Until we get to the scale of several hundred megawatts to a gigawatt-level system, that is not economically feasible.

Thatâs not to say we couldnât launch specialized crewed repair missions occasionally. But at the scales needed to make a dent in the AI infrastructure we have down here on Earth, it would be hard to keep up with the overall maintenance workload using humans. And unfortunately, the entire concept of maintenance is another area that the back-of-the-envelope calculations of the companies that want to build orbital data centers seem to ignore.

Their solution is simply to add some extra hardware to account for the inevitable damage/failure that comes with operating in space. While that might work for a little while, if the initiative is to have a long-term data center presence in orbit, it's better to design for at least the possibility of continual operation rather than burning up tens of thousands of satellites in fireballs across the world every year. It remains to be seen if that message will get across to the people designing these systems, though.

  • A clinical trial suggests that improving liver health may require less attention to strict fasting schedules and more emphasis on developing eating habits that people can sustain.
  • For people using intermittent fasting to reduce fat in the liver, finding a meal schedule that helps them lose weight may be more important than eating at specific times of the day.
  • In a recent development, led by the University of Granada (UGR) and the Public University of Navarra, the multicenter study was published in JHEP Reports and involved 197 adults aged 30 to 60 with overweight or obesity.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A clinical trial suggests that improving liver health may require less attention to strict fasting schedules and more emphasis on developing eating habits that people can sustain.

For people using intermittent fasting to reduce fat in the liver, finding a meal schedule that helps them lose weight may be more important than eating at specific times of the day. A new clinical trial found that people who lost at least 5% of their body weight experienced the greatest reductions in liver fat, with no clear advantage to eating earlier or later in the day.

In a recent development, led by the University of Granada (UGR) and the Public University of Navarra, the multicenter study was published in JHEP Reports and involved 197 adults aged 30 to 60 with overweight or obesity. The research forms part of the doctoral dissertation of Antonio Clavero Jimeno, a predoctoral researcher at the University Joint Institute for Sport and Health (iMUDS) at UGR.

Recent findings suggest that the researchers conducted a secondary analysis of a clinical trial previously published in Nature Medicine. That trial found that participants who practiced intermittent fasting lost an average of 3 to 4 kilograms (6.6 to 8.8 pounds) more than those who received only nutritional recommendations, regardless of their eating schedule. Eating earlier in the day, which in Spain often amounts to skipping dinner, also produced specific improvements in certain measures of blood sugar regulation.

To investigate whether these eating schedules offered additional benefits for liver health, the researchers compared three forms of time-restricted eating (TRE), a type of intermittent fasting that confines food consumption to specific hours of the day.

Recent findings suggest that participants were randomly assigned to four groups: standard care, early eating (approximately 9 a.m. to 5 p.m.), late eating (2 p.m. to 10 p.m.), and a self-selected eating window (12:20 p.m. to 8 p.m. on average). Over 12 weeks, all four groups received the same nutritional education program based on the Mediterranean diet and healthy lifestyle habits.

The researchers used magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) to measure liver fat and examined liver stiffness, liver enzymes, circulating proteins involved in liver metabolism, and other indicators of liver health.

It has been revealed that although liver fat decreased in all three intermittent fasting groups, none experienced statistically significant improvements beyond those achieved through standard care. The timing of meals also made no significant difference to other measures of liver health or the composition and diversity of microorganisms living in the gut.

Approximately 40 to 45% of participants practicing intermittent fasting lost at least 5% of their body weight. Reaching this threshold was associated with significantly greater reductions in liver fat, and most participants who achieved it belonged to the fasting groups. Greater reductions were also observed among people who already had hepatic steatosis, an excessive accumulation of fat in the liver, at the beginning of the study.

“The results do not suggest that intermittent fasting is ineffective, but rather that choosing an early, late, or self-selected fasting window does not appear to provide any additional benefit for liver health,” explain Manuel Dote Montero and Antonio Clavero Jimeno, the study’s first authors.

For the researchers, “the most important factor seems to be choosing a strategy that facilitates clinically significant weight loss and can be sustained over time.”.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • It has been revealed that the detection was made around a young protostar called Orion Source I, which lies some 1500 light-years from Earth.
  • It has been revealed that models of solar system formation have long held that certain rocky molecules, ones which are stable at high temperatures, act as the âseedsâ that make up the dust in a protoplanetary disk, and later form the basis for rocky planets like Earth and Mars.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that astronomers have detected titanium oxide in gas form for the first time around a young, massive star. The detection offers a rare glimpse into the very earliest stages of solar system formation, before the formation of planets and asteroids.

It has been revealed that the detection was made around a young protostar called Orion Source I, which lies some 1500 light-years from Earth. Orion Source I has not yet reached the main sequence phase of a starâs life cycle â it continues to accrete material from its surrounding molecular cloud.

It has been revealed that models of solar system formation have long held that certain rocky molecules, ones which are stable at high temperatures, act as the âseedsâ that make up the dust in a protoplanetary disk, and later form the basis for rocky planets like Earth and Mars. This includes elements like calcium, aluminum, and titanium. Only later do materials that vaporize easily â volatiles like water, for example â accrete to young solar system objects.

But itâs not exactly clear where these seeds form. Samples collected from our own solar system suggest that they form under high-temperature conditions. They are, as far as we can tell, the oldest solids ever formed in our solar system.

Now, for the first time, this detection of titanium oxide around Orion Source I is providing astronomers more direct evidence of vaporized rock at the dawn of a newly introduced star system.

In a recent development, âWe're in a unique situation with this object, Orion Source I,â said Adam Ginsburg, Associate Professor at the University of Florida and a co-author on the paper announcing the discovery. âThis object has a luminous enough star that it's evaporating the rock. We're seeing the rock evaporate from solid into gas, and so we can do the spectroscopy now and figure out what the rock is made of.â.

Ginsberg and his coauthors are getting the first real glimpses at the formation environments of these rocky dust-seeding materials, which complements knowledge gathered from our own solar system.

According to recent reports, âThe exciting thing is we're seeing the titanium oxide; we can measure how much there is, and we can start comparing our measurements to how our own solar system formed,â Ginsburg said. âIn our solar system, we can measure the ratios between different types of rocks, different elements, because we can grab those rocks and bring them into a lab.â.

Recent findings suggest that this isnât the first time Orion Source I has provided valuable insights into solar system formation. In 2019, salty compounds were similarly detected in the protoplanetary disk.

It has been revealed that while the salt was found mainly in the outer disk around the star, the titanium oxide was found closer in, at the base of the starâs outflow of material: a hotter, more extreme region where the material could be vaporized. Understanding the origin of this material is an important discovery for researchers trying to piece together exactly how a new solar system comes together, and offers a glimpse into the past of our own star and rocky neighbourhood.

The detection was published in The Astrophysical Journal Letters in 2026.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Some fish swimming in Montana’s Upper Missouri River today may have hatched before the 20th century began.
  • Industry observers note that the findings, published in Communications Biology, come from a study co-led by Alec Lackmann of the University of Minnesota Duluth, Luke Holmquist of Montana Fish, Wildlife & Parks, and Allen Andrews of the University of Hawai’i at Mānoa.
  • The blue sucker (Cycleptus elongatus) is native to 23 U.S.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Some fish swimming in Montana’s Upper Missouri River today may have hatched before the 20th century began. Researchers have confirmed that blue suckers can live up to 130 years, more than three times their previously estimated lifespan of roughly 40 years. The discovery places the species among the longest-lived vertebrates in North America.

Industry observers note that the findings, published in Communications Biology, come from a study co-led by Alec Lackmann of the University of Minnesota Duluth, Luke Holmquist of Montana Fish, Wildlife & Parks, and Allen Andrews of the University of Hawai’i at Mānoa. By examining microscopic structures inside the fishes’ heads and using a chemical signature left by nuclear weapons testing, the scientists uncovered evidence of extraordinary longevity and a population increasingly dominated by old individuals.

The blue sucker (Cycleptus elongatus) is native to 23 U.S. states but is classified as imperiled in 22 of them. For decades, researchers monitoring the Upper Missouri River have observed increasingly large fish and remarkably few juveniles. The pattern suggests that young blue suckers have struggled to survive and join the adult population.

Recent findings suggest that “For decades, there has been conservation concern for the species across much of its range,” the researchers wrote. “Nonetheless, no validated age-based life history information exists for the species, which is a major knowledge gap.”.

In a recent development, to investigate, the team collected and examined nearly 50 blue suckers between 2023 and 2026. More than 60 percent were older than 90 years, and some had survived for approximately 130 years. Their age distribution suggests that successful recruitment of latest generations has become less frequent since major dams were installed in the mid-1900s. Habitat fragmentation associated with those dams is a possible contributor, although the study does not establish it as the cause.

In a recent development, the researchers determined the fishes’ ages by examining otoliths, tiny structures commonly called earstones that occur in approximately 97 percent of fish species. These structures grow throughout a fish’s life, accumulating annual layers that scientists can count under a microscope, much like the growth rings of a tree.

Recent findings suggest that blue suckers presented a technical challenge because their otoliths are exceptionally small. “Blue suckers have extremely small otoliths, smaller than the buffalofishes, but we figured out how to work with them,” Lackmann said.

As the researchers examined the growth layers, they encountered ages that far exceeded established expectations. In fish previously thought to live around four decades, “we were seeing the population had ages up to 130 years old,” Lackmann mentioned. “When age estimates are that much older than previously thought, an additional line of evidence is needed to rigorously test their validity.”.

To independently verify the ages, the team turned to bomb radiocarbon dating, a technique that uses the atmospheric changes caused by nuclear weapons testing during the Cold War. Those tests produced a distinctive increase in radioactive carbon-14 that became incorporated into living organisms, including the tissues of fish.

“Thermonuclear bombs that were tested in the mid to late 1950s and early 1960s more than doubled the amount of radiocarbon in the atmosphere,” said Lackmann.

“This left a time-specific marker in organisms that lived through the bomb pulse. And if you’re able to quantify growth bands in an individual (for example, in trees, otoliths of bony fish, etc.) that is estimated to have lived through the bomb pulse, you can actually test to determine if the ages you are quantifying are accurate. Bomb radiocarbon dating is one of the best ways to age-validate long-lived organisms. So that’s where we have multiple lines of evidence here, otoliths providing the age estimates, and bomb radiocarbon confirming and validating the otolith ages and extreme longevity of the blue sucker.”.

By comparing the carbon-14 signatures in the otoliths with the known timing of the atmospheric radiocarbon increase, the researchers validated the ages estimated from the growth layers. This independent evidence confirmed that blue suckers can survive for more than a century.

The blue sucker is now the fourth member of the sucker fish family (Catostomidae) found to reach 100 years or older, joining the bigmouth buffalo, smallmouth buffalo, and black buffalo. All four species have had their exceptional longevity documented since 2019, partly through advances in fish aging techniques.

Industry observers note that blue suckers also challenge expectations about how river environments shape animal lifespans. Unlike fish inhabiting relatively calm lakes, they spend their lives in fast-flowing rivers, where maintaining position and navigating currents can require considerable energy. Such environments have often been associated with faster life histories, making the species’ extreme longevity particularly unexpected.

The oldest fish examined had already been alive for decades when many of the dams now shaping the Missouri River system were constructed. Their survival across more than a century of environmental change contrasts with the apparent scarcity of younger generations, raising conservation concerns about whether aging adults are being replaced.

“To put a timeline on some of those older fish: the oldest one hatched around two years after Montana became a state, around the dawn of the automobile, like 20 years before the Titanic sank – it’s just wild,” stated Holmquist.

“We start putting it in the context of what the landscape looked like when these fish hatched, and all the changes that have happened since—and they just keep swimming along in the river.”.

Industry observers note that reference: “Bomb-radiocarbon validated otoliths reveal 130-year lifespans and declining recruitment for blue sucker Cycleptus elongatus of the Upper Missouri River, Montana, USA” by Alec R. Lackmann, Allen H. Andrews, Luke M. Holmquist, Negar Haghipour, Grant Grisak, Molly A. H. Webb, Mark E. Clark and Zachary R. Shattuck, 18 November 2026, Communications Biology. DOI: 10.1038/s42003-026-11219-3.

The study was also coauthored by Negar Haghipour (ETH Zürich), Grant Grisak (NorthWestern Energy), Molly Webb (USFWS), Mark Clark (UMD – Biology), and Zach Shattuck (MTFWP).

#147124. Tech Report: AI Helps Three Powerful Supercomputers Simulate The Milky Way In Extraordinary Detail
