The 6 Best Portable Generators Give You Power Whenever and Wherever You Need It

📅 25 Mar 2022 | ⏱️ 17 min read (3455 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Popularmechanics

⏱️ ~17 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review.
  • Industry observers note that generators come in all sizes, but when you need power for camping or tailgating, or to power tools when you’re too far from an outlet, a large one meant for home backup is just too much.
  • When you’re shopping for a portable generator, there are a few important things to consider, including power, weight, and fuel type.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Industry observers note that generators come in all sizes, but when you need power for camping or tailgating, or to power tools when you’re too far from an outlet, a large one meant for home backup is just too much. Power stations are handy, but once they run out of power, they take a long time to recharge. That’s where a smaller-sized portable generator can really shine. So long as you have the fuel, they can keep running.

When you’re shopping for a portable generator, there are a few important things to consider, including power, weight, and fuel type. For portable power, models that output 2,000 to 5,000 watts will generally be simple enough to lift in and out of a truck, though some models that generate more are designed to be lightweight. Anything over 100 pounds starts to buck the idea of something being portable, even if it has wheels.

It has been revealed that fuel type matters, too. All generators run on gas, but dual-fuel models can also run on propane. The drawback is that propane delivers slightly less power output and shorter running time, but it runs a lot cleaner and is much less messy to deal with.

If you’re powering sensitive electronics like digital equipment or TVs, you’ll also want to look for an inverter generator, which delivers more stable “cleaner” power that won’t damage your gear. They also run quieter than standard models. For these reasons, all of the picks on our list are inverter generators.

Keeping portability in mind, the models we cover in this story are all 7,500 watts and under. For the models that we tested, we based our methods on our experience using generators for backup power with and without transfer switches, on construction sites to run power tools and equipment, as well as running sound systems and lighting at outdoor events. We measured the sound levels of these generators idling with no load, and while running under load at two feet and 25 feet. We then used an oscilloscope to observe the sine wave of the alternating current generated by these machines, and a clamp meter to check voltage output.

Industry observers note that some examples of devices we used with large starting and running loads include a large air conditioner and a portable table saw. In one case, we even tested it paired to a solar inverter-charger. We evaluated these generators based on ease of starting, power response, sound levels, value, safety, and reliability to select the top performers.

According to recent reports, the Honda EU2200i inverter generator has just about everything you want from a portable generator. It’s half the size and weight of comparable generators in its class; it’s very quiet and clean when operating; and it’s fully enclosed so you can swiftly and easily transport it and move it around without worrying about it getting caught on anything.

That enclosure is an important feature, as it protects the inverter electronics and helps contain noise—the EU2200i is remarkably quiet. In testing, we measured sound levels of 68.9 decibels at the generator under no load. When we switched it to “eco” mode, which reduces engine speed when power isn’t called for, the sound was reduced to 76 decibels.

When we used an oscilloscope to look at the sine wave of the current generated, the curves were smooth and symmetrical, an indicator of “clean” power. This remained true even when running heavy loads from devices like a table saw or an air conditioner.

Recent findings suggest that there are some nice design features, too. The vent on the gas cap closes so fumes or fuel cannot escape. You could breathe freely packing this in the passenger compartment of an SUV. Likewise, the power on/off switch doubles as a fuel shutoff, so it can’t be forgotten.

Lastly, the EU2200i has ports for parallel operation. With the correct cable kit, it connects to a second EU2200i to double the output to 4,400 starting and 3,600 running watts. The EU2200i is ideal for camping and other outdoor events where generator noise might be frowned on.

In a recent development, we like the GD400BN because it’s powerful, quiet, and portable at a reasonable price point. The interesting thing about this inverter generator is how much power it can deliver, yet it’s still as compact as similar generators that deliver half as much output. Even when running on lower-output propane as the fuel source, it can run up to 3,000 watts, which is considerable for a generator that only weighs 47 pounds.

In a recent development, another plug or two would’ve been nice, however. Its single AC outlet limits you to plugging one power tool or appliance at a time, despite having enough output to power more than one device. It does have a 120-volt, 30-amp outlet for connecting to an RV, though, so that does make up for it a bit, but only if you have that need. The 1.1-gallon fuel tank is also a bit limiting regarding runtime for gasoline, but that’s easily overcome by using propane. For all intents and purposes, this is a very nice dual-fuel generator, and at a list price of $600, it comes at a reasonable price to boot.

The Wen DF360iX offers a considerable amount of utility for an affordable price. You have the option to run the generator on gasoline or propane with a running output of up to 2,900 watts. While propane delivers a bit less at 2,600 watts, that’s plenty of power for a job site or camping use and even enough electricity for small to midsize RVs.

It has been revealed that while this generator is fairly light at 49 pounds, it doesn’t cut back on ports, including a 30-amp port for direct connection to an RV. There are also two three-prong AC ports, a 12-volt DC receptacle, and two USB-A ports. Like most inverter generators, it produces less noise. This model is rated at around 65 decibels of noise at a quarter load, which is quiet enough that it shouldn’t bother the neighbors. There are some nice safety features, too, including auto-shutoff if the fuel runs too low and a carbon monoxide (CO) sensor that detects if dangerous levels are present.

Of course, with any generator in this price range (under $500), there are compromises. This model has a pretty small fuel tank—only 1.5 gallons—so you won’t be able to run this on gasoline for long periods (around five hours with a half-load) without having to stop and refill. You can mitigate this, however, by relying on a larger tank of propane. For example, a 20-pound tank should enable you to run it for up to 14 hours.

According to recent reports, GENERATOR SAFETYWhile not hard to run, generators present dangers, so you need to follow basic safety rules. Never operate them in a closed space, like a garage or shed. Exhaust gases contain carbon monoxide (CO), a lethal, odorless, colorless gas. Most manufacturers offer models that shut down when they detect carbon monoxide building up. Do not run a generator in a garage with the door open, or in front of the garage with the door open, because carbon monoxide can still get trapped and seep into the house. Run generators at least 20 feet away, including from windows and doors, with the exhaust blowing away from the house.

It has been revealed that RV owners need a generator outfitted with at least a 120-volt, 30-amp outlet, but it also helps to have a decent amount of power to go with it, so that you can run things like a heater or an air conditioner. This model from Champion offers both, with the outlet and up to 3,500 running watts, which is enough to power a small- to medium-sized RV.

It also offers great fuel flexibility. With a full 2.3-gallon fuel tank, it should be able to run for up to 14 hours, but it’s dual-fuel, so with a full 20-pound propane tank, this generator can supply 21 hours of uninterrupted power.

It has been revealed that in addition to being a solid companion for camping and RVing, this generator could serve as a useful tool in an emergency at home where power is needed. Using a manual transfer switch, you could power a few 120-volt circuits using the 30-amp connection. And the inverter will help to keep it running more quietly, which is helpful at home or the campground.

It has been revealed that one of our test editors picked up this generator when faced with a home emergency where he needed a generator with specific features, quickly, and on a budget. A failed generator at a solar-powered off-grid cabin necessitated the quick acquisition, and, happily, the Pulsar 7,250-Watt Dual-Fuel Inverter Generator indicated up on the doorstep in only two days.

Industry observers note that in about 15 minutes, with minimal assembly and after adding oil, the generator was connected to a propane cylinder by a hose and was running on the first cycle of the starter. Since then, it’s run steadily at 500 watts, up to 5,500 watts, at 240 volts (great for powering high-voltage appliances like dryers or water pumps), to charge a battery bank during the winter when sunlight wasn’t enough to get the job done.

This Pulsar puts out very clean power, too, with a claimed total harmonic distortion (THD) of less than 3 percent, which met the requirements of the solar inverter-charger it was paired with.

Using the inverter to monitor the current frequency, we found that it was indeed very stable with minimal variance, between 59.97 and 60.09 Hz. All things considered, the Pulsar 7,250-Watt Dual-Fuel is a good value for the specs, capacity, and features.

Recent findings suggest that generac’s iQ3800 Portable Inverter Generator is a great example of what we love about dual-fuel, inverter generators. This type of generator can deliver cleaner power than a standard model, meaning there’s less distortion in the electrical current frequency. That’s ideal for powering sensitive electronics, such as TVs, computer equipment, and smart household appliances. This is also a closed-frame inverter generator, which tends to be quieter; the iQ3800 is one of the quietest generators we’ve tested of this size.

We were very impressed with how easy the iQ3800 is to operate. The electric start and auto choke worked perfectly, taking only about four to five seconds, while the manual pull-start also fired up the generator with minimal effort. Switching between fuel types was also very simple to perform. Once running, you can view important information on an easy-to-read LED display that lists the total hours the machine has run, the fuel level for the gasoline tank (there’s no gauge for propane), and a load gauge that uses a bar graph to show power output level—knowing that helps to avoid overloading the generator.

It has been revealed that the inverter technology might be the most notable feature of the iQ3800. This generator has a total harmonic distortion (THD)—a level of variance in the current frequency—of less than 3 percent, which is very low. Essentially, anything with a screen or any smart device would be best powered using an inverter generator like the iQ3800. It’s an ideal generator to power RVs in campgrounds or off-grid, and a great option for emergency backup in urban areas.

Full Generac iQ3800 Portable Inverter Generator Review.

It has been revealed that these generators, sometimes called backup generators, are used to provide temporary power when and where it is needed. Portable is a relative term; some are more portable than others. While the smallest models can be picked up and carried, most have wheels and a handle to make transport easier. However, at 100 pounds or more, picking them up to load or move may take two people. Appliances, power tools, or other devices can be plugged directly into standard outlets on the generator’s front panel.

Sources indicate that additionally, many models have a twist-lock plug that can provide up to 240 volts and be used to power circuits in a home via a manual transfer switch. You may hear generators like these referred to as “open frame” generators, which simply means that the engine, fuel tank, and generator components are not enclosed in bodywork.

Though inverter-type generators are—like their standard cousins—typically portable, we group them separately because they’re significantly and technically different in terms of how they work.

Like most generators, inverter generators provide 120/240 volts of AC power. They generate AC current just like the others, but it’s then converted to DC (Direct Current), and then inverted back to AC. The conversion and inversion is controlled by circuitry which acts like a filter, flattens surges, and cleans up the sine wave (or oscillating wave) of the electrical current.

Recent findings suggest that typical generators have varying degrees of distortion in the sine wave of the alternating current. This isn’t usually an issue for most electrical devices, though sensitive electronics like tablets, laptops, televisions, and other smart devices can be damaged by current distortion or surges. These devices will last longer with “clean” power and steady voltage. Because of that added complication, inverter generators can be significantly more expensive.

In a recent development, standby generators are permanently installed and connected to a home. These may power selected, critical circuits during a power outage, or may provide power for the whole home. Standby generators have systems that monitor power supplied by a utility and start automatically in the event of an outage. Since they’re not portable or easily moved, we didn’t include any here.

It’s crucial to know what you intend to power with a generator in order to choose the right size. Manufacturers list two figures for generators: starting watts and running watts. Starting watts include the initial surge required to start appliances or tools with powerful electric motors or compressors. Once started, these devices require far less power to run continuously.

Many manufacturers have a chart with estimated power requirements for common appliances and tools to help you figure out what you need. For a more precise measurement, you can also calculate the figure yourself by adding up the power consumption of specific appliances and adding them together.

To calculate watts, multiply voltage (usually 120 volts) by the amps (amperage) required to run the appliance (usually found on a tag attached to the appliance). Do this for each item that the generator will power.

Sources indicate that most portable generators are powered by gasoline, the most commonly available fuel. However, when using generators for emergency power, their infrequent use presents some problems to consider.

Recent findings suggest that the first is that when major, catastrophic storms hit and power outages last for days, gas stations may struggle to meet demand, resulting in long lines. The second glitch has to do with the infrequent use of backup generators, which may sit for months to years between uses.

Gasoline sitting in a carburetor will slowly evaporate over time, leaving gummy deposits that can block fuel from getting through, making it difficult or even impossible to start your generator without servicing. You can avoid this by closing the fuel valve and letting the generator run until it stalls, using up the remaining fuel in the carburetor. Also, over time, gasoline can oxidize or become “stale,” losing combustibility. It may also absorb water, which can then corrode fuel tanks and other metal components in the fuel system. Starting a generator regularly, as well as treating fuel with a stabilizer, can help fight these problems.

Ethanol-free gasoline, available at some gas stations, is also less susceptible to degradation over time than standard 87-octane pump gas; however, it’s still a good idea to mix the fuel going into your generator with stabilizer.

Dual-fuel generators can run on gasoline or liquified petroleum gas (LPG), commonly known as propane. Switching between the fuels is simple, and you won’t be tied to the availability of one type of fuel.

It has been revealed that A big advantage of propane is that it’s very stable when stored for long periods of time. It won’t go stale, and it won’t gum up carburetors from sitting. Plus, some homes that use propane for other purposes may already have large storage tanks on the premises, foregoing the need to make repeated trips out for fuel.

Sources indicate that the downside to propane is that it creates fewer BTUs (British Thermal Units, a measurement of energy) than the same amount of gasoline. So, a generator running on propane will have slightly reduced starting and running watts. On the plus side, though, it will also run a little quieter than those that run on gasoline.

Recent findings suggest that while not as common, tri-fuel generators add an option to connect by natural gas. Some propane-powered generators can be converted to run on natural gas, as well. Like propane, natural gas can run cleaner and a little quieter. However, it also creates fewer BTUs than gasoline and propane, so it will also produce reduced starting and running watts.

Natural gas also requires a dedicated line for the generator, which most homes that have access to natural gas will not have, and thus will need to be professionally installed.

If you’re powering appliances, tools, or other devices by plugging them directly into the standard outlets on the generator, the answer is no. If the generator is being used to power circuits in your home, maybe. It’s always best to consult the operator’s manual, a licensed electrician, or your local building officials about township ordinances—some localities may have requirements that differ from the National Electrical Code (NEC).

Electrical circuits need to be grounded to operate devices safely, so that any current that shorts out or has a fault is directed to the ground, i.e., the actual, literal earth, so the user doesn’t become the conduit to “ground.”.

According to recent reports, there are two ways that generators are grounded: neutral-bonded and floating neutral. Neutral-bonded means the neutral wire is connected (i.e., bonded) to the generator frame. With a floating neutral, the neutral is not connected to the frame. In the latter case, the generator should be grounded by connecting the ground terminal to a grounding rod driven into the ground.

Sources indicate that generators with ground-fault circuit interrupter (GFCI) outlets, when used to power circuits in your home, require neutral switching and a manual transfer switch, and must be grounded by connecting the ground terminal to a ground rod driven into the soil. Neutral-switching transfer switches are also referred to as three-pole transfer switches.

Recent findings suggest that there could be numerous reasons for difficulty starting a generator. The first things to check are whether or not there's any fuel in the tank, and if the fuel valve is turned open. Then, check for any obstructions in the air cleaner box. If that’s clean, move on to check that the engine has spark.

If your generator has sat for a long time without treated fuel, the carburetor may be clogged up and require cleaning—if you’re unfamiliar with any of these steps, it may be best to take it to a shop for service.

In an emergency, use what you can get, but as a general rule, 87 octane fuel will be fine—just don’t go lower than that.

As long as we’re talking fuel, it’s always best to use ethanol-free fuel in equipment with small gas engines—if that’s not possible, nothing more than 10-percent ethanol. Ethanol can attract moisture, which will then separate and settle in the gas tank or carburetor, where it can corrode and clog the fuel system. For this reason, it’s also a good idea to treat gas with a fuel stabilizer.

Much like your lawn mower, generators need regular maintenance. However, since they often see less use, maintenance intervals tend to be farther apart. Typical maintenance would include changing oil, checking the air filter and changing it if needed, changing the fuel filter if so equipped, and checking the spark plug.

The best source of specific maintenance and troubleshooting information for your generator is the owner’s manual.

Trump administration ups ante on aviation funds after ground stop

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (781 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy leaves a House Republican Conference meeting in the Capitol on July 21.
  • Top administration officials doubled down on calls for Congress to supply additional funds for an ongoing air traffic modernization effort after they mentioned old equipment contributed to the need for a nationwide ground stop of flights on Friday.
  • Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin increased their ask to $50 billion on Friday night, a day after Duffy and White House budget chief Russ Vought formally requested $30.1 billion.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy leaves a House Republican Conference meeting in the Capitol on July 21. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

Top administration officials doubled down on calls for Congress to supply additional funds for an ongoing air traffic modernization effort after they mentioned old equipment contributed to the need for a nationwide ground stop of flights on Friday.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin increased their ask to $50 billion on Friday night, a day after Duffy and White House budget chief Russ Vought formally requested $30.1 billion.

The increased allotment, which the administration officials didn’t fully flesh out, comes after the nation’s air traffic control system experienced “instability” in its radar and communications at certain facilities earlier in the day, Duffy told reporters.

He said “inconsistency in the data” being issued by those systems led to implementation of the nationwide ground stop, saying the order was given out of “an abundance of caution” before being lifted about four hours later.

During a Friday night White House briefing, Duffy and Mullin explained the complications were driven by “an incredibly old air traffic control system.”.

Recent findings suggest that earlier in the day, the stoppage had caused mass confusion and raised questions about potential terror attacks, or artificial intelligence breakouts resulting from upcoming software the agency is rolling out. While Mullin noted “we’re not ruling out anything,” he explained that “the public was never at danger through this process.”.

Still, Duffy called the incident “an emergency” while calling for additional modernization funds.

“This is an emergency,” he stated. “I want $50 billion. President Trump is a builder. He’s going to build this network and deliver for the American people. But the president can’t deliver for America unless the Congress delivers the money to make it happen.”.

The latest figure is $19.1 billion higher than the figure Duffy and Office of Management and Budget Director Russ Vought called on congressional appropriators to approve in a Thursday letter.

Mullin said the new $50 billion figure was an administration estimate for a “complete overhaul of the system” which has been going through a “patchwork” upgrade process that may have overwhelmed the older equipment still being used.

“We need someone to come in and build the whole system," Mullin noted. "Nickel and diming it together does not work.".

Industry observers note that thursday’s call for $30.1 billion echoes a White House-backed bill that Sen. Eric Schmitt, R-Mo., introduced in September, which would provide $10.1 billion for air traffic control upgrades, including $2 billion for "cloud computing and national airspace system telecommunications.".

Those funds would come after $12.5 billion allocated to the effort through the July 2025 reconciliation law that Duffy and Vought called a “down-payment.".

Sources indicate that senate Commerce, Science and Transportation Committee Republicans touted those already-appropriated funds in a social media post. They pointed to $1.9 billion provided in the reconciliation law that would go toward upgrading air route traffic control centers, which guide planes across long distances after departure and which the FAA had cited as the cause of the problem.

Sources indicate that the 22 air route traffic control centers across the country guide aircraft using instrument-dependent flight plans. Under such plans, pilots use instruments, electronic navigation and air traffic control assistance to guide them and maintain separation from other aircraft in certain airspaces.

The committee’s majority stated Friday's outage highlighted the need to prioritize modernization of the air route traffic control centers, arguing that President Lyndon B. Johnson was in office the last time a newly introduced one was built.

Commerce ranking member Maria Cantwell, D-Wash., said in a statement Friday night that the panel is looking into FAA and airspace telecommunications concerns.

“Technology complications related to how planes communicate through primary frequencies, backup frequencies, and other issues will be something the Commerce Committee will be reviewing,” Cantwell stated.

Cantwell is poised to take the committee's gavel come January as Democrats assume the majority in the Senate.

In a joint statement Friday night, House Transportation and Infrastructure Chairman Sam Graves, R-Mo., and ranking member Rick Larsen, D-Wash., called the communication failures “concerning” and remarked their committee would “thoroughly review the issues that led to this nationwide ground stop.”.

Both committees have also been in monthslong negotiations over dueling aviation safety bills responding to the January 2025 midair collision near Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport that killed 67 people.

It has been revealed that at concern in those negotiations is which location transmission technology should be mandated to aid in air traffic control operations and allow aircraft to maintain appropriate distance. Leaders have remarked they hope to reach a deal in the lame-duck session.

Donkeys help families survive droughts, but governments often overlook them

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1476 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Donkeys help East African families survive severe droughts, yet governments and aid organizations often overlook their essential needs.
  • It has been revealed that families in East Africa depend on donkeys for many everyday tasks.
  • In a drought their job gets even more key.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Donkeys help East African families survive severe droughts, yet governments and aid organizations often overlook their essential needs.

It has been revealed that families in East Africa depend on donkeys for many everyday tasks. The animals carry water, feed for livestock, and household belongings. They have also been part of local culture for generations.

In a drought their job gets even more key. Once the water close to home has dried up, donkeys trek long distances to bring it back.

Yet when drought relief arrives, donkeys are rarely part of it. Aid has tended to go to the food-producing animals, and donkey-owning households end up worse off for it.

A team from the University of Portsmouth, Maasai Mara University and Haramaya University looked at how far that neglect goes.

They went through 77 documents and talked with 41 people on the ground. Donkeys, it turned out, are mostly missing, from the policies right down to the vet schools.

Sources indicate that from 2020 to 2023 East Africa was hit by drought. Crops failed widely and some places lost up to 70% of livestock.

Around 26 million people were threatened with food shortages, and conflict over the dwindling resources went up.

Many of the worst affected families are pastoralists, meaning their living depends on herds that often move with them.

Donkeys have been part of that life since they were domesticated in Africa thousands of years ago.

When nearby sources dry up, the water a donkey brings back keeps people, crops and herds going. Donkeys also get people to health facilities, aid distribution centers and markets.

According to recent reports, kenya and Ethiopia both rely heavily on them. Ethiopia has about 10.8 million donkeys, and Kenya around 1.2 million.

Professor Leanne Proops works on animal behavior and welfare at the University of Portsmouth and supervised the project.

“Working donkeys are a lifeline for many communities during drought, helping people access water, transport essential supplies and sustain their livelihoods,” said Proops.

“Yet their contribution is largely overlooked in the policies and support systems designed to help communities cope with these crises.”.

Of the 77 documents, 51 were Kenyan and 26 Ethiopian, issued anywhere from 1964 up to 2025.

Sources indicate that animal health, agriculture, climate change, disaster risk and water were the areas covered. Equids, that is donkeys, horses and mules, came up in just 17.

Quite often the donkey got one mention in a species list and was absent from the rest of the policy.

It has been revealed that “Livestock” was a word used a lot, but most documents never remarked what species it took in. In reality it meant cattle, sheep and goats.

Donkeys, on the occasions they did appear, sat outside conventional livestock under labels such as “working animals” or “emerging livestock.”.

Not one of the documents made a link between donkeys and drought, even though camels were mentioned in that role.

On welfare the picture is not much better. Kenya’s Animal Welfare and Protection Bill has been in deliberation since 2019 without being enacted.

Up until 2025, Ethiopia’s criminal code only made cruelty an offense when it happened where the public could see.

A 2025 proclamation now prohibits overloading or overworking any working animal, though no penalties are set out in that part.

References to animals in the policies were heavily based on use, with meat, milk, hides and exports driving them. Kenya’s 2024 Livestock Bill does define donkeys as draught animals but welfare hardly features.

The interviews pointed the same way. If a drought is forecast, preparedness prepares kick in with worming and vaccination for the other livestock.

Recent findings suggest that “The donkeys were generally left out. Nobody was thinking about them,” one participant in Kenya told the researchers.

Later on, supplementary feed rations get handed out in both countries and again the donkeys are not counted.

A participant in Ethiopia said that when fodder runs short, “the priority is not for donkeys, not for mules, just for animals with salvage value.”.

In the only program one Kenyan participant had worked on with donkeys included, they got rabies vaccination and no food. The rest of the animals were counted for supplementary feeding.

Recent findings suggest that participants also noted that droughts are far more frequent than before. Money often comes towards the end, when much has died.

Pastoralists summed this up in their own words: “money comes with the vultures.”.

Industry observers note that dr. Emily Haddy, lead author of the paper, did the work at Portsmouth and is now at the University of Nottingham.

“Recognising donkeys in livestock and disaster planning is not just an animal welfare glitch,” stated Haddy.

“By including working donkeys in drought preparedness and emergency responses, governments and aid organisations can help protect animal welfare and strengthen community resilience.”.

It has been revealed that the veterinarians taking part spoke of getting little or no training on donkeys. One participant in Kenya mentioned they try to extrapolate from horses, which does not always hold.

“We try to extrapolate what we know from the horse to the donkey, which is not always true,” the participant said.

Vets specializing in donkeys are few and tend to be in urban areas such as Nairobi. Pastoralist communities therefore often have no access, and lose animals that could have been treated.

Medications suitable for donkeys are also in short supply, particularly anesthesia and pain relief.

“I don’t even think there is any firm in Kenya which makes feeds for donkeys,” another participant mentioned.

Recent findings suggest that it should be noted the vets interviewed were older graduates. Donkey medicine in the Kenyan vet curriculum has recently improved, though its effect on the ground may take time.

According to participants, the priority for government is animals bringing in foreign currency directly, through sale of meat and hides.

Recent findings suggest that the services of a donkey are largely invisible. That makes them hard to quantify and keeps them out of national economic reports.

One participant described a child-focused relief scheme for milk. Donkeys play a vital role in that milk chain, but they were not taken into account.

“They see the human being first, and they see the cattle, the producer of the milk, and the consumer of the milk, the in-between connection they don’t see,” the participant said.

Donkey deaths are also not systematically recorded, so they usually do not appear when authorities list the animals that died.

In a recent development, international guidelines do mention working equids. The Livestock Emergency Guidelines and Standards, aimed at livestock projects in humanitarian crises, include them as pack animals.

Sources indicate that the World Organisation for Animal Health gives advice on managing equids during feed shortage too. These were poorly reflected in the national documents.

Professor Tesfaheywet Zeryehun of Haramaya University put the two kinds of welfare side by side.

“Our findings reinforce the fact that donkey welfare cannot be separated from human wellbeing,” noted Zeryehun.

“In drought-prone communities, protecting working donkeys is equally about protecting the livelihoods, resilience and dignity of the families who depend on them.”.

“Their contribution must therefore be recognized in policies and emergency preparedness programs.”.

According to recent reports, documents had to be online and in English to be included. That likely cut the Ethiopian count, as many are in Amharic.

Only one pastoralist representative from Ethiopia was interviewed, so those views are probably underrepresented. Fewer than 15% of participants were women.

People were found by snowballing through the authors’ own contacts, and that could bring some selection bias with it.

What’s missing above all is hard evidence on how much donkeys are worth economically. Several interviewees felt numbers on that are what would capture the minds of policy makers.

Sources indicate that the authors recommend that equids be explicitly included in livestock definitions. Doing that would make donkeys eligible for the feed and veterinary support that other livestock can get.

They also suggest fodder reserves kept for donkeys, donkey modules in vet training and welfare laws that are actually enforced.

The impact of severe drought on donkey health is named as a research priority.

In a recent development, dr. David Obiero of Maasai Mara University remarked the gaps reach beyond policy itself.

“The lack of recognition of working donkeys extends beyond policy into veterinary training, access to healthcare and vaccination programmes,” said Obiero.

In a recent development, “These animals are vital to community livelihoods, yet the systems designed to support livestock often overlook them. Addressing these gaps is essential to supporting pastoralist communities during time of drought and beyond.”.

With recurrent droughts expected to intensify, the animal fetching the water is still largely outside the plans to help.

The full study was published in the Journal of Rural Studies.

#147066. Artificial intelligence could fundamentally change how we grow our food

📅 26 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1269 w)

Artificial intelligence could fundamentally change how we grow our food

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1269 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A latest review explores how generative AI could transform crop breeding and help address future agricultural challenges.
  • In a recent development, modern plant breeding runs on genome data and decades of catalogued crop genes.
  • Conventional crossbreeding largely relies on existing genetic variation.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A latest review explores how generative AI could transform crop breeding and help address future agricultural challenges.

In a recent development, modern plant breeding runs on genome data and decades of catalogued crop genes. For all that, it still takes 10 to 15 years to turn a promising cross into a variety a farmer can plant.

Conventional crossbreeding largely relies on existing genetic variation.

A new review states the next round of breeding won’t start with a plant at all. It will start with a model that writes DNA no plant has ever carried, and a lab that builds the sequence to see whether it works.

Feng Xu, Jun Yan, Xiangfeng Wang and their colleagues at China Agricultural University went through 67 generative AI tools built for biological design.

They sorted the tools by the part of breeding each one could serve, and hardly any were made with crops in mind.

Most were trained on microbes or mammalian cells, and the authors wrote that carrying them over to a maize or wheat genome is unfinished work.

The appeal lies in what the older tools couldn’t do.

Yield that holds up in a dry year is controlled by many genes at once, and a model that only ranks the variants nature supplied has a short reach.

Plant breeders mark their own history in stages, and the review counts four before this one. Choosing by eye and crossing came first.

Molecular markers came next, then genomic selection, then the omics work of the past decade, which filled catalogs with crop genes and the traits attached to them.

Every stage improved the odds of picking well. None of them changed the basic move, which was to choose among variation that already existed in a species.

Breeders have worked those catalogs for particular traits, from tomato flavor to seed size to crops that fertilize themselves.

According to recent reports, breeding 5.0, the authors’ name for what comes next, is meant to change the move itself. Design the genetic part first, then build it.

Artificial intelligence in plant science has mostly sorted things. It scored variants, predicted traits and ranked candidates a breeder could already have grown.

Industry observers note that generative models work the other way around. Trained on enough DNA and protein structures, they produce new examples that fit the patterns they learned.

That buys two things the authors care about: sequences beyond anything in nature, and screening that happens before a seed goes in the ground.

In a recent development, four kinds of model do most of this work. One compresses sequences into a map a researcher can move through in small steps, which suits fine-tuning how strongly a gene switches on.

According to recent reports, one trains two networks against each other. The first writes sequences, and the second tries to spot the fakes.

A third starts from noise and strips it away a step at a time, which gives tight control over three-dimensional shapes.

The fourth treats DNA as a language, with bases as letters and genes as sentences.

Those language models are the ones that can take an instruction in plain words.

In a recent development, the clearest results involve the short stretches of DNA that decide when a gene switches on and how strongly. Biologists call them promoters.

In cyanobacteria, 95% of the promoters one model designed turned out to be active. In E. coli, a second model wrote promoters that worked 70.8% of the time and looked little like anything in nature.

The authors call that design from scratch. Designs can be tuned as well as built. A third model raised promoter activity by as much as 33.43-fold, and in yeast a fourth moved expression across a thousandfold range.

Of that fourth model’s designs, 57% beat the strongest natural promoters they were measured against. Not one of those organisms is a crop.

According to recent reports, that pattern runs through the review. The proof exists, and it exists in microbes. Plant-specific models are appearing, and most of them still score sequences instead of writing them.

Genome editing lets breeders change a gene directly, and Cas9, the enzyme behind most of that work, came out of bacteria.

Profluent Bio fine-tuned a protein language model until it produced OpenCRISPR-1, the first openly available Cas9 designed this way.

It has been revealed that it cut DNA about as well as the standard enzyme, with better specificity, and it still read the short tag that marks where to cut. A separate model produced another Cas9 variant that worked in mammalian cells.

Protein design has gone further outside plants. One model produced 310 proteins that folded as predicted once made, and tools like AlphaFold made that check routine.

In plants, almost all the published work is redesign of existing proteins, including a refined enzyme in Arabidopsis and an improved potato protein.

The authors remarked design from scratch has rarely been validated in crops.

The authors also raised safety and regulatory questions about AI-designed proteins in crops, including their potential unintended effects, how long they persist under field conditions, and whether they are safe to consume.

So the authors suggested starting small, with designed proteins used as laboratory probes rather than put straight into a crop.

The authors’ own contribution is a framework they call DESIGN, named for six capabilities: discover, engineer, simulate, integrate, generate and navigate.

In plainer words, find the patterns in existing data and pull together information of different kinds.

Then design molecules that fit a set of constraints, make parts nature does not, test candidates in simulation, and weigh competing goals.

The authors set out two worked cases. One designs a maize promoter that stays quiet in a watered field and drives a drought-response gene hard when water runs short.

The other designs a protein that traps a molecule the stripe rust fungus uses to switch off the defenses of wheat.

Neither case is a finished experiment. Both are intends, detailed enough to name the tool at each step and the filter a candidate must clear.

The six capabilities don’t run in a line, the authors wrote. They run as a loop: learn, design, build, test, then feed the results back into the model.

Recent findings suggest that three problems sit between the framework and a field. Plant datasets are scattered across species and growing conditions, and well-annotated ones are thin for most crops.

Sources indicate that many models don’t transfer between domains or explain their output. Testing in plants is slow, so designs pile up faster than anyone can check them.

Plant genomes make the data problem worse, being larger and more repetitive than the genomes most of these models learned from.

Sources indicate that the same gap shows up in single-cell work. One plant model, built for Arabidopsis, labeled cell types it had never been shown with 0.91 accuracy.

The goal is to simulate how a root cell handles salty soil before planting.

The authors emphasized that AI is not meant to replace plant breeders. Breeders will continue to set agricultural goals and evaluate real-world results, while AI helps explore new possibilities.

What hasn’t happened yet, by the authors’ own accounting, is the validation of even one designed protein or regulatory element in a greenhouse or a field.

In a recent development, they named the benchmarks and shared datasets that would get the field there. That greenhouse result is the thing to watch for.

The full study was published in the journal Science China Life Sciences.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Recent findings suggest that these days, Jessica Yih spends a lot of time talking to women about testosterone.
  • Industry observers note that some non-hormonal treatments are now available, but the U.S.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .).

Recent findings suggest that these days, Jessica Yih spends a lot of time talking to women about testosterone. Interest is “coming from all directions,” says the University of California, Irvine Health urologist. A major source: women who hope testosterone can boost the female libido. Only about a decade ago, women looking for libido treatments had few medical options — even though women of all ages struggle with low sexual desire.

Industry observers note that some non-hormonal treatments are now available, but the U.S. Food and Drug Administration has yet to approve a female testosterone product, despite years of research suggesting it can boost sexual function and desire among postmenopausal women. Female testosterone products are approved in countries including the United Kingdom and Australia.

Industry observers note that not many studies have looked at testosterone’s effects on libido in premenopausal women, but preliminary data in that area are also promising, according to a 2026 research review in The Journal of Sexual Medicine that Yih coauthored. “I have seen it change people’s lives,” Yih notes. The hormone seems to make the female brain more receptive to sexual stimuli; it also promotes physical effects that enhance sexual pleasure, such as increased blood flow to the genitals. Right now, American women interested in these potential benefits have to look for them off-label. But that may change. In September, the FDA held a public meeting on testosterone use among menopausal women, “with the goal of informing future research and potential drug development in this area,” says Kaveeta Vasisht, the FDA’s associate commissioner for women’s health.

According to recent reports, the hormone has a rocky regulatory past. In 2004, an FDA advisory panel unanimously voted against approving a testosterone patch for women, citing a lack of safety data. There are still outstanding questions on that front, Yih says—like how, if at all, long-term use affects risk of conditions such as breast cancer and heart disease. Then, in 2011, a pair of Phase III trials found that testosterone therapy didn’t significantly outperform a placebo — a benchmark the FDA looks for when deciding whether to approve a new drug. That’s not to say testosterone didn’t work, says Tami Rowen, an ob-gyn at UC San Francisco. Rather, it seemed that hype about the hormone was so strong that study participants went in with sky-high expectations, leading even the placebo group to report benefits. The treatment was a “victim of its own success,” Rowen says.

It has been revealed that interest hasn’t let up, though. By one estimate, the U.S. female prescription rate for all uses rose from 0.4 out of every 1,000 women in 2018, to 1.8 out of every 1,000 women in 2026. That’s an increase of nearly 400 percent. With so much buzz, the potential placebo effect remains “the biggest problem with testosterone right now,” Rowen says.

Another outstanding question, Yih says, is whether using testosterone long-term increases the risk of breast cancer and heart disease.

It has been revealed that women seeking a libido boost do have non-hormonal options. In 2015, the FDA approved Addyi, the first treatment for low libido in premenopausal women. The drug seemingly raises levels of neurotransmitters that promote sexual desire while tamping down those that block it. A competitor, Vyleesi, hit shelves in 2019. Then, last year, regulators expanded Addyi’s use to postmenopausal women younger than 65. An international group of experts, including Rowen, issued recommendations for treating low female libido in 2025 in Sexual Medicine Reviews. Psychological therapies and Addyi are backed by the strongest evidence, the group found.

Rowen at the moment has her eye on in-development products including Lybrido. The drug, which is slated to enter a Phase III clinical trial in Europe, aims to rev sex drive in the brain and enhance physical arousal. The demand for new treatments is there, Rowen says. “Women deserve better than placebo.”.

#147063. An overlooked brain region offers latest clues to how memory works

📅 26 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1007 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Earth ↗ Open Full Page

An overlooked brain region offers latest clues to how memory works

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1007 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In mice, a thin brain sheet called the claustrum kept a smell or a touch in working memory for 30 seconds, and quieting it cut performance.
  • In a recent development, anyone following a conversation holds the last sentence in mind while the next one arrives.
  • Part of that job, at least in mice, belongs to a sliver of nerve cells wedged between the cortex and the structures beneath it.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In mice, a thin brain sheet called the claustrum kept a smell or a touch in working memory for 30 seconds, and quieting it cut performance.

In a recent development, anyone following a conversation holds the last sentence in mind while the next one arrives. The sound is gone within a moment, yet the brain keeps using it for seconds, and where it keeps it is only partly understood.

Part of that job, at least in mice, belongs to a sliver of nerve cells wedged between the cortex and the structures beneath it.

Sources indicate that the sliver is called the claustrum. In mice, it kept a trace of a smell or a touch for up to 30 seconds. Quieting it cut the animals’ scores on a memory task by roughly 40% to 60%.

Alan Carleton and Ivan Rodriguez of the University of Geneva led the work, with Anindya Bhattacharjee as first author.

Carleton’s lab in the Department of Basic Neurosciences studies how the brain handles the senses, and the claustrum caught the team’s attention because of its wiring.

“Its neurons are connected to almost all regions of the cortex, which puts it in a good position to receive and influence information from very different networks,” Carleton remarked.

The short-term hold the study tested is called working memory. Reading and deciding both depend on it, and it is impaired in disorders such as schizophrenia and ADHD.

It runs on brain circuits spread across many regions, and how those circuits hold information over time isn’t clear.

The team trained head-fixed mice on a game of same or different.

It has been revealed that A tone marked the start of each trial. Then came a one-second cue. It was one of two odors, or a puff of air on the left or right whiskers.

After a delay of 5 to 60 seconds, a second cue arrived. If it differed from the first, the mouse earned a drop of water by licking a tube. If it matched, licking earned nothing.

Thirty mice learned the odor version, and within about 400 trials they were scoring above 70%. Twenty-three of the 25 mice given the whisker version learned it too.

Scores fell as the delay grew. The memory faded at the same rate for both senses, with a half-life of about 20 seconds in the typical mouse.

In seven mice, the team watched claustrum cells through a tiny lens while the animals played. Each cell carried a sensor that glows when the cell is active.

According to recent reports, about a quarter of the cells fired at the cue, and about 60% fired during the wait. Roughly a quarter responded to one cue but not the other.

It has been revealed that the cells’ activity shifted as the wait went on. Even so, a computer program reading the whole population could still tell which cue the mouse had received, right up to the second cue, at every delay tested.

On trials the mouse got wrong, the program did far worse.

“Far from being a static memory, neuronal activity changed over time,” Rodriguez said. “Nevertheless, the identity of the stimulus remained sufficiently present to be decoded up to 30 seconds later.”.

Only a small share of the cells tracked licking or movements of the nose, mouth or forepaw, about 8% at most for any one of them.

The findings suggest that the memory trace was not simply a reflection of the animal’s movements.

In a recent development, to test whether the claustrum was needed, the team dialed its cells down in two ways. A drug that acts only on cells carrying an engineered receptor cut scores by about 40%.

Optogenetics, in which cells carry a light-sensitive protein and a fiber delivers light for about one second, cut them by 40% to 60%.

The light trials were mixed in with ordinary trials in the same session, and performance suffered regardless of when the light was delivered.

Dimming the claustrum during the first cue, early in the wait, late in the wait or during the second cue hurt in every case.

“The result was similar regardless of the type of stimulus, olfactory or tactile, and regardless of when the disruption occurred during the waiting period between the two stimuli,” Carleton said.

Mice carrying a harmless protein instead of the light-sensitive one played as well with the light on as off.

Sources indicate that the same mice then played a version with no delay, telling two odors or two puffs apart on the spot. The light had no effect on that.

The mice’s pupils, body movements and licking looked the same with and without it, and they didn’t lick early during long waits. What fell was the rate of correct licks on trials where the cues differed.

“Disrupting the claustrum specifically impairs the ability to use temporarily held information to guide behavior, without affecting perception itself,” Carleton stated.

Industry observers note that the sliver is thin and poorly bounded, so the team could only partly quiet it, and the mice still scored well above chance. Other regions carry short-term memories too, and this study doesn’t say how the work is shared.

In a recent development, A second team reported in June on a set of cells in and around the claustrum that connect to the prefrontal cortex. Mice needed those cells while holding a location in mind in a maze.

Silencing them during the decision itself improved performance, the opposite of what the Geneva team saw.

The two groups used different tasks and targeted different cells, and neither result settles which cells do what.

How the claustrum keeps a memory steady while its own activity drifts is the open question.

The next step, Carleton stated, is to work out how the claustrum talks to the cortex, and how that exchange keeps a held memory from degrading.

The full study was published in the journal Nature Communications.

#147061. Violent star collisions may have created the earliest giant black holes

Violent star collisions may have created the earliest giant black holes

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1449 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Crowded early star clusters could merge stars into one giant, and a fresh model shows how that giant may become a black hole seed.
  • Space is so empty that two stars almost never hit each other.
  • A new model suggests those crashes could merge stars until one carried the mass of the whole cluster.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Crowded early star clusters could merge stars into one giant, and a fresh model shows how that giant may become a black hole seed.

Space is so empty that two stars almost never hit each other. In the first star clusters, though, stars were packed so tightly that they may have crashed into one another again and again.

A new model suggests those crashes could merge stars until one carried the mass of the whole cluster. A star that heavy may have no way to die except by collapsing into a black hole.

That matters because the James Webb Space Telescope keeps finding enormous black holes far earlier in cosmic history than astronomers expected.

The new work, led by Claire Williams, a doctoral student at UCLA, is a calculation rather than an observation. It maps where colliding stars could have made the seeds of those black holes.

Webb’s deep images show extremely compact star clusters in the early universe, and computer simulations of that era produce the same crowding.

Williams and her colleagues in the UCLA Division of Astronomy and Astrophysics built a model to ask what happens to the stars inside them.

Co-authors of the study came from Northwestern’s CIERA and seven other institutions.

The model clusters ranged from about two-thirds of a light-year in radius to roughly 300 light-years.

In a recent development, they held anywhere from ten thousand to a billion times the mass of the Sun. Some had a black hole at the center and some did not.

Industry observers note that for each one, the team worked out how often stars would run into each other before something stopped them. That could be the stars burning out or a neighboring clump of matter crashing in.

Industry observers note that even with the strictest assumptions, collisions should have been common in many of these systems. Test simulations tracking 1,000 individual stars near a cluster’s center agreed on where they happen.

Sources indicate that in an interview with Earth.com, Williams remarked star collisions matter today only in rare, extreme places, such as the cores of galaxies. So astronomers usually don’t treat them as central to how stars live.

“We were surprised to discover how ubiquitous these collisions might have been,” she said.

Industry observers note that what a collision does depends on how fast the two stars meet. If they meet at speeds below the escape speed at a star’s surface, they can merge into one bigger star.

At higher speeds, collisions can strip material from both stars or destroy them entirely, releasing gas from their interiors.

In a cluster with no black hole, the model found no system where stars moved fast enough to destroy each other. Every collision was a merger.

And because the merged stars are heavier than their neighbors, they sink toward the center swiftly, where they collide again.

“Perhaps the strangest outcome of our simulations is that stars can merge repeatedly within the cluster until they form one gigantic star with a mass equal to that of an entire cluster,” Williams noted.

“When a star this huge reaches the end of its life, models suggest that it may have no option but to collapse into itself and form a massive black hole.”.

How substantial that merged star gets depends mostly on how tightly the cluster is packed.

In the model’s standard setup, the central star passes 200 times the Sun’s mass only once a cluster holds roughly 100,000 suns’ worth of stars per cubic parsec. A parsec is about 3.3 light-years.

Above that line, nearly all of the lightest clusters in the model produced one. In the densest cases, the merged star passed 100,000 solar masses.

When the team filled the clusters with heavy stars instead of Sun-like ones, only 22 systems built a giant at all, and the largest reached 512 solar masses. Heavy stars burn out quickly, so the collisions ran out of time.

If each giant collapses into a black hole of the same mass, the result is an intermediate-mass black hole, a size astronomers have struggled to find.

Other groups have already proposed stellar mergers as a route to early black holes, and the team’s giant-star masses broadly agree with theirs.

The upcoming part is one framework that runs from an ordinary early cluster to a black hole star wrapped in gas.

Once a black hole is at the center, the outcome changes. Its gravity speeds up the stars closest to it, so collisions there happen too fast to merge.

The stars are torn apart instead, and the gas from their interiors piles up in a tiny region around the black hole.

According to recent reports, the Milky Way’s center is the nearby example. “One place in the nearby universe where collisions between stars are common is the galactic center,” Williams said.

“In our model, once these very massive stars turn into intermediate-mass black holes, the system resembles our own galactic center, which is a black hole surrounded by a dense star cluster.”.

That dense, gassy core is why the authors connect the model to Webb’s little red dots.

Astronomers believe these compact objects hold a rapidly growing black hole, and several recent studies describe that black hole as buried in dense gas.

In the model, a cluster as dense as a little red dot would build a central star of 10,000 to 100,000 solar masses. Once a black hole formed, collisions would keep feeding gas toward it.

Williams remarked other researchers had already proposed that very massive stars might be connected to the dots.

“Little Red Dots may represent the densest extreme of a continuum of stellar systems that formed naturally in the early Universe, rather than an entirely separate class of object,” she told Earth.com.

Smadar Naoz, a UCLA astrophysicist and co-author, compared the research on the dots to the tale of blind people each describing an elephant by the part they touch.

“Our research connects several of those perspectives together and may help us see more of the elephant,” Naoz remarked.

Asked by Earth.com what Webb could see to confirm the picture, Williams said there may not be a single “smoking gun.”.

The most direct test, she mentioned, is spectroscopy, which splits an object’s light into its component wavelengths.

The bright and dark lines in that spectrum reveal the temperature, chemical makeup and motion of the material giving off the light.

With better theoretical predictions, those lines could help tell light from very massive stars apart from light reworked by gas around a black hole that is actively feeding.

One clue would be unusual amounts of certain elements, thrown out when collisions expose the insides of stars. The gas from these collisions may be unusually rich in nitrogen, which has already turned up in some early clusters.

Sources indicate that A second test would look for leftovers. If collisions built very massive stars that later collapsed, some of the resulting black holes may now wander near the edges of galaxies.

In a newer preprint that has not been peer reviewed, Williams’s team reports that upcoming sky surveys could find them.

Surveys by the Rubin Observatory and the Roman Space Telescope may spot the black holes when they destroy stars that pass too close.

“Finding a larger population of these events would provide independent evidence that dense early clusters formed intermediate-mass black holes through runaway stellar collisions,” Williams noted.

The authors list what their simplified model leaves out. It ignores any gas left over from the cluster’s birth, which they expect would pull merged stars inward even faster.

It doesn’t enhancement the stars’ masses as mergers happen, so it may miss runaway growth.

It has been revealed that its estimate of how much material a fast collision strips from a star is also likely too high. So the gas densities around black holes may be overstated.

Sources indicate that the model also stops at the giant star. It doesn’t follow whether that star collapses, how much of its mass ends up inside a black hole, or how fast the black hole grows afterward.

Industry observers note that williams said the team’s next step is following the gas that fast collisions throw into the middle of a cluster. The current model estimates how much gas that makes, but not where it goes.

The gas could stay trapped, cool and feed the black hole, change the orbits of nearby stars, or be driven out. Each outcome would leave a different signature for telescopes to look for.

The full study was published in the journal The Astrophysical Journal.

#147060. The 8 Best Home Generators Are a Significant Investment. These Deliver Reliable Power During an Outage.
