The 8 Best Home Generators Are a Significant Investment. These Deliver Reliable Power During an Outage.

📅 07 Nov 2018 | ⏱️ 25 min read (4927 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Popularmechanics

⏱️ ~25 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review.
  • Recent findings suggest that stronger and more frequent severe weather events are making a compelling argument for investing in a home generator.
  • The term “home generator” can be confusing.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Recent findings suggest that stronger and more frequent severe weather events are making a compelling argument for investing in a home generator. A large portable generator or a permanently installed standby generator can keep your entire home powered and operational for several days, or at least keep a few critical appliances such as a refrigerator running until the power comes back on. The cost of emergency power is never a small investment, though it is an increasingly vital one.

The term “home generator” can be confusing. It’s an unofficial category that includes larger portable generators capable of powering several appliances or a few critical circuits using a transfer switch (not all portable generators are built for this task). It also includes permanently installed standby generators that can automatically switch to whole-home backup power when the lights go out. Choosing the right size generator primarily comes down to how much power you think you’ll need in an emergency.

In a recent development, there are many reliable home generators that deliver a great deal of power. Some offer you the choice of running on multiple different fuels, while other models use an inverter that can give you quieter and “cleaner” operation. There is a nice range of prices available, too, so you can easily find a generator below that fits your needs as well as your budget.

For the generators on this list that we tested, we considered the difficulty of unboxing, assembling, and starting each generator for the first time, because few things are as frustrating as buying a tool that turns out to be unnecessarily complicated from the get-go.

Once set up, the generators we reviewed were subjected to different load conditions, including things such as power tools, home appliances, and even recharging large power stations. We assessed the features that distinguish these generators from each other, including safety features, app connectivity, and portability, among other things.

A few picks on our list have not been tested, but we included them here after considerable research, taking into account the brand’s reputation, our knowledge of its product lines, various outside reviews, and our own experience testing similar models from those same brands.

The DuroMax XP11000iH is a powerful midsize dual-fuel inverter generator, capable of keeping most homes up and running for an extended period of time. Inverter generators are a step above traditional generators because they convert alternating current (AC) to direct current (DC) and then back again to AC. This process creates cleaner, more efficient power and enables the generator to run more quietly and fuel efficiently.

Having two fuel options—gas and propane—provides a big boost of convenience by allowing you to use whatever’s handy. No gasoline? You can use the same tank of propane you use for your gas grill. It’s also parallel-capable, so you can daisy-chain it with another generator if you need extra power.

It has been revealed that the generator is enclosed in a large, sturdy plastic casing, which makes it durable and provides a fair amount of sound dampening. Of the many gas generators I’ve tested, it may be the quietest model that’s capable of backing up a whole home, especially when it’s running on propane, which trims it down by another few decibels. At 61 decibels on a 20 percent load, it’s about as loud as a dishwasher. Most comparably sized generators go up to around 80 decibels—about the same volume as a police siren.

Industry observers note that in addition to a full suite of essential modern safety features such as a carbon monoxide shutoff and low-oil shutoff, it goes the extra mile with lots of little touches, like remote start. The integrated battery tender keeps it ready to start, no matter how long it’s been sitting, which can be a lifesaver, too. When you do run out to check it, an onboard display demonstrates you key stats such as hours run, current load, and voltage output.

Industry observers note that the only downside I could find was its weight. At upward of 200 pounds, it isn’t easy to carry. It does have wheels and sturdy handles, though, so it isn’t hard to wheel around on flat, paved ground—if you can push a loaded wheelbarrow, you can push this. Not that you’ll need to move it much; it’s a very sturdy generator, and it comes assembled with the wheels and handles attached (not all generators come with those pre-attached). —Reviewed by Nick Hilden.

Industry observers note that technically, there are cheaper generators out there, but the Generac GP9500E offers an outstanding blend of capability, quality, and durability at a very reasonable price. As such, this is where I’d steer you if you’re trying to shave down your spend.

In a recent development, its 9,500-watt running capacity is slightly higher than the DuroMax’s, and it’s capable of powering all but the largest of homes. It can get a little noisy under a heavy load, but that’s common with units this size. It let out a relatively moderate purr when it was just powering the lights and a few appliances, but it became more of a roar when the heat kicked on.

With three fuel options—gas, propane, and natural gas—you get about as much versatility as you could possibly expect from a generator. A relatively large 7.5-gallon gas tank delivers a long runtime between fill-ups. And, while I was initially skeptical as to the necessity of the third fuel option, having natural gas support showed its value when a storm knocked out the power, and I didn’t have gas or propane on hand. All I needed to do was plug it into the natural gas line, and suddenly my house was the only one on the block with lights on.

Beyond that, though, it’s a fairly basic model. It has essential safety features such as low-oil and CO shutdown, but lacks elements such as a fancy digital display, remote start, or app. I don’t necessarily think that’s a problem: It can be helpful to get a piece of machinery that doesn’t go overboard with features. Its control panel is about as straightforward as can be, and it’s a cinch to get up and running.

Like my top pick, the GP9500E is exceedingly heavy. It’s also quite sturdy, though, which feels like a fair trade. The outlet covers aren’t as flimsy and breakable as with many other models of a similar price point. It isn’t completely immobile: It has wheels and handles that make it easy to cart around short distances. Realistically, though, weight is almost always going to be an glitch with any generator capable of backing up your house.

In a recent development, ultimately, its selling point is the price. It’s hard to find a quality tri-fuel generator for around $1,100, and the GP9500E performs well if you don’t mind losing out on some bells and whistles.

Whether you’re connecting devices individually, powering an RV, or running home backup power during a storm, this generator from Westinghouse (model WGen9500DF) covers all the bases. In addition to being dual-fuel (gas or propane), it includes both 30- and 50-amp outputs capable of powering 120- and 240-volt circuits. That means you could connect this generator to a transfer switch installed in your home using either option. And with 9,500 running watts of power, it’s enough for several critical circuits in your home, including the ones that run on 240 volts, such as a heating/ventilation/air-conditioning system, electric dryer, or well pump.

Several other features caught our attention, including a push-button electric start and stop (no need to mess with a pull cable), plus a remote start key fob. There’s an automatic low-oil shutoff, and the display provides the voltage output, frequency, and lifetime hours (this can run up to 12 hours on a 6.6-gallon tank of gasoline). The only drawback is the 74-decibel noise level. While that’s typical of generators of this type, if you're planning on using this to power an RV or camper, it may be too loud for some parks, as many limit generator noise to under 70 decibels.

While it does not offer as much power as some of the choices on our list, Champion’s 4,750-watt generator has enough capacity to run three or four critical 120-volt circuits in your home during an outage. It will also power small to medium campers and RVs via a dedicated 30-amp, 120-volt RV receptacle. Listed at around $600, this generator gives you a lot for the price you pay.

In a recent development, this generator uses a 224-cc engine with a 4.7-gallon fuel tank, enabling it to run for up to 14 hours (up to 10 hours using propane). A gauge displays a readout of the runtime hours and voltage output, and there’s an automated shutoff feature if the oil starts to run low. Since it’s dual-fuel, this generator can run off propane in addition to gasoline. For instance, if you are using it with an RV, you can run it off a camper’s propane tank without having to pack and haul a gas can. Likewise, with the included adapter hose, you can hook it up to a 20-pound propane tank.

There are a few drawbacks. Beyond the somewhat low wattage output for whole-home backup, there are no 240-volt outlets, so if you need that many volts to power circuits in your home for something such as a dryer or water heater, this model won’t be right for you. But if you just need something to keep some lights on and run a few appliances, this generator will get the job done and not cost you a ton of money up front to do it. — Reviewed by Bradley Ford.

Industry observers note that there are many reasons to opt for an inverter generator, but the two biggest ones are: cleaner, more stable power (crucial for powering electronics safely) and less noise. Loudness becomes a major factor with larger generators, as more power requires a more powerful engine. That’s why we were so impressed with this model (EU7000iS) from Honda. It delivers a lot of power but at notably low loudness levels.

It has been revealed that it’s vital to note that this is not a small generator. It weighs in at 263 pounds, making it one of the heaviest on our list. That noted, we found it fairly comfortable to move around. The metal frame that houses the generator has a folding handle that locks into place and is capped with soft grips, while on the front of the frame there are strong 10-inch rubber wheels. This made it fairly easy to roll around, even up some gradual slopes.

In a recent development, it’s also quite sturdy. The outer casing is constructed of stamped metal and impact-resistant composite hard plastic, with two large, hinged maintenance doors that lock into place.

Once we fired up the generator, it was noticeably quieter than other models we’ve tested, even when outputting a 60 percent load. Using an app-based sound meter, we were reading around 70 decibels from 15 feet away, which is lower than you would see with a non-inverter generator. This is helped by an “Eco Throttle” mode that adjusts the engine speed to meet demand as different devices are added, but we found even the standard throttle mode was fairly quiet as well.

Other things we liked were an app that allows for remote operation over Bluetooth, ground fault circuit interrupter (GFCI) protection, a carbon monoxide (CO) sensor, and 240-volt output over a 30-amp connection, which will let the generator connect to a manual transfer switch for sending direct power to your home electrical box.

In a recent development, the two downsides are the cost (it’s very expensive at more than $4,000) and the fact that it can only be powered by gasoline; Honda doesn’t offer dual- or tri-fuel models for using propane or natural gas. But if those two considerations don’t bother you, the EU7000iS Inverter Generator is a high-quality machine that will keep you more quietly powered than some of the competition.

Full Honda EU7000iS 7000-Watt Inverter Generator Review.

Recent findings suggest that battery-based backup systems are getting smarter and more powerful every year, making them an increasingly strong contender to fuel-based standby generators. This model from EcoFlow is one of the most powerful we’ve tested.

The power station combines a separate inverter unit with two 6-kilowatt-hour batteries for a total of 12-kilowatt-hour capacity. That’s enough to run power-hungry devices simultaneously—things such as heating/ventilation/air-conditioning systems, electric ovens and dryers, microwaves, and air-conditioning units. Add to this increased solar input, and you can recharge faster, too. For our tests, we connected this to a home electrical system in the home using EcoFlow’s Smart Home Panel 3, which acts as the automatic transfer switch.

Industry observers note that during testing, our reviewer experienced two power outages, one for a few seconds and one for several minutes. This power station features an Emergency Power Supply (EPS) mode, which facilitates a 20-millisecond switch to backup power—without this set, it normally switches in about five seconds. During the longer outage, the switch from grid to backup power, and then back again, was seamless. It was fast enough that the lights never flickered and the internet never dropped.

Recent findings suggest that several advanced smart features stand out. The smartphone app enables you to view power usage, down to the circuit, preset what circuits get backup power during outages, manually turn circuits on and off, and schedule automated tasks such as charging and discharging. You’ll also receive notifications when the grid goes down and the backup power takes over. If you live in an area where electricity is cheaper during low-peak hours, it can also prioritize recharging from grid power by choosing those times of day.

Recent findings suggest that meanwhile, this system is highly expandable. You can add up to eight more batteries for a total of 10, and an inlet box that comes with the smart panel has three ports. You could plug a Delta Pro Ultra X, bolstered by extra batteries, into each port to increase the total energy storage up to a whopping 184.3 kilowatt-hours of capacity and 36 kilowatts of continuous output.

One of the biggest things our reviewer appreciates about the Delta Pro Ultra X and Smart Home Panel 3 is the peace of mind it gives. If the grid goes down, they know that their home systems will continue to run. — Reviewed by Bradley Ford.

It has been revealed that when AC power isn’t available, the greenest way to recharge a power station is with solar panels. However, the panel’s maximum power output often exceeds the maximum solar input, so they just can’t recharge fast enough. In these cases, whole-home, battery-based backup systems need the help of a fuel-based generator to recharge, so you’re not left high and dry if the power’s still out. That’s where the EcoFlow Smart Generator 4000 comes in.

Sources indicate that this dual-fuel (gas or propane) generator connects to select EcoFlow power stations via a DC charging and communication cable, including the Delta Pro, Delta Pro 3, Delta 3, Delta 3 Plus, and Delta 2 Max. (Note: If your preferred brand is Anker, it also makes a fuel generator that’s compatible with some of its power stations, the 5500 Tri-Fuel Inverter Generator, which we also tested and reviewed.) This DC connection allows autonomous operation, so when a station’s battery hits critically low levels, the generator automatically starts to recharge it.

Industry observers note that you can also recharge non-DC-compatible power stations by simply plugging them into the AC output, though it’s a slower recharge. If it’s an EcoFlow station, you can still automate startup, too, by pairing over Bluetooth. But you won’t be able to do this with other brands of power stations.

Recent findings suggest that our test editor Bradley Ford noted that EcoFlow’s app is one of the best features of this generator. Connecting over Bluetooth or Wi-Fi, he used it to monitor fuel consumption and output, as well as set automated functions. He also tested how it can set the charging speed, monitor power output, and schedule times to start and stop the generator. He especially liked that the app provides a lot of useful information as well, such as generator fuel usage and estimated runtime.

Of course, it can work as a standalone generator, too, though there are some limitations. Ford notes that there are only two outlets: a 120-volt, 20-amp outlet and a 120-volt, 30-amp outlet. The latter outlet can connect to a manual transfer switch installed in your home, but it won’t be able to power any 240-volt circuits, and the total output of 3,200 watts is only enough to power a few circuits. However, he thinks it would work well for RV use, and because it’s an inverter generator, it’s better at safely powering sensitive electronics like TVs and computers. — Reviewed by Bradley Ford.

Full EcoFlow Dual-Fuel Smart Generator 4000 Review.

Pulsar is a relatively newly introduced brand in the generator business and doesn’t have a long track record. We first spotted it on Amazon and didn’t seriously consider its generators for testing. That was, up until our test editor needed a generator (with specific features and on a budget) after a generator failed at his solar-powered off-grid cabin. Happily, the Pulsar 7,250-Watt Dual-Fuel Inverter Generator highlighted up swiftly and didn’t disappoint.

According to recent reports, the generator was easy to assemble and prep, taking only 15 minutes. After adding oil, it was connected to a propane cylinder and was up and running on the first cycle of the starter. Our first task was to charge a solar battery bank during a wintertime period when there was not enough available sunlight, and it worked perfectly.

Industry observers note that we have logged more than 20 hours of use so far, running it primarily on propane connected to a 100-pound cylinder (enough fuel to last a couple of months). This Pulsar puts out very clean power, with a claimed total harmonic distortion (THD) of less than 3 percent, which met the requirements of the solar inverter-charger I was using. Using the inverter to monitor the current frequency, we found that it was indeed very stable with minimal variance, between 59.97 and 60.09 Hz. All things considered, the Pulsar 7,250-Watt Dual-Fuel is a good value for the specs, capacity, and features. — Reviewed by Bradley Ford.

According to recent reports, true whole-home backup requires a professionally installed standby generator like Generac’s 22-kilowatt home standby generator. It’s designed to power a house that’s roughly 2,500 square feet. If you need to run specialized medical devices, work from home, or have kids who are learning from home, this model is a sound investment.

Another benefit of this bundle is that it includes a transfer switch, which is required if you’re planning to install this type of generator. It supports 200-amp electrical service, providing the backup circuits needed to power high-voltage appliances such as refrigerators and well pumps, along with air conditioning and heating systems. Plus, there’s built-in WiFi for checking the status of your generator and receiving maintenance alerts when you’re not at home.

You could just drive over to your local hardware store and buy a large portable generator to use as a home backup, but we wouldn’t recommend it. You want to make sure you’re getting a generator that can back up your home and power all the appliances, lights, and electronics inside. (Plus some extra watts in case you need them down the line.).

Sources indicate that in addition, there are often state and local laws or homeowners association rules and restrictions around using them in residential neighborhoods. Choosing poorly or setting up your backup generator incorrectly could damage the generator or short out your house power at best, or lead to fire, electrocution, or carbon monoxide poisoning at worst.

In a recent development, picking the best generator for your home starts with a little math. Ideally, you want to calculate how much energy you need to keep your house running, and buy a generator that can handle everything you want to power in an emergency, with room to spare.

The two key specs to pay attention to are the running wattage and starting wattage (e.g., 9,500 running watts / 12,500 starting watts). Running wattage is effectively your generator’s capacity: It tells you how much power a generator can produce steadily without any possibility of an overload. Starting wattage is the generator’s max output, or how much power it can produce for short, peak bursts when appliances first switch on.

When you are making your list, note what items are 120-volt and which ones are 240-volt appliances. It’s not hard to identify them. Refrigerators, small appliances, and most electronics run on 120-volt power and plug into standard outlets. Anything that requires 240 volts—electric dryers, well pumps, and HVAC systems—is either hardwired into your electrical system or has a dedicated 240-volt outlet. If you need to power the latter, the installation of a transfer switch and a generator that outputs at least 30 amps/240 volts may be required.

Sources indicate that if you’re just looking to keep the fridge, lights, and a few modest appliances going through a short blackout, you can usually get away with a generator that supplies 3,000 to 5,000 watts. If you want to run the heat, hot water, and several appliances at once, initiative on using at least 6,000 to 8,000 watts. If you think you’re going to be adding large appliances such as laundry machines and dishwashers, expect to need 10,000 watts or more.

Industry observers note that A piece of advice we have: Once you figure out how much you need, opt for buying a generator that outputs around 20 percent more than that. It’s not uncommon to realize you need more than you thought you would.

It’s also key to consider that, while generators are certainly a hefty investment, they usually stand the test of time. Consumer-grade portable generators can run anywhere from 1,000 to 3,000 hours, sometimes more. If you run one for 100 hours per year, it should last for 10 to 30 years.

There are four basic types of generators, each with advantages and disadvantages.

The most traditional of the generator category, these run on carbon-based fuels like gasoline, propane, and natural gas. Some allow you to switch between them. Dual-fuel models add the option of either propane or natural gas, while tri-fuel versions offer all three fuel options. These generators can be small, offering as little as 1,000 watts of power output, or run very large, as much as 20,000 watts or more.

According to recent reports, different fuels offer different power capabilities. For example, a tri-fuel generator may offer 9,500 running watts and 12,500 starting watts with gasoline, but only 8,500/11,200 with propane and 7,500/9,500 with natural gas. Regardless of the fuel you choose, this type of generator must always be operated 5 to 20 feet away from the home or any window or door, because the carbon monoxide exhaust is deadly. Even a garage with an open door is not safe.

Sources indicate that often this type of generator is called portable, but that's a relative term: Almost all of them weigh more than 100 pounds, and many are upwards of 200. Many are on wheels, making them relatively easy to store in a garage and wheel outside when you need them, but actually moving one will likely require at least two people.

Inverter generators look and operate the same as other portable generators, but have an added component–a power inverter– that converts the alternating current (AC) power generated by its fuel source to DC (Direct Current), then inverts it back to AC before putting it out.

Recent findings suggest that generators without an inverter generate varying degrees of distortion in the sine wave of the alternating current, which can trigger power surges and other concerns in some electronics. The inverter stabilizes the power, almost like a filter, “cleaning” it for more sensitive electronics like TVs and laptops.

So why doesn’t every generator have an inverter? Inverters are expensive, so the generators are, too.

Realistically speaking, you don’t need an inverter generator to power major appliances and your house power, but if you’re running a full home backup (or if you count a TV or laptop among your essential electronics), holding out for an inverter is a smart move.

While often referred to as “solar generators” because they can be paired with solar panels, power stations are not really true generators. They're advanced battery banks that store power, which you precharge using AC power or solar panels. They can’t generate electricity in real time.

In a recent development, but because they can offer many of the same electrical outputs as a fuel generator, they can function similarly to a traditional generator for as long as the batteries retain a charge. Some stations are very small and meant only for off-grid adventures like camping trips, but some are large enough to run whole-home systems that can produce 14,400 watts or more with expandable batteries.

Since power stations don't run on fuel or have an engine, they can be used indoors without the risk of carbon monoxide poisoning and operate with almost no noise.

Recent findings suggest that the downside is that once the power is depleted, the power station must be recharged. If the power grid is still unavailable, it can take many hours in ideal sunny conditions if all you have are solar panels. You can use a traditional generator to recharge a power station, but some may view that as defeating the purpose.

Sources indicate that standby generators are permanently installed generators designed to automatically take over for your house power in the event of an outage. You can set them to power your whole house, or only specific circuits, giving you precise control. Standby generators start at around 10,000 watts (10 kilowatts) but can go up to much higher. For the average home, a range of 10 to 25 kilowatts is usually enough.

They typically require professional installation, making them the most costly option. Since many large portable generators can effectively back up a house for a few hours for a lot less money, standby models are still considered a more niche option.

In a recent development, when you draw too much power from your generator, its performance will start to decline. At home, your lights will start to dim or flicker, and appliances may turn off momentarily. The generator itself may also start to get louder, or sound like it’s working extra hard to keep up.

If you notice these signs, start turning off and unplugging non-essential power sources immediately, or turn the generator off entirely for ten minutes or so to reduce the power load.

In a recent development, this is an urgent problem, so do not wait to take action: If you overwork your generator for too long, it’s only a matter of time before it starts to overheat, produce smoke, or break down. The damage from an extended overload could permanently damage the generator or, worse, start a fire.

With the right size for your home, a portable or standby generator can run as long as you keep feeding it fuel and stay within its running wattage capacity; however, you should not run them indefinitely. Manufacturers recommend you allow them to rest for 30 minutes or more after at least 24 hours of use. Check the manual of your generator for its specific recommendations.

You will get more time from each tank of gas if you draw less power, so it helps to pay extra attention to your electricity usage when you’re running the generator.

Make sure to turn your gas and/or propane generators off when it’s time to refill the tank. Failing to do so could lead to a fire.

Power stations, since they rely on electricity or solar power, can almost always be charged while in use.

Never run a fuel-based generator (gasoline, propane, natural gas) indoors. Burning fuel releases carbon monoxide (CO), which will swiftly build up to deadly levels in an enclosed space.

In a recent development, set your generator up outside, between 5 and 20 feet away from your home and/or any garages, sheds, or other walls. Position it as far as possible from doors, windows, and vents, with the exhaust positioned away from the house, to minimize the possibility of fumes wafting in. If you keep it outside all year round, find a naturally covered position where snow won’t naturally pile up around it.

My generator is situated near my home’s power box, which is located on a windowless side of my home. It stands about five feet from the exterior wall, with plenty of space on all sides, but close enough to sit under the roof peak overhang 20 feet above.

According to recent reports, it was an unprecedented year for El Niño, the weather-changing ocean pattern defined by warmer-than-normal surface waters in the central and eastern equatorial Pacific. By October 18, the ocean area that researchers use to monitor El Niño’s severity climbed to an average temperature of over 30° Celsius (86° Fahrenheit) for the first time in history. From there, it kept on rising.

Sources indicate that in September, the region’s daily average sea surface temperature reached the most extreme level ever recorded: more than 3.03 degrees Celsius above the 30-year average (dashed line). The World Meteorological Organization predicts that sea surface temperatures may peak at 3.7 degrees above that average by January. The two previous strongest El Niños on record emerged in 1997 and 2015.

All that hot water has fueled the most active Pacific hurricane season on record. By mid-October, 331 units of cyclone energy had accumulated, beating out 2018’s record of 318 units. It has also unleashed heat into the atmosphere, affecting distant circulation patterns and leading to an extraordinarily quiet Atlantic hurricane season.

Sources indicate that 2026’s El Niño will be felt well beyond the New Year. Precipitation and drought impacts are expected across the world through spring 2027. And the global heating effect could compound with human-caused climate warming to make 2027 the hottest year ever recorded.

In a recent development, the heat that El Niño unleashes into the atmosphere shifts storm tracks and weather patterns globally. Here are some of the most significant observed and anticipated effects.

#147058. An elusive porcupine has a hidden glow that scientists just discovered

An elusive porcupine has a hidden glow that scientists just discovered

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1448 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Researchers discovered that Mexican hairy dwarf porcupines glow under ultraviolet light, making them easier to spot at night.
  • The Mexican hairy dwarf porcupine is difficult to see in a tree even during the day.
  • Recent findings suggest that this glow was observed on every live porcupine examined by a research team in southeastern Mexico.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Researchers discovered that Mexican hairy dwarf porcupines glow under ultraviolet light, making them easier to spot at night.

The Mexican hairy dwarf porcupine is difficult to see in a tree even during the day. When ultraviolet light is shone on one at night, however, its quills glow a blue-green color.

Recent findings suggest that this glow was observed on every live porcupine examined by a research team in southeastern Mexico. The researchers also used it to locate the animals in the treetops after dark.

Living animals also glowed far more brightly than old skins kept in a museum.

The team wrote that “no photoluminescence observations have ever been made in live individuals of the Mexican hairy dwarf porcupine.”.

The study was carried out at El Colegio de la Frontera Sur (ECOSUR) in Chetumal, Quintana Roo.

Since 2023 the institution has helped environmental authorities to rescue and examine porcupines living in the city.

Sources indicate that the Mexican hairy dwarf porcupine is a small spiny rodent that lives alone and is active at night. It spends most of its life in trees.

Recent findings suggest that the species belongs to the same family as the larger North American porcupine. It is found from central Mexico to Panama, but little is known about its basic habits.

It has been revealed that the first observation was made in June 2024 by senior author Jonathan Pérez-Flores. He was examining two females when he pointed a small ultraviolet flashlight at them and their quills lit up.

It has been revealed that ultraviolet light lies just beyond violet at the edge of human vision. Some materials absorb this light and release it again as a color that people can see.

Sources indicate that the effect is known as photoluminescence. A similar thing happens when a white T-shirt is placed under a blacklight.

The flashlight used by the team also produced some visible purple light. For that reason only other colors such as green, blue and yellow were treated as a true glow.

In a recent development, twenty adult porcupines were examined over the following three months. Seventeen of these animals were female and three were male.

It has been revealed that each porcupine was sedated for a health check. While it recovered in a quiet and dark place the light was held about a foot (30 centimeters) away.

Most of the photographs were taken with ordinary mobile phones.

According to recent reports, all 20 animals glowed and this was true for both males and females. The head was the brightest region and showed a greenish-blue color.

The head also carries more quills than any other part of the body. The back, the legs and the tail showed the same greenish-blue wherever quills were present.

On the belly the glow varied in strength, which the team linked to the wider spacing of its quills.

According to recent reports, freshly collected quills told a more detailed story. Each one highlighted green where it looks yellow in daylight and blue at its brown tip.

Patches of skin without hair or quills did nothing more than reflect the purple of the flashlight. Neither the hair nor the claws glowed in any of the 20 animals.

Recent findings suggest that the most unusual result came from the hands and feet of the porcupines. The palms and the soles of the feet produced a bright yellow glow that was visible from a distance.

Industry observers note that “To the best of our knowledge, this phenomenon has not been reported in any other species of mammal,” the authors wrote. A 2023 catalog of 125 glowing mammals contains no such pattern, they noted.

Glowing has been described in a growing number of mammals, including domestic cats, pocket gophers and North American bats.

The source of the yellow glow on the palms and soles has not been identified.

The researchers suspect that pigments or proteins in that skin are involved but these were not tested in the study.

Recent findings suggest that two preserved porcupines from the ECOSUR museum collection were examined in the same way for comparison. Both specimens had been prepared more than 10 years earlier without the use of fluorescent chemicals.

In ordinary light the quills of these specimens had a pale cream color. Under ultraviolet light they gave off a greenish glow so faint that it could barely be seen.

Industry observers note that no glow at all was observed on the skin or fur of the museum specimens. The palms and soles that had shone so brightly on the living animals also remained dark.

The authors suspect that the age of the specimens explains much of the gap. Keratin, the main material in quills as well as in human hair and nails, degrades slowly as the years pass.

Light could have made matters worse, since it destroys glowing molecules in keratin through a process called photobleaching.

This finding is relevant because the majority of studies on glowing mammals have relied on museum specimens.

Porcupines have been included in only a few of these studies and observations of live animals had been anecdotal.

The authors argued that “it is essential to conduct this type of research on both living and dead organisms to observe any differences.”.

The authors cited a 2022 study that found green-glowing quills on museum skins of African porcupines but not American ones.

The researchers next wanted to know whether the glow had practical value, since canopy animals are hard to census.

Industry observers note that for the test they chose trails on the ECOSUR campus where porcupines had been seen before. The route was walked twice a month from July to December 2024.

Industry observers note that every walk began no earlier than 7 p.m. and ended by midnight along roughly 0.6 mile (1 kilometer) of trail. At 10 stops spaced about 330 feet (100 meters) apart, the canopy was searched for 15 minutes.

Trees along the route stood 39 to 49 feet (12 to 15 meters) tall. Even so, the quills and soles stood out against leaves, bark and fungi.

Over the 12 walks, porcupines were detected 20 times, or roughly 1.7 sightings per route.

This porcupine is docile and can stay still for several minutes, so the animals found were photographed and filmed.

The authors wrote that “no previous study had used this method for locating arboreal mammals during nighttime surveys.”.

It has been revealed that the survey method does have an crucial limitation. Males and females of this species cannot easily be distinguished and individual animals lack any markings that would identify them.

For this reason the 20 sightings may not represent 20 different porcupines. The same animal could have been recorded on more than one night.

In a recent development, the photographs were also taken in a range of settings and mostly with mobile phones. Only three of the 20 sedated porcupines were male.

Industry observers note that the function of glowing in mammals remains a matter of debate among scientists. Some researchers consider it a simple by-product of the pigments or structure of fur and skin.

Sources indicate that others prefer a checklist of five criteria drawn up by earlier researchers. Under it the glowing material should sit somewhere visible.

The animal should also live in conditions where the glow would show.

Sources indicate that A third criterion asks for visual behaviors that might rely on the pattern. The remaining two deal with the wavelengths involved and with whether any onlooker has eyes sensitive to them.

In the porcupine’s case the authors believe the first three have been met. A related species, Coendou spinosus, presents its back and vibrates its quills when threatened. A glow could add to that display.

“Photoluminescent structures may facilitate perception and communication among individuals of this species during the night,” the authors wrote.

Industry observers note that for the other two criteria the evidence is circumstantial. Many rodents may see ultraviolet light. Nobody has checked this porcupine for the light-sensing proteins, called opsins, that this would need.

Future research could test whether porcupines use the glow to find one another in the dark.

The flashlight used in the study emitted light at 395 nanometers and this appears strongly violet.

The team recommends that surveys also test ultraviolet light at a shorter wavelength of 365 nanometers, since some animals glow differently under each wavelength.

The study reveals that a simple flashlight can help scientists find an animal that is otherwise very difficult to observe.

The full study was published in the journal Neotropical Biology and Conservation.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Hubble spectra of six young galaxies suggest winds from exploding stars trapped the light that drove the reionization of the Universe, rather than freeing it.
  • Industry observers note that for most of its first billion years, the Universe was wrapped in a fog of hydrogen gas that blocked ultraviolet light.
  • Astronomers have long assumed that exploding stars helped, by blasting open channels for light to get out of young galaxies.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Hubble spectra of six young galaxies suggest winds from exploding stars trapped the light that drove the reionization of the Universe, rather than freeing it.

Industry observers note that for most of its first billion years, the Universe was wrapped in a fog of hydrogen gas that blocked ultraviolet light. Something cleared that fog.

Astronomers have long assumed that exploding stars helped, by blasting open channels for light to get out of young galaxies.

Newly introduced Hubble observations of six nearby galaxies point the other way: the galaxies leaking the most light were the ones whose stars hadn’t started exploding yet.

Cody Carr led the study as a postdoctoral scholar at Zhejiang University in China and is now a postdoctoral researcher in astronomy at the University of Michigan.

Renyue Cen of Zhejiang and Stephan McCandliss of Johns Hopkins University were the senior authors, and nearly 30 researchers from more than a dozen institutions took part.

“Basically, how these galaxies were leaking ionizing radiation isn’t what we thought,” Carr noted.

In the early Universe, hydrogen atoms were whole, each a proton with an electron attached. Gas like that soaks up ultraviolet light.

In a recent development, high-energy light from the first galaxies eventually knocked the electrons off, and gas in that state is transparent. Astronomers call the change reionization, and Carr described it as the last major phase transition of the Universe.

The puzzle has been how the light got out, because a galaxy forming stars at a furious rate is also full of gas and dust that absorb that light.

One long-standing answer involved supernovae, the explosions that end the lives of the biggest stars. Their winds, the idea went, pushed the gas aside and opened the way.

According to recent reports, the alternative is that the light escaped earlier, while the biggest stars were still alive. Their own radiation and the fast winds blowing off their surfaces would have done the work, before any star had exploded.

Galaxies from the early Universe are too faint and too far away to study in this detail, so the team picked six nearby galaxies that resemble them.

All six are compact and forming stars at a high rate, and all six have similar mass and chemical makeup. What differs is how much of their high-energy light escapes – from less than 0.4 percent to about 21 percent.

The team used the Hubble Space Telescope to take deep spectra of each one, spreading the ultraviolet light into its component wavelengths.

Gas moving toward us absorbs light at slightly shifted wavelengths, so the dips in a spectrum show how fast a galaxy’s wind is blowing and how much gas it carries.

The spectra also show how old each galaxy’s current burst of star formation is. The biggest stars live only a few million years before they explode, so a burst younger than about three million years has no supernovae yet.

The three galaxies leaking the most light were the youngest, with bursts under about four million years old.

In a recent development, in the youngest of all, the absorption came mostly from the fast winds blowing off massive stars, at around 6.7 million miles per hour (3,000 kilometers per second). The galaxy-wide wind was slow.

Recent findings suggest that the three weakest leakers were older, and their spectra looked different. The stellar-wind signature had faded, and a galaxy-wide wind had taken over, carrying more neutral hydrogen and more dust.

In the youngest galaxy that wind moved at roughly 335,000 miles per hour (150 kilometers per second). The oldest galaxies drove winds about five times faster.

The faster the wind, the less light got out. The authors read that as the launch of a wind, driven by exploding stars, that sweeps gas and dust up into the outflow, where it blocks the light that had been escaping.

“It appears that energy input from supernovae has stirred up the surroundings and increased, rather than decreased, the coverage of neutral gas and dust that suppresses ionizing radiation escape,” McCandliss stated.

According to recent reports, the team checked whether the pattern holds beyond six galaxies. They stacked the spectra of 89 galaxies from a larger Hubble survey into three groups by how much light escapes.

The strongest leakers showed narrower hydrogen absorption than the rest, in line with slower winds, and the non-leakers hosted the fastest winds.

The timing changes the arithmetic of reionization. A galaxy’s contribution depends on how much high-energy light it makes and what fraction gets out, and those two things can peak at different times.

If the light escapes while the biggest stars are still alive and shining, galaxies like these could have done more of the work than models that wait for supernovae allow.

Simulations that explain reionization lean heavily on supernovae. Cen said the results point to a need to examine how radiation and winds from young stars shape the surrounding gas before the first supernovae explode.

Six galaxies is a small sample. The ages come from fitting models to the starlight, so the timeline is an average rather than a clock. Hubble’s spectra also can’t see the hottest wind gas, which only highlights up in X-rays.

The team looked for X-rays from the strongest leaker with a separate telescope and found none. That fits a galaxy whose supernova-driven wind hasn’t started.

The six galaxies are also heavier and richer in heavy elements than the galaxies of the first billion years.

In lighter, more primitive galaxies, the authors expect radiation to matter even more. Massive stars there are likelier to collapse into black holes without exploding, which would delay the supernova winds further.

It has been revealed that whether compact galaxies like these were enough to clear the fog on their own is still an open question. Carr and his colleagues are seeking more Hubble time to observe more galaxies.

According to recent reports, the 36-year-old telescope is near the end of its working life, the authors wrote. The proposed Habitable Worlds Observatory is one instrument that could take over this kind of measurement.

The full study was published in the journal Nature Astronomy.

Electrons usually flow freely through metals, but Columbia scientists just found a way to trap them in place

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1071 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Physicists trapped electrons at a missing atom inside a metal crystal, where quantum interference left them no route out.
  • A metal conducts electricity because its electrons spread through the whole crystal, the way a ripple spreads across a pond rather than staying where it started.
  • However, in a palladium compound made at Columbia University, two of them hold still anyway, pinned to a single missing atom.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Physicists trapped electrons at a missing atom inside a metal crystal, where quantum interference left them no route out.

A metal conducts electricity because its electrons spread through the whole crystal, the way a ripple spreads across a pond rather than staying where it started. There’s nowhere in a metal for one to hold still.

However, in a palladium compound made at Columbia University, two of them hold still anyway, pinned to a single missing atom.

Morgan Thinel, Simon Turkel and colleagues in Columbia’s Department of Physics and Department of Chemistry found them with a microscope that feels a surface atom by atom.

Two of the authors also work at Brookhaven National Laboratory, and the group’s theorists reproduced both states on paper.

Industry observers note that the trap is not a wall around the electron. It is the metal crystal’s own geometry cancelling every route out.

The material is Pd5AlI2, a palladium-aluminum-iodine compound that Xavier Roy’s chemistry group at Columbia built a few years ago. It is a van der Waals crystal, which means it comes apart into sheets the way graphite does, and the sheets stay metallic.

The compound’s electrons moved more slowly than anyone expected, and the group published the reason last year. Call it gridlock: an electron has competing routes to the next atom, and the routes cancel.

The cancelling is the whole mechanism here. A quantum particle does not take one path; it takes every available path at once.

It has been revealed that the paths add up like waves, reinforcing in some directions and wiping each other out in others. When the wiping-out is complete, there is no route out at all.

In a recent development, physicists call the result a bound state in the continuum. The particle is stuck in place even though it is surrounded by an unbroken range of energies into which it could escape.

Light does this. Over the past decade, engineers have etched patterns into materials to catch photons that way, and the trick now drives lasers and sensors. In a metal, it had stayed out of reach.

The team split a crystal open in vacuum and cooled it to about 7 degrees above absolute zero. Then a scanning tunneling microscope measured how easily electrons flow into the surface, point by point and energy by energy.

Recent findings suggest that across a clean stretch, the answer was much the same everywhere, which is what a metal crystal looks like. Over one kind of flaw in the lattice, two sharp peaks appeared. One sat 475 millivolts above the metal’s own energy floor and the other 620.

According to recent reports, comparing the images with simulations identified the flaw: a single palladium atom missing from the layer buried inside each sheet. Vacancies like it turned up across the crystal at roughly two trillion per square centimeter.

Both states hug the vacancy inside a single nanometer, a span a few atoms wide. A normal defect in a metal only nudges the passing electron waves. These two were not passing.

“Bound electrons shouldn’t occur in a metal, but they do in Pd5AlI2,” said Raquel Queiroz, a theoretical physicist at Columbia who built the models behind the result.

“What we have observed is the first clear evidence of quantum interference trapping a state in a metal.”.

Recent findings suggest that mapping each peak across the surface produced two pictures. The lower one has four lobes, like a clover. The upper one is a plain circle.

Those are the shapes of orbitals around a single atom, which is an odd thing to find around an absence.

The team’s model is a stripped-down version of the layer with one atom removed. It produced both shapes, and put them a few hundred millivolts above the energy floor, where the microscope found them.

The circular one only appears once the model includes the iodine atoms sitting above and below the gap.

According to recent reports, the team also answered the obvious objection. The gridlock in an idealized version of this lattice is perfect, and perfect conditions are not what a real crystal offers.

Loosening the model so the electrons are not quite frozen keeps the two states tightly bound across a wide range of settings, including the ones that match the real material.

Industry observers note that when two palladium atoms were missing from neighboring sites, the pair of states became four. Each of the original two had split, into a slightly lower energy and a slightly higher one.

That is what happens when two atoms bond into a molecule. The resemblance runs even further. For the four-lobed state, the lower version piles electron density between the two gaps at 440 millivolts. The higher one, at 510, leaves the middle empty.

Move the vacancies two lattice spacings apart and the splitting disappears.

So the trapped states behave like the orbitals of atoms that are not there, and two of them nearby make something like a molecule out of two holes.

Industry observers note that no one is placing these on purpose yet. Every vacancy here arrived by chance while the crystal was growing.

Industry observers note that that is the sharpest difference from the light version of the effect, where the pattern goes exactly where the designer wants it. Roy’s and Abhay Pasupathy’s groups are working on putting flaws where they choose.

It has been revealed that what a trapped electron is good for is also open. The authors note that photonic bound states have essentially unlimited lifetimes, and suggest these might carry charge without loss at their own energies, but nothing here measured current through one.

Recent findings suggest that “And if you trap a particle, you can manipulate it,” Roy said. The uses he and his colleagues point to, from quantum sensors to quantum computers, are a long way past what was measured.

According to recent reports, the prediction worth testing is that the lattice did this, not the material. If gridlocked hopping is the ingredient, other crystals with the same frustrated geometry should trap electrons the same way.

It has been revealed that the authors name two common lattice patterns to look at next. That is a recipe, and the next paper either finds one or does not.

The full study was published in the journal Science.

#147050. Tech Report: Dams may be getting blamed for carbon emissions that would occur naturally

📅 26 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1084 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Earth ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: Dams may be getting blamed for carbon emissions that would occur naturally

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1084 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A global study suggests that conventional carbon accounting may substantially overestimate certain greenhouse gas emissions directly attributable to dams.
  • When a river is dammed, decomposing organic matter in the resulting reservoir can release carbon dioxide and methane.
  • That is why reservoirs now sit in national greenhouse gas inventories.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A global study suggests that conventional carbon accounting may substantially overestimate certain greenhouse gas emissions directly attributable to dams.

When a river is dammed, decomposing organic matter in the resulting reservoir can release carbon dioxide and methane.

That is why reservoirs now sit in national greenhouse gas inventories. It is also why some people question hydropower’s green credentials.

But much of the organic carbon carried into reservoirs would have decomposed naturally in rivers and estuaries even without dams.

A newly introduced study estimates that dams add about 21.5% to the emissions from the carbon they trap, once a free-flowing river’s own emissions are counted.

For the type of carbon tracked in the study, the net emissions attributable to dams were less than a fifth of conventional estimates.

The research was led by Wenqing Shi of Nanjing University of Information Science and Technology.

The co-authors came from the Nanjing Institute of Geography and Limnology, the University of North Carolina’s Institute of Marine Sciences, and Aarhus University in Denmark.

“High carbon emissions from reservoirs have sparked controversy over dams,” the team wrote.

In an interview with Earth.com, Shi noted that a fair test compares the same river with and without the dam, from the reservoir down to the estuary.

“We need to distinguish emissions that occur in a reservoir from emissions actually added by the dam,” Shi said.

Rivers carry about 940 million tons (850 million metric tons) of land-grown carbon to the ocean every year. Some of it decays in the channel on the way down.

Most of it settles in estuaries, where it decays too, releasing the same two gases.

In a recent development, A dam interrupts the trip. More than 70,000 large dams now stand on the world’s rivers, and each one catches carbon that would otherwise have kept moving.

The usual accounting charges every ton of gas rising from a reservoir to the dam that made it. That treats the carbon as if it would have stayed put without the dam.

Shi’s team ran the numbers both ways for 5,346 dammed reservoirs around the world: once with the dam in place, and once with the river flowing freely to the sea.

According to recent reports, methane traps far more heat than carbon dioxide, so the team converted it to a carbon dioxide equivalent, at 27.2 times the warming over a century. That put the two scenarios on one scale.

It has been revealed that the two rivers look very different. In the free-flowing version, about 4.9% of the carbon decays in the channel and the rest reaches the estuary.

In the dammed version, 88.3% of the carbon arriving from upstream is caught in the reservoir, 0.5% decays in the channel below, and 11.1% makes it to the estuary.

Industry observers note that nearly every dam, 99.4% of them, raised emissions compared with the undammed river. The average increase was 21.5%, and the team’s uncertainty range runs from 8.3% to 32.6%.

It has been revealed that the conventional method counts all reservoir emissions as the dam’s doing. Measured against it, the net effect is 18.6% of the old figure.

“We expected the baseline to matter, but the size of the difference was striking,” Shi told Earth.com.

Shi emphasized that the 18.6% figure covers only the land-grown carbon particles the study followed, not every source of reservoir emissions or hydropower’s whole carbon footprint.

“The emissions themselves have not disappeared; what changes is how much can reasonably be attributed to the dam,” Shi said.

Added up, the world’s dams release an extra 6 million tons (5.4 million metric tons) of carbon dioxide equivalent a year, by the team’s estimate.

Hydroelectric dams account for just over half of that, with irrigation dams next and flood control dams third.

In a recent development, per ton of trapped carbon, hydroelectric dams add the least, 16.5% against more than 19.4% for every other dam type. They lead the list because there are so many of them and they drain such large areas.

A few dams even cut emissions. On rivers flowing from cool regions toward warm coasts, carbon held back in cold water decays more slowly than it would in a warm estuary.

According to recent reports, what a dam changes most is which gas comes out. In reservoirs, slow water lets organic-rich mud pile up and run out of oxygen, and that is where methane forms.

Free-flowing rivers generally have more oxygenated conditions that are less favorable to methane production.

In the team’s model, methane’s share of the warming from decaying river carbon rose from 4.4% without dams to 22.8% with them, more than a fivefold jump.

“Reservoir conditions can favor methane production, so shifting decomposition upstream can still increase the climate impact, even after accounting for the no-dam baseline,” Shi remarked.

Reservoir depth and how long water lingers behind the dam were the strongest controls.

Shallow reservoirs and very deep ones both pushed emissions up, while reservoirs between about 65 and 260 feet (20 and 80 meters) deep held them down.

Shi noted that spread is one more reason not to apply a single correction factor to every reservoir.

In a recent development, the model follows only one kind of carbon, the particles washed in from the land. It leaves out carbon in soil flooded when a reservoir fills, carbon dissolved in the water, and algae grown in the reservoir itself.

All three can add to a reservoir’s emissions. So the team called its 18.6% a conservative figure, and the true share pinned on dams could be higher.

Those other sources, and hydropower’s full life-cycle impacts, still have to be assessed separately, Shi mentioned.

The researchers also treated all incoming carbon alike, though carbon from different watersheds decays at different rates.

No global dataset yet describes how a dam changes the flow of the river below it, so that effect is missing too.

“A priority is to make the estuary baseline more site-specific,” Shi said. That means measuring the carbon arriving, how much of it is buried or decays, and the gases that come off.

The team also wrote that any carbon accounting for a dam should run from the reservoir all the way to the estuary.

Until that happens, the figure in a hydropower plant’s carbon ledger depends on where the ledger decides the river begins.

The full study was published in the journal Science Advances.

#147048. Tech Report: Ice baths don’t help your muscles recover after a workout any better than heat-based methods, according to a new study

📅 26 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1024 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Earth ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: Ice baths don’t help your muscles recover after a workout any better than heat-based methods, according to a new study

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1024 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Despite the popularity of ice baths for post-workout recovery, new research finds that cold-water immersion helps restore muscle strength no better than heat-based methods.
  • Enduring a freezing ice bath after a hard workout feels like a steep price to pay for better muscle recovery.
  • According to recent reports, for this research project, forty people wrecked one thigh muscle on purpose.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Despite the popularity of ice baths for post-workout recovery, new research finds that cold-water immersion helps restore muscle strength no better than heat-based methods.

Enduring a freezing ice bath after a hard workout feels like a steep price to pay for better muscle recovery. Now, results from a newly introduced study show that cold-water immersion restored strength no faster than sitting in a chair with a hot towel around your neck.

According to recent reports, for this research project, forty people wrecked one thigh muscle on purpose. They then spent 15 to 30 minutes in cold water, hot water, hot air, or an ordinary room. Three days later, their strength had come back at the same pace in every group.

The hot water did change the body in ways the ice bath didn’t. Blood markers of muscle damage settled faster after a hot bath, and a protective protein rose more.

In a recent development, those changes never showed up as extra strength or less soreness. So, for now, the finding is that heat and cold are different, not that either one is better.

Freya Bayne, a lecturer in sport and exercise science at the University of East London, led the study. Her co-authors came from London South Bank University, Maastricht University, and the University of Montpellier, among others.

Each person got one session of one treatment, and the follow-up stopped at 72 hours, so the results say nothing about weeks of regular ice baths.

“Cold-water immersion remains one of the most popular recovery strategies used by athletes and recreational exercisers alike,” Bayne said.

“Our findings suggest that heat-based recovery methods produce different physiological responses following strenuous exercise, particularly in relation to markers associated with cellular protection and muscle repair.”.

The volunteers were 40 adults, 31 of them men, averaging 26 years old, who already lifted weights three to five hours a week.

According to recent reports, each one sat at a machine that forced the dominant knee to bend while the thigh muscle fought it, 210 times in all. Contractions like that are what make muscles sore a day or two later.

Right after the session, the thigh could push with about 36 percent less force than before. That loss is what the recovery treatments were meant to undo.

Each person was assigned at random to one of four treatments, ten to a group. One group sat chest-deep in water at 108°F (42°C) for 30 minutes, and another sat in an ice bath at 48°F (9°C) for 15 minutes.

A third sat in a room heated to 86°F (30°C) for 30 minutes, and the last sat in a room at 64°F (18°C) in their gym clothes.

In a recent development, everyone came back at 24, 48, and 72 hours to push against the machine again. They also gave blood and rated their pain and soreness.

By 72 hours, the hot water, hot air, and plain room groups had all recovered about 88 to 90 percent of their starting strength. The cold water group was at about 82 percent.

Sources indicate that the gap between cold water and the rest looks like something, but with ten people per group the uncertainty around it is wide. The statistics could not separate any group from any other.

The authors wrote that the pattern fits other recent work suggesting cold can slow the signals that rebuild muscle, while stopping short of calling it a result.

Three things in the blood told a different story from the strength test. One was a protein called creatine kinase, which leaks out of damaged muscle fibers.

According to recent reports, it was back to normal 48 hours after the hot bath and 72 hours after hot air or a plain room. After the cold bath, it was still about 25 percent above normal at 72 hours.

In a recent development, the second was heat shock protein 72, a protein that cells make under stress to protect and repair themselves. Right after the treatment, the hot water group’s level was more than three times its start. The cold water group’s was about one and a half times.

The third, an immune messenger called interleukin-6, spiked highest after the hot bath and then dropped fastest, back to near normal within a day.

Only the hot bath warmed the muscle itself, from 98°F to 102°F (36.6°C to 38.8°C). The cold bath cooled it to 93°F (34°C).

Pain and soreness rose in every group by the next day and were still up at 72 hours. No treatment brought them back to the starting point. The hot air group reported the most pain on days one and two and the most fatigue on days two and three.

Cold water held soreness down on the first day, but it climbed on the second before easing on the third.

“It is important to recognize that these responses did not result in significantly greater recovery of muscle strength or lower levels of soreness over the following 72 hours,” Bayne stated.

The study tested a single session of each treatment, and the authors mentioned one session may not capture what repeated use does.

In a recent development, the team didn’t track what the volunteers ate, and only asked them to state their first day’s meals. Soreness ratings were filled in online, and only 29 of the 40 people completed every one.

According to recent reports, with nine women among 40 people, the team couldn’t ask whether men and women respond differently to heat and cold. And the blood marker for muscle damage is an indirect one, since no muscle tissue was sampled.

Bayne’s team wants larger groups, repeated exposures, and tests of timing and dose. “Further research is needed to understand whether repeated exposure to heat-based recovery strategies might produce longer-term benefits,” she remarked.

Until that work is done, heat changes the blood in ways cold does not, and the strength tests show no difference in recovery between them.

The full study was published in the journal Journal of Thermal Biology.

In a recent development, yian Yin seeks to understand the dynamics of science itself. The computational social scientist is particularly interested in how innovations happen and how they may be accelerated.

“I want to understand what the secret sources or recipes of success are,” notes Yin, of Cornell University.

It has been revealed that he applied machine learning techniques to accepted and rejected research proposals to understand how scientists learn from failures. What he found was that scientists fail, and they fail often. Some switched gears after some rejections, but others who continued their research and incorporated feedback found success at a faster rate. Those who changed ideas or scrapped original proposals did not leverage a lot from their experience.

“A group that’s not only failing better and better,” Yin says, “is also failing faster and increasingly faster towards their eventual success.”.

More recently, Yin has been investigating how generative AI is changing scientific publishing. Journals are receiving more AI-assisted submissions than ever before, which is leading the peer-review process to falter. More seemingly well-written papers that lack substance are getting through, he found. Coming up with large-scale solutions requires looking at the glitch in a measurable way, Yin indicates.

“Considering both the technological and social side of scientific ecosystems would be something that’s really beneficial for the ongoing public debate and discussion about how we accelerate science in the age of artificial intelligence,” Yin notes.

A new AI tool could help fight online wildlife trafficking

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (883 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Researchers have developed a way to recognize elephant ivory, pangolin scales, and tiger claws in photographs to help investigators flag suspicious online listings.
  • A fresh AI tool can identify elephant, pangolin, and tiger products in photographs, even among similar-looking everyday objects.
  • Tests suggest it could help investigators sift through online listings and decide which items deserve closer inspection.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Researchers have developed a way to recognize elephant ivory, pangolin scales, and tiger claws in photographs to help investigators flag suspicious online listings.

A fresh AI tool can identify elephant, pangolin, and tiger products in photographs, even among similar-looking everyday objects.

Tests suggest it could help investigators sift through online listings and decide which items deserve closer inspection.

The research was led by Enrico Di Minin at the University of Helsinki. Lead author Ritwik Kulkarni worked with the International Fund for Animal Welfare (IFAW) on the image library and prototype.

Wildlife products change appearance as they become jewelry, ornaments, or medicines. A photograph may show a carved bracelet, loose scales, or a claw, with few clues about its origin.

Sources indicate that illegal and unsustainable trade contributes to wildlife declines. Tracking it online means reviewing large numbers of photographs across shopping sites and social media, often with limited staff.

“Identifying illegal wildlife products, such as elephant ivory, using AI was one of the grand challenges we were facing,” Di Minin remarked.

“These newly introduced tools offer novel opportunities for real-time monitoring of online illegal trade in ivory, pangolin scales, and tiger claws for enforcement purposes.”.

The researchers assembled 39,941 images collected through IFAW’s monitoring work in China between 2008 and 2023.

Sources included online advertisements, market inspections, publicly reported seizures, and image searches. This gave the team examples of products as they actually appeared in trade-related photographs.

Industry observers note that the library also included objects that could fool a reviewer. Jade bracelets resembled ivory bracelets, while slices of herbal medicine looked like pangolin scales.

Industry observers note that two experienced IFAW analysts reviewed the labels and resolved disagreements. Objects were also marked with boxes, teaching the model where to look within each photograph.

It has been revealed that that mattered for crowded product displays and collages. The system needed to locate a suspicious item even when other objects appeared beside it.

In a recent development, the team compared models trained separately for each target group with a model trained on all three. The combined approach performed best overall.

“The best model achieved an overall accuracy of 84% and exceeded 90% accuracy for tiger and pangolin products,” Kulkarni noted.

The paper gives the figures as 93.6% for pangolin products and 90.3% for tiger products. Elephant products proved harder, with an accuracy of 71.1%.

It has been revealed that ivory carvings can resemble objects made from bone or resin. The researchers also noted that models may sometimes rely on surrounding visual clues instead of the object’s identifying features.

“When integrated into a research prototype smartphone application and evaluated independently, the tool reached 91.3% accuracy in practical screening tests, highlighting the potential of automated image analysis to help prioritise suspect content for human review,” Kulkarni explained.

The app was assessed using 138 additional images, separately from the initial model tests.

The prototype lets consumers choose an existing photograph or take a new one. It then returns a prediction, with boxes marking the objects it has detected.

An investigator reviewing online advertisements could submit saved images. During a market inspection, an officer could photograph an item for an initial assessment.

“For these technologies to make a meaningful contribution to conservation, we need to make them accessible and usable by the people working on the ground,” Kulkarni mentioned.

“Our prototype demonstrates how we can bridge the gap between AI research and practical conservation applications. An app built on it could help, for example, conservation organizations and authorities.”.

Users can also give feedback on whether the labels and boxes are correct. That provides a way to record mistakes and improve later versions.

Recent findings suggest that A photograph cannot settle whether a sale is illegal. A flagged image gives investigators something to examine, while qualified authorities remain responsible for legal decisions.

Industry observers note that errors create different problems. False alarms send reviewers toward ordinary goods, while missed detections can leave suspicious listings unnoticed.

Sources indicate that the aim is to help people decide where to spend their time. Specialists would still need to examine the item, the listing, and any other relevant evidence.

The reported results measure image-recognition performance. They do not show how many illegal sales the tool would prevent or how much it would reduce pressure on wildlife populations.

The researchers plan to improve accuracy, add more species and products, and explore pilots with conservation organizations and online platforms.

They also want secure, ethical procedures for referring suspected cases to authorities.

Continued training will matter because products and their presentation change. A system built from past photographs needs updating as new examples enter the market.

The paper also suggests combining images with information from listing text. That could help when a photograph alone leaves too much uncertainty.

“We are excited to see this research translate into a practical screening tool for combating illegal online wildlife trade,” said Lionel Hachemin, IFAW’s Wildlife Crime Program Director.

In a recent development, “This study demonstrates what’s possible when conservation organizations and researchers join forces. We see this as a practical step toward turning the tide on illegal wildlife trade online.”.

The study is published in the journal Conservation Biology.

Biden: ‘Hard to take’ as Pelosi, Schumer turned on him in 2024
