💡 Key Takeaways
  • President Joe Biden, Speaker Nancy Pelosi, and Senate Majority Leader Charles Schumer, D-N.Y., arrive for The CHIPS and Science Act of 2022 bill signing at the White House, on Aug.
  • Industry observers note that in conversations with Democratic strategists in recent months, I heard a strikingly similar sentiment when the topic turned to Joe Biden’s forthcoming memoir.
  • Spoiler alert: Biden offers only a full-throated defense of his decision to seek reelection in 2024, and expresses deep disappointment over what he casts as a disloyal pressure campaign orchestrated by party leaders to force him out of the presidential race despite what he cites as his successes in the office.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

President Joe Biden, Speaker Nancy Pelosi, and Senate Majority Leader Charles Schumer, D-N.Y., arrive for The CHIPS and Science Act of 2022 bill signing at the White House, on Aug. 9, 2022. In his new memoir, Biden mentioned he was disappointed when Pelosi and Schumer urged him to drop out of the presidential race in 2024. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

Industry observers note that in conversations with Democratic strategists in recent months, I heard a strikingly similar sentiment when the topic turned to Joe Biden’s forthcoming memoir. The consensus view, even among some who’d worked for the former president, was that if he did anything other than accept some responsibility for his role in Donald Trump’s return to the White House, they didn’t have much appetite to hear what he had to say about anything else.

Spoiler alert: Biden offers only a full-throated defense of his decision to seek reelection in 2024, and expresses deep disappointment over what he casts as a disloyal pressure campaign orchestrated by party leaders to force him out of the presidential race despite what he cites as his successes in the office.

But while his perspective on the climactic moment of his political career will be the most scrutinized portion of Biden’s new book, “Promise Me, America” seems primarily intended to offer the former president a platform he has otherwise not had since leaving office: to catalog what he sees as his historic achievements and offer his perspective on how he wrestled with the major issues of our time.

Recent findings suggest that it’s often stated that the only thing better than being president is being a former president. That has hardly been the case for Biden in the nearly 22 months since he left the White House, especially as he’s endured what his son Hunter has described as “debilitating” physical pain following a cancer diagnosis last March.

But where “Thanks, Obama” became a popular mantra nearly a decade ago for Democrats seeking to defend and celebrate the 44th president’s record in contrast with the first Trump administration, no such widespread nostalgia has emerged around Biden, as the party is loath to revisit the trauma of the summer of 2024.

Recent findings suggest that the sheer length of his new book — more than 400 pages — seems an implicit acknowledgment that presenting a positive portrait of Biden’s single term in office is largely to be a solitary effort. Over 15 chapters, Biden offers sometimes mechanical descriptions of specific policies and their impact, but also new details of the sausage-making required to pass major initiatives like the Inflation Reduction Act. That legislation, he writes, was revived thanks in part to an Italian dinner hosted by Commerce Secretary Gina Raimondo to make peace between West Virginia Sen. Joe Manchin III and White House Chief of Staff Ron Klain.

Biden writes in sweeping terms about other accomplishments like responding to the COVID-19 crisis he inherited, calling his administration’s work “one of the most monumental achievements in public health history.” He repeatedly defends his frequent efforts to warn Americans about the need to safeguard our democracy even as critics in the press and his own party suggested he focus more on economic concerns.

Supporting Ukraine in its war against Russia gets the most extensive treatment of any single concern in the book, including a detailed account of Biden’s clandestine trip to Kyiv in February 2023. And the former Senate Foreign Relations Committee chairman takes great effort to delve into the complexity of the U.S.-China relationship and his relationship with President Xi Jinping, while asserting that Taiwan “will likely be the most important foreign policy challenge in the world over the next generation.”.

According to recent reports, recurring throughout the book are expressions of optimism that under his administration, Washington was beginning to work again like it was supposed to, that America’s global leadership was being restored through its alliances, and that he was tackling problems that previous presidents had sidestepped. And in offering this comprehensive presentation of his record, Biden also offers his primary rationale for running again.

“We had accomplished so much —  I wanted to finish the job. And yes: I believed I was the best person to do it,” he claims. “I was the only person who had ever beaten Donald Trump. And I felt I was the best person to do it again.”.

In a recent development, one of Biden’s top advisers put it to me a different way in the months leading up to his decision to seek another term. “He has been running for president for 50 years. And the idea that he would actually be president and stop running for president is almost laughably preposterous.”.

The biggest question, of course, was his age, something Biden, who was 81 when he dropped out of the race, asserts he gave serious consideration.

Industry observers note that “I knew better than anyone how old I was. I knew what I was —  and wasn’t —  capable of doing. I carefully monitored how I was meeting the demands of the job. And there is not a single example of me failing to handle my responsibilities,” he writes.

The June 27 debate, of course, created a very different perception, as Biden acknowledges that his flubbed comment that “we finally beat Medicare” was to become “Exhibit A that I was too old to do the job.” But he tries to argue it was no different than the poor showings of previous incumbent presidents, including President Barack Obama, in their first debates.

Sources indicate that “The difference was that every other president was given the chance to redeem themselves in a second debate. As it turned out, that chance would not be available to me,” Biden writes.

He argues the response he was seeing from voters at his public events after the debate didn’t justify the panicked response of elected Democrats in Washington, and that public polling highlighted only minor slippage after the debate, until a steady drumbeat of elected Democrats publicly began calling for him to step aside.

In a recent development, describing separate visits from former Speaker Nancy Pelosi, D-Calif., and then-Senate Majority Leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y., personally urging him to step aside, he says there was a “yawning gap between what I was seeing with Democratic voters and what I was hearing from the Democratic leadership in Washington.”.

“I have to admit it was personally hard to take so many old friends turning on me,” Biden says. “I told Schumer he had a lot of gumption (I may have noted it differently at the time), coming to my home and telling me to get out of the race. Loyalty matters to me. If I give you my word, I stick with you. If I say I’m with you, I’m with you to the end.”.

At one point, Biden seems to reflect some resentment that some of the Democrats who would ultimately call on him to drop out of the race had themselves been too afraid to challenge him in the first place, saying: “Anyone who was scared off from running has no business being president.” While there was a constant narrative about the weakness of his candidacy, Biden acknowledges, the lack of a serious challenger was in fact a sign of his strength.

Recent findings suggest that “I had it on good authority that several big names in Democratic politics had looked at running. They held meetings and took polls and talked to donors and to potential staff. If they thought I was weak or vulnerable, they would have taken their shot. But they didn’t,” he writes.

Biden’s defiant tone, and his insistence that the lack of party unity was a greater threat to his continued candidacy than his own performance, may be dismissed by Democrats who don’t want to revisit this difficult chapter. But as Schumer and other Democratic leaders are now facing their own internal challenges, “Promise Me, America” may also serve as a cautionary note for an ambitious crop of potential candidates hoping to reclaim the presidency in 2028.

  • Industry observers note that gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review.
  • Power stations (i.e., solar generators) have become increasingly popular because they are easy to run, cost less over time than gas generators, and offer eco-friendly, emission-free operation, especially when paired with a solar panel.
  • Unlike fuel-based generators, solar generators can’t create electricity in real time.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Power stations (i.e., solar generators) have become increasingly popular because they are easy to run, cost less over time than gas generators, and offer eco-friendly, emission-free operation, especially when paired with a solar panel. Some are small and compact, ideal for off-grid adventures, while larger ones are able to back up critical home circuits during a blackout.

Unlike fuel-based generators, solar generators can’t create electricity in real time. They’re giant battery packs, not true generators, and need to be recharged using alternating current (AC) power or solar panels, the latter of which often takes many hours in ideally sunny conditions.

In a recent development, despite those distinctions compared to portable generators, there’s nothing more convenient than a power station for charging or running everything you need for day-to-day life—phones and laptops, lights, and even a small appliance or two. Plus, it’s nice to have a device that doesn’t produce carbon emissions and replenishes itself freely from the sun’s rays. Whether you’re seeking a highly portable option or need one that’s heavy-duty enough for extended use, these are the best solar generators we’ve tested and researched to date.

To pick the best solar generators, we tested some of these power stations for charging capacity, ease of use, weight, and different use cases. Our picks were reviewed by Popular Mechanics editor Brad Ford, who provided input for the larger-capacity units. Other models on this list were reviewed by test editor David Dritsas or freelance writer Maggie Slepian.

Our primary concerns were portability and convenience. Ease of use was also crucial—was the display easy to read? Did the screen readouts make sense? Bonus points if we could tell how much power is available at a glance. In the past few years, these criteria have become easier to meet. There are now plenty of compact, affordable units that have better charging capabilities than before.

It has been revealed that very few power stations of this size can handle as much solar input power as the Bluetti Apex 200. With two input types—low-voltage XT60 (up to 1,000 watts) and high-voltage MC4 (up to 2,000 watts)—it can accept up to 3,000 watts of solar power. If you had the panels and ideal weather, you could fully charge this station in less than 2 hours—even faster than plugging it into the wall. That’s impressive.

It also balances nicely between being a portable station and a home backup solution. It offers 3,200 watts of continuous power (it indicates 3,600 on the front, but that’s only if it’s connected to an expansion battery). We were able to power a refrigerator for a full 27 hours on a single charge, and estimated the battery efficiency at 90 percent, which is very good. Meanwhile, the 2,560-watt-hour battery capacity is expandable by adding up to six additional batteries. Using Bluetti’s largest battery, the B500K, you could build a massive 33-kilowatt-hour system.

Sources indicate that while 3,600 watts isn’t enough to power a whole home, you could power a couple of circuits through a manual transfer switch using the 120-volt 30-amp output. But keep in mind that there’s no 240-volt support, so you can’t use it to power high-voltage appliances like electric dryers.

As a portable station, the Apex 200 has a lot to offer. At 59 pounds, it’s not too hard to move around the house or in and out of a vehicle. And there are several great DC power options, including a bank of USB outlets (two are high-power USB-C) and both 10- and 30-amp, 12-volt outputs. We also love that the AC ports can individually be turned on and off using the mobile app; this helps improve overall runtime.

Since very few stations can match its max solar input capacity, we concluded that the Apex 200 is definitely a top choice for anyone who wants a power station that can recharge using the sun’s rays, but also offers the versatility of being used on the road or at home.

Full Bluetti Apex 200 Power Station Review.

Recent findings suggest that this model replaces the original Jackery 1000, but many of the same observations made of the first model still apply. The new version has a slightly higher capacity of 1,070 watt-hours and uses a newer lithium iron phosphate (LiFePO4) battery, which is a newer battery technology that offers a longer lifespan (4,000 cycles versus 500 cycles for this model) and better performance in extreme temperatures.

Recent findings suggest that expert Maggie Slepian used the previous model on a media trip where she had to keep multiple camera batteries charged during a weeklong outing. She found that while the capacity was lower than you'll find with others on this list, it actually powers items for longer than some higher-capacity models. She also charged her photographer’s camera batteries while charging the power bank on solar power (it was a very sunny winter day), which proved effective and efficient.

The newer V2 model has seven ports, including three AC outlets, two USB-C ports (one 30-watt and one 100-watt), a 12-volt car port, and one standard 18-watt USB-A outlet. It charges a typical laptop eight times or powers a small refrigerator or an electric cooler for over 15 hours.

It has been revealed that the Jackery Explorer 1000 V2 charges with a 200-watt solar panel or a 12-volt outlet in your vehicle while you’re on the move. It has fairly standard charging times, with 11.5 hours in a car outlet, 6.5 hours for solar panels, and just 5.5 hours to fully charge in a wall outlet. This won’t be your best bet for powering larger appliances, but it’s an ideal power station for smaller items and off-grid camping.

In a recent development, this power station takes solar recharging seriously. The Elite 300 can accept up to 1,200 watts of input, which is a high amount for a station this size. We paired it with a 250-watt portable panel and, on a fully sunny day, got around 260 watts of input. That’s the typical efficiency of a portable panel (again, you’ll never get 100 percent). But pair it with some larger panels, and you’ll get even more.

It also boasts an impressive battery capacity of just over 3,000 watt-hours and 2,400 watts of output, which is high for a station of this size. Plus, it includes a 120-volt 30-amp port, which is handy for connecting it to a small RV or pop-up camper, allowing you to run small appliances and water pumps. It’s not enough power to run a heating or cooling system for a significant amount of time, but for lights, small appliances, and other items that need power, this station will deliver.

Sources indicate that if there’s one downside we found, it’s that there’s no way to add an expansion battery to increase your capacity. That’s not a huge detractor, but it’s something we’ve seen in stations even smaller than this one. But at the end of the day, the Bluetti Elite 300 solar generator offers the right balance between a midsize power station that delivers a lot of power and run time, and a station that is compact and portable enough to be perfectly suited for an outdoor adventure.

Full Bluetti Elite 300 Solar Generator Review.

The EcoFlow Delta Pro is a large portable power station with an output that rivals some gas portable generators. When sold in a bundle with solar panels, like the package with two 220-watt portable panels we tested, it becomes a powerful solar generator. With an output of 3,600 watts, the Delta Pro can charge multiple appliances, and the output has the ability to bump up to 4,500 watts with its built-in X-Boost technology if more power is needed.

Industry observers note that to get an idea of the run time, we used the Delta Pro to power a full-size, 25-cubic-foot refrigerator—which it did for a remarkable 51 hours and 24 minutes. When recharged from a standard outlet, it took only two hours and 36 minutes. But it also charges with the included adapter, at electric vehicle charging stations, with a DC car adapter, or with the solar panels that come with the unit. Through the 30-amp connection, you can also connect this to a transfer switch to directly power select circuits in your home.

Like any power station with a large battery capacity, it will take a long time, perhaps nearly two days, to recharge this station using the bundled 220-watt solar panels. The good news is the Delta Pro accepts up to 1,600 watts of solar input, so it can charge faster by connecting more panels.

The heavy-duty wheels and telescoping handle on Anker’s Solix F3000 are easy to use, allow you to stand upright when pulling, and are a dream for people who regularly find themselves moving their power station around, whether it’s at a campsite or to different parts of the house during a power outage.

Along with convenience, this generator is a powerhouse with the capacity to easily run your refrigerator or a greenhouse heater, or keep your RV bright and warm.

We were impressed with Anker’s app, which allows us to check the charging status or power being generated without continually going outside to check. The app also lets you turn the power to the AC and USB ports on and off remotely, keeping tabs on how much energy is being utilized.

The Solix F3000 has 11 ports, including two car ports, an RV-specific outlet, four AC ports, three USB-C charging ports, and two USB-A. In sunny conditions and moderate temperatures, it recharges with a 400-watt solar panel in just a few hours and supports up to 2,400 watts of solar input.

Recent findings suggest that one of Jackery’s most recent solar generators is also its most rugged, able to withstand the elements better than most. It achieves this with an IP65 weatherproof rating, molded rubber port covers, a shockproof enclosure, and a bottom drainage system, which is part of a titanium alloy cooling structure that helps keep water out of the enclosure.

In a recent development, we got a chance to see these features up close and were impressed by them all, as well as a very sturdy enclosure that, thanks to the cooling system design, eliminates any side vents that could allow water to get inside. It feels strong; you could bang this station around without worrying too much about damaging it. The only downside is that this denser construction adds a bit of weight.

Recent findings suggest that as a power station, it delivers 1,800 watts of output with a battery capacity of 1,536 watt-hours. That’s enough power for a weekend camping trip or for running low-powered small appliances and some lighting during an emergency. As a solar generator, it can handle up to 800 watts of input from a portable panel. We paired it with a Jackery 200-watt panel, and it worked well. Overall, if your off-road adventures often get a little dirty, but you need some extra power, the Jackery Explorer 1500 Ultra Power Station is a good one to have at your side.

Full Jackery Explorer 1500 Ultra Power Station Review.

The latest version of the Goal Zero Yeti 1500 is a well-designed power station that’s ideal for off-grid camping situations where dust, wind, and potentially wet conditions are always on the table. This 2,000-watt power station is weatherproof with an IPX4 rating and features outlet shields that cover the ports and inputs. Each section is well-lit by an LED light that’s individually turned on or off using a manual button or the mobile app (and will shut off if not used after a certain period).

There’s a healthy number of outputs on the Yeti 1500, including four 120-volt AC outlets, four (two are high-powered) USB-A ports, and four 12-volt connections. We simulated an emergency blackout and managed to run a cable modem with a WiFi router, a lamp, a TV, and a tower fan, while charging a phone and a laptop through the USB-C ports. Given the station’s output and capacity, there was enough power for over two days of use (conveniently shown on the main display), and there was plenty of room to spare for a few more devices.

To test its solar capabilities, we paired the Yeti 1500 with a Nomad 200-watt portable solar panel and connected it using the high-voltage DC input, which accepts up to 600 watts; however, it also features a low-voltage input that accepts up to 300 watts for smaller panel arrays. Because both inputs can be used simultaneously, you could theoretically pair with two arrays for up to 900 watts, which is a high amount of input for a station of this size.

Of course, no portable panel operates at 100 percent efficiency. Even on a sunny, cloudless day with no shade-causing obstructions, the input readings showed anywhere from 125 to 145 watts. After initiating a recharge with only 5 percent capacity left, it would take at least 10.5 hours in those conditions to recharge. That’s actually not bad. An average of about 70 percent efficiency for a portable panel is good.

Full Goal Zero Yeti 1500 Review.

Sources indicate that the Anker Solix C2000 power station can deliver the full 2,400 watts of output to the bank of five AC outlets—something similar stations don’t offer. This allows you to power several things at once, like a refrigerator, toaster, router, and chargers, all at the same time.

During our tests, we were able to take full advantage of this, powering a refrigerator (by itself for up to 18 hours), along with some high-powered appliances, like a four-slot toaster and an electric kettle (though not the last two at the same time).

Another interesting ability of the C2000 is that you can fast charge it from AC power up to 1,800 watts, but that recharging rate remains consistent if you’re powering other devices at the same time (we confirmed this with a wattmeter). For example, we ran a 1,400-watt space heater while still recharging at the full 1,800-watt rate. Other power stations offer similar fast charging but will throttle the amount of power coming into the station while powering devices.

For solar recharging, we were a bit disappointed that this station can only accept 800 watts of input; other stations of this size accept more. But when solar was plugged in, it worked well. We connected it to a 200-watt Anker portable panel, and in full sun, we were getting around 125 to 145 watts of input, which is pretty good as these types of panels go. The C2000 is not IPX-rated for any type of weather resistance, however, so we would not recommend leaving this station sitting outside if the weather turns wet.

Full Anker Solix C2000 Power Station Review.

Recent findings suggest that power stations use watts and watt-hours to express size and capacity. Watts (size) refer to how much power it produces. For example, if you need to run a 900-watt microwave, you’ll need a station that outputs at least that much power (ideally more, since factory specs are never exact).

Sources indicate that meanwhile, watt-hours (capacity) give you an idea of how long devices can be powered continuously, though how much time depends on the amount of power being drawn—watt-hours don’t dictate a set time frame. Higher-powered devices will drain the battery a lot faster than lower-powered ones.

That may seem confusing, but a simple equation gives you an approximate idea of how it works: total watt-hours (of the generator) ÷ watts (of the device) = hours the power station runs.

For example, if you had a power station with a 2,048-watt-hour capacity and wanted to run a 750-watt space heater consistently at its highest setting, it would probably run for around 2.5 hours, so long as nothing else is plugged in. But for a refrigerator, whose power draw fluctuates between 10 and 300 watts (depending on how often the compressor turns on), you might be able to run it for nearly 24 hours.

According to recent reports, keep in mind that manufacturer specs are taken from perfect conditions; in the real world, you’ll likely see slightly less capacity from your power station. If you’re not sure how much power the different devices in your home draw, sometimes it’s written on a label, or you can use a device like a wattmeter.

Recent findings suggest that just as a power station has specifications on output size and capacity, solar panels are rated by how many watts they produce for a device after they convert the sun’s rays into electrical current (e.g., 100 watts, 200 watts, etc.). Because real-world conditions are never perfect, it’s not uncommon for panels to only output 50 to 75 percent (or even lower) of their total potential.

Your panels must also be within the acceptable input range of the power station. For example, connecting a 400-watt solar-panel array to a power station that only accepts 110 watts of solar input can cause an overload and damage the station.

Sources indicate that while weight and size don’t directly correlate to the technicalities of power banks, they impact the convenience of each model. Many camping and overlanding setups have limited space, so the more compact models likely have a higher appeal as a result.

Industry observers note that that noted, most units weigh at least 10 pounds, and the weight and size increase rapidly with greater capacities. Before purchasing, consider where you plan to store the power bank and the space in your vehicle or camper where it will live while you’re on the road. If you plan to use this power bank solely as a home backup option, portability will matter less, but consider how much effort it will take to move it around within your home or in your outdoor space.

Industry observers note that I am a low-maintenance camper, and most of my background is in lightweight backcountry travel. That means I prioritize space-saving and ease-of-use, so my go-to power banks have between 250 and 600 watt-hours, and weigh less than 15 pounds.

According to recent reports, this is perfect for a weekend trip, with the on-the-go (car or solar) charging capabilities to put my mind at ease for longer trips. Mostly, I’m charging small items, so one charge lasts a long time. However, plenty of people in the van-life and remote-work world are powering their RVs and vans, and relying on multiple laptop charges. For that, I’d recommend one of the larger units.

In a recent development, A solar-powered generator charges and runs almost anything that requires power—it just depends on the capacity. These generators can charge power tools in the shop, laptops for remote work, and personal devices like Bluetooth headphones and speakers.

Industry observers note that A solar-powered generator with a higher power capacity can even power household appliances in the event of a power outage. And the fact that these are solar-compatible means you aren’t reliant on the electrical grid to recharge them.

Industry observers note that every unit on our list has multiple charging options, including wall (AC outlet), car (12-volt), and solar. Each input method charges your unit at a different speed, and solar also depends on the conditions. AC power is the fastest, followed by 12-volt, and then by solar (though a larger solar array could potentially be faster than 12-volt).

According to recent reports, I try to charge up my power banks whenever I can, so I’m never caught off guard trying to leave on a trip with a dying power bank. If this happens (which it has), I’ll charge it in my vehicle’s 12-volt port while I’m driving, though this is often slower than solar or a wall unit.

Sources indicate that solar power is the most sustainable and typically fastest way to power these—just be sure you have enough wattage in the solar panels to make it effective. I recommend keeping the generator stored with at least an 80 percent charge, and unplugging it once it’s fully charged—keeping it plugged in longer than necessary degrades the battery.

Most units will have a simple readout display showing the remaining battery charge, and it’s a good practice not to allow your battery pack to get below 20 percent.

#147043. Benjamin Franklin mocked the bald eagle in a 1784 letter and praised the turkey, but never asked for it to be the national bird

Benjamin Franklin mocked the bald eagle in a 1784 letter and praised the turkey, but never asked for it to be the national bird

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1084 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The letter, never mailed to his daughter, was not published in full in English until 1817.
  • Industry observers note that A popular Thanksgiving story holds that Benjamin Franklin wanted the turkey, not the bald eagle, to be the national bird of the United States.
  • It has been revealed that the story traces back to a letter dated January 26, 1784, and addressed to his daughter, Sarah Bache.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The letter, never mailed to his daughter, was not published in full in English until 1817. The bald eagle became the national bird by law only in 2024.

Industry observers note that A popular Thanksgiving story holds that Benjamin Franklin wanted the turkey, not the bald eagle, to be the national bird of the United States. It is a good story, but it is not what Franklin actually wrote.

It has been revealed that the story traces back to a letter dated January 26, 1784, and addressed to his daughter, Sarah Bache. In it, he poked fun at the eagle on the badge of the Society of the Cincinnati and noted a few kind words about the turkey. In that letter, he never proposes the turkey as a national symbol.

According to the editors of his papers, Franklin never even sent the letter to his daughter. And the bald eagle itself was officially designated the national bird by law only in 2024, more than two centuries later.

Industry observers note that when Franklin wrote the letter, the bald eagle was already on the Great Seal of the United States. It had been adopted for the seal on June 20, 1782.

In the winter of 1783 to 1784, Franklin, the American minister, was too ill to travel and isolated at Passy, in France, according to the editors of his papers.

In a recent development, on January 26, he saw the founding document of the Society of the Cincinnati, a hereditary order of American army officers. John Paul Jones had sent it to him along with a pamphlet attacking the society.

The letter that Franklin wrote that same day was, in the view of the editors of The Papers of Benjamin Franklin, a satire meant as a public essay.

Addressing it to his daughter, with whom, the editors note, he never corresponded about politics, made it look like a private note.

According to recent reports, he took aim at the idea of passing honors down to children. He objected to “an order of hereditary Knights, in direct opposition to the solemnly declared sense of their country.”.

Sources indicate that he even did the math. In nine generations, he wrote, a member’s share in his descendant would be “but a 512th part.”.

Industry observers note that the birds come up near the end, when Franklin turns to the society’s badges, which had been made in France. “To me they seem tolerably done; but all such things are criticised,” he wrote.

Some critics, he reported, disliked the Latin mottos. “Others object to the bald eagle, as looking too much like a Dindon or turkey,” he wrote, using the French word for turkey.

In a recent development, then Franklin gave his own opinion. “For my own part I wish the bald eagle had not been chosen as the representative of our country,” he wrote. “He is a bird of bad moral character. He does not get his living honestly.”.

He described the eagle sitting on a dead tree, “too lazy to fish for himself,” while it watched another bird, which he called the fishing hawk. When that bird caught a fish and carried it toward its nest, he wrote, the eagle “pursues him, and takes it from him.”.

According to recent reports, he went further. “Besides he is a rank coward,” Franklin wrote. The “little king bird not bigger than a sparrow attacks him boldly and drives him out of the district.”.

Sources indicate that only then does Franklin praise the turkey. He wrote that he was “not displeased” that the figure on the badge was not recognizable as a bald eagle and looked more like a turkey.

“For in truth, the turkey is in comparison a much more respectable bird, and withal a true original native of America,” he wrote. Eagles, he noted, “have been found in all countries, but the turkey was peculiar to ours.”.

In a recent development, he did not spare the turkey entirely. He called it “a little vain and silly,” though “not the worse emblem for that,” and “a bird of courage” that would attack a grenadier of the British guards who dared to invade its farmyard “with a red coat on.”.

It has been revealed that nowhere in the letter does Franklin ask for the turkey to replace the eagle on the seal or anywhere else. The comparison is part of a joke about a badge.

It has been revealed that according to the editors of his papers, Franklin revealed the letter only to his grandsons before sending it, around March 1784, to the abbé Morellet in France to translate it into French. Morellet advised against publishing it. Franklin agreed and promised it would not appear while he was alive.

Recent findings suggest that A partial French translation came out in Paris in 1790, months after Franklin’s death. The full English text was not published until 1817, when William Temple Franklin included it in his edition of Franklin’s writings.

In other words, the letter that so many people now quote was almost unknown in Franklin’s lifetime.

The bald eagle’s official title came with a bill that Sen. Amy Klobuchar of Minnesota introduced on June 20, 2024, exactly 242 years after the eagle was adopted for the Great Seal.

Industry observers note that the Senate passed it by unanimous consent in July 2024, and the House approved it by voice vote on December 16, 2024. It was signed into law on December 23, 2024, as Public Law 118-206.

It has been revealed that the law adds a new section to the U.S. Code. It reads: “The bald eagle (Haliaeetus leucocephalus) is the national bird.”.

In its findings, Congress noted that the bald eagle is unique to North America and that federal, state and local governments, nonprofit groups and individuals had all contributed to its recovery.

Even so, eagles still face problems, including the lead poisoning that is common in eagles.

The turkey’s history with people goes back much further than Franklin. Scientists have found that turkeys were domesticated at least 1,500 years ago.

The information was obtained from Benjamin Franklin’s letter to Sarah Bache of January 26, 1784, as published by the National Archives in Founders Online from The Papers of Benjamin Franklin, the record of S.4610 on Congress.gov, and the enrolled text of the bill published by the U.S. Government Publishing Office.

  • In a recent development, in an increasingly fire-prone western North America, Jennifer Grenz, an ecologist and member of the Lytton First Nation, looks at fire with a holistic eye.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .).

In a recent development, in an increasingly fire-prone western North America, Jennifer Grenz, an ecologist and member of the Lytton First Nation, looks at fire with a holistic eye. She considers her work with landscapes recovering from catastrophic wildfire to be “deliberately unfocused,” spanning soil microbial ecology, restoration ecology, invasion biology and historical biology.

Grenz analyzes historical ecological records, like how Indigenous people have shaped and cared for ecosystems over time, to paint a comprehensive picture. “I’m interested in how those histories leave ecological legacies and hints of the stewardship of the past,” notes Grenz, who leads the Indigenous Ecology Lab at the University of British Columbia in Canada. “What changed on the land that made it more vulnerable?”.

Grenz spends time with many kinds of specialists, such as archaeologists, anthropologists and Indigenous elders who provide oral histories.

Moving forward, her lab will examine ecology below ground, including soil, microbial communities and root networks. The goal is to understand the role of underground ecology in critical topics like carbon sequestration, climate change, biodiversity and sustainable management.

“My motivation is in our interior Salish Territories in the southern interior of British Columbia, where my ancestors rest and where my people are,” Grenz notes. “The responsibility I feel to them and to our Tmícw, which means our lands, [is] to not take us back to the past, but to show that we have the deep knowledge to help us move forward.”.

#147040. The biggest concern about toddler screen time may be what children are missing

📅 26 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1563 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Earth ↗ Open Full Page

The biggest concern about toddler screen time may be what children are missing

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1563 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Many toddlers use screens daily, potentially missing valuable opportunities to play, talk, and learn through real human interaction.
  • Recent findings suggest that at 18 months, children are learning to name things, put words together and make sense of the world around them.
  • In Hungary, researchers found that 49% of children around this age used screens every day.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Many toddlers use screens daily, potentially missing valuable opportunities to play, talk, and learn through real human interaction.

Recent findings suggest that at 18 months, children are learning to name things, put words together and make sense of the world around them. Many are also becoming quite familiar with television and smartphones.

In Hungary, researchers found that 49% of children around this age used screens every day.

Recent findings suggest that there has been plenty of debate over how much screen time is appropriate for young children. A new review, however, looks at a different side of the problem.

How much time is left for talking, playing and being with other people?

Krisztina Kopcsó, a researcher at the HCSO Institute for Quantitative Population and Economic Research in Budapest, led the review.

Kopcsó and her colleagues drew on data from a Hungarian national survey and research from around the world published since 2015.

Among the authors was Ákos Pogány from the Department of Ethology at Eötvös Loránd University (ELTE).

“Young children learn primarily through actively exploring the world and interacting with others, rather than through screens. One of the greatest risks of introducing digital devices too early is that their use takes time away from precisely these essential experiences,” Pogány mentioned.

Screen exposure before age two is discouraged by the World Health Organization and the American Academy of Pediatrics. Video chatting with distant family members is treated as an exception.

A more restrictive position has been adopted in France. Complete screen abstinence until age three was recommended by an expert committee appointed by the French President.

A recent Hungarian expert guideline also recommends avoiding screens before age three.

Despite these recommendations, early screen exposure is widespread. A 2022 meta-analysis included 63 studies and more than 89,000 children.

Only 24.7% of children under two were found to meet the guideline of no screen use.

It has been revealed that in the United States, children under two averaged 63 minutes of screen media per day in 2024. These data were reported in the Common Sense Media census. By age two, 40% of children owned their own tablet.

Objective measurements were used in the Australian EUiLO cohort, described by Brushe and colleagues in 2023. A child-worn device recorded electronic noise for 16 hours on a typical day.

Families with lower educational attainment were oversampled among the 207 children. At 24 months, no screen exposure was recorded for only 2.4% of them.

Mean daily exposure in that cohort was 76.1 minutes at 6 months and 148.3 minutes at 24 months.

Industry observers note that the Hungarian data were obtained from the Cohort ’18 Growing Up in Hungary panel study. A representative sample was recruited during pregnancy.

Maternal reports for 2,569 children were collected in 2019 and 2020 and analyzed by Kopcsó and colleagues in 2024. The children were aged between 15 and 23 months.

The database was weighted for maternal age, education, parity and marital status.

In a recent development, daily screen exposure was reported for 49% of the children. More than one hour of exposure on a typical day was recorded for 37.5%. No exposure was reported for 14%.

Among daily owners, mean screen time on a typical day was 122.5 minutes.

Most children were cared for at home. Only 6.7% attended formal childcare at the time of the survey.

Industry observers note that television viewing was identified as the most frequent screen activity. It was watched every day by 43.6% of the children.

Sources indicate that videos on mobile devices were watched daily by 21.2% of children. Active touchscreen use on a daily basis was reported for 18.7%.

Higher screen time was observed in lower-income households and among children of less educated mothers. Both gradients were statistically significant in the 2024 analysis.

A similar gradient was reported in a 2024 German study of 3,035 children by Paulus and colleagues. Parents there described using screens when time was short.

The contexts of screen use were also recorded in the Cohort ’18 survey.

Screen use while having fun with the child was reported by 62.1% of mothers.

Screens were allowed during household chores by 53.5%. Use for perceived developmental purposes was reported by 52.8%.

In a recent development, background television was reported as a regular practice in 31.4% of families. It was rare or absent in 39.1%. The mother’s own relaxation was cited as a reason by 13.9%.

In Hungary, 19.6% of toddlers watched screens during meals, and 12.4% used them while falling asleep.

Children who spent more time with screens were read to and played with slightly less often, even after accounting for family income and mothers’ education.

However, busy parents may have less time for these activities, regardless of screen use.

A 2017 study linked screen use during more daily routines to delays in social and emotional development.

Another study in 2018 found that children who spent less time with screens at age two had better self-control at age four.

Apps and streaming content for babies are often marketed as educational.

A 2021 meta-analysis published in Child Development examined how well young children learn from videos compared with real-life demonstrations. Children aged 0 to 6 were included.

Less learning was found from video than from equivalent live demonstrations, and the gap narrowed with age.

Word learning from video was supported by adult co-viewing in a 2018 study by Strouse and colleagues.

Video chat was examined by Myers and colleagues in 2017 and by McClure and colleagues in 2018. Reciprocal interaction and joint attention cues are preserved in that format.

Screens were used to soothe or distract the child by 43% of Hungarian mothers. Frequent reliance on this strategy may reduce chances to practice self-regulation, the authors wrote.

Reciprocal associations between device use for calming and emotional reactivity were reported in a 2023 JAMA Pediatrics study.

Children aged 3 to 5 were followed. Similar associations were reported by Konok and colleagues at ELTE in 2024.

Recent findings suggest that autoplay, infinite scrolling and algorithmic recommendations are listed in the review as persuasive design features. Rapid cuts and high visual salience may also place heavy demands on immature attention.

A parent’s phone can interrupt even the simplest moments with a child. In 2018, researchers McDaniel and Radesky used the term technoference to describe these interruptions.

Studies conducted in restaurants and public places in the United States and Israel found that parents paid less attention to their children while using phones.

Some even responded rather sharply when their children sought their attention.

A 2015 study found that just hearing a phone notification was enough to distract someone, even if they ignored it.

According to recent reports, babies seem to notice these interruptions, too. In a 2018 study, infants whose mothers frequently used phones had a harder time returning to a happy mood, even after their mothers put the devices away.

In the French ELFE cohort, mean daily screen time at age two was 49 minutes in 2013, among 12,099 children.

Television exposure during family meals at age two was associated with poorer expressive language.

In a recent development, less advanced general cognitive development was found at age 3.5, Yang and colleagues reported in 2024. Overall screen time was not the factor identified.

According to recent reports, earth.com has previously covered how a parent’s own phone use relates to vocabulary growth. The role of eye contact in infant language learning has also been reported.

A harm-reduction approach to infant media use was proposed by Heller in Infant Behavior and Development in 2021.

Age-appropriate limits combined with harm-reduction strategies are recommended in the review.

Industry observers note that background and parallel media use during caregiving routines and play should be reduced. Screen exposure during meals and before bedtime should be avoided.

Caregiver co-use is prioritized when screens are introduced in the second or third year.

Information could be provided to expecting parents through obstetric, prenatal and primary care services. Complaints about the no-screens-before-two rule have also been reported by parents.

Recent findings suggest that the European Union has rules to keep children safe online. Article 28 of its Digital Services Act focuses specifically on protecting young customers.

On July 14, 2025, the European Commission also issued guidelines addressing features that could make it difficult for children to stop using digital platforms.

However, these measures do not specifically address the needs of babies and toddlers.

The authors argue that keeping children safe from the potential harms of digital media should not be the responsibility of parents alone.

Reducing screen time sounds like a sensible idea, but researchers still have much to learn about its benefits for very young children.

A 2025 review of experiments involving preschoolers found that programs teaching parents about screen habits helped reduce children’s screen use.

Few studies, however, have tested similar approaches in children under two. Even fewer have followed children long enough to see whether their language skills, sleep or ability to manage emotions improved.

Future studies could test whether replacing screen time with play and reading improves language development in children under two.

For young children, what they do after the screen goes off may be just as key as switching it off in the first place.

The review was published in the journal Biologia Futura.

#147038. Tech Report: A newly introduced discovery could give the world 12 months to prepare for extreme El Niño and La Niña weather events

📅 26 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1488 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Earth ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: A newly introduced discovery could give the world 12 months to prepare for extreme El Niño and La Niña weather events

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1488 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Researchers have found the conditions needed to predict some El Niño and La Niña events 12 months ahead of time.
  • Most El Niño forecasts are only reliable about six months ahead of time.
  • That is because the Pacific Ocean becomes so sensitive to tiny shifts in the spring that forecast models easily lose track of what comes next.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Researchers have found the conditions needed to predict some El Niño and La Niña events 12 months ahead of time.

Most El Niño forecasts are only reliable about six months ahead of time. Predicting a full year in advance has long been considered nearly impossible.

That is because the Pacific Ocean becomes so sensitive to tiny shifts in the spring that forecast models easily lose track of what comes next.

Now, researchers have found that certain 12-month El Niño forecasts really do hold up, depending on the state of the Pacific on the day the prediction is made.

Forecasts issued during a La Niña held up a year in advance in all nine climate models an Australian team tested. Forecasts issued when the Pacific was in neither phase did worse than a forecast built from nothing but the historical odds.

For farmers and water managers, that could mean months of extra warning before some El Niños.

Nandini Ramesh of CSIRO, Australia’s national science agency, and UNSW Sydney led the work. Her co-author Mandy Freund is at the University of Melbourne and the ARC Centre of Excellence for the Weather of the 21st Century.

According to recent reports, the team graded about 7,500 past forecasts rather than building a fresh forecasting system. Ramesh mentioned the researchers are still a few steps from applying the findings to agency models.

In an interview with Earth.com, Freund stated the accuracy of forecasts that started during a La Niña surprised the team most. Routine checks of forecast performance, she said, often don’t sort forecasts by their starting state.

El Niño, La Niña and the neutral years between them make up a cycle scientists call the El Niño-Southern Oscillation, or ENSO.

“Separating forecasts according to their starting state, we were able to uncover a much clearer picture of when long-range ENSO predictions can be trusted,” she noted.

Industry observers note that the warm phase of that cycle is El Niño, when the surface of the central and eastern tropical Pacific runs warmer than usual. La Niña is the cool phase. Both tend to peak around December, and both change weather patterns around the world.

Recent findings suggest that A declared El Niño or La Niña can set off drought warnings for farmers and water managers, the authors wrote. It can move the prices of farm commodities and start public health planning.

By one estimate they cite, seasonal forecasts influence companies worth a combined $13 trillion.

The trouble is the spring. From March to May the tropical Pacific is unusually sensitive to small disturbances. A forecast made before those months and aimed at the winter after them loses much of its skill.

Forecasters call this the spring predictability barrier. It is a big part of why predictions beyond about nine months have stayed so difficult.

In a recent development, the team worked from an archive of decade-long climate simulations run by modeling centers in nine countries. Those include the United States, the United Kingdom, Japan and Canada.

These are physics-based models, which simulate the ocean and atmosphere from physical laws rather than past statistics.

The centers started a fresh batch every year from 1961 to around 2020, and the team used the runs that began between October and January.

Rather than judging the simulations on exact temperatures, the researchers asked one question of each: would the following winter land in La Niña, neutral or El Niño?

Sources indicate that they sorted every year into one of those three bins using sea surface temperatures in a patch of the central Pacific. The coolest third of years counted as La Niña and the warmest third as El Niño.

Sorting the years that way left about 7,500 one-year forecasts to grade against NOAA‘s record of what the ocean actually did. Then the researchers split the results by which of the three states the Pacific was in when each forecast began.

In every one of the nine models, forecasts that began during a La Niña scored higher than forecasts that began during an El Niño or a neutral year.

Their skill a year out matched what seasonal forecast models manage three to four months ahead, a range forecasters already rely on.

Forecasts that began from a neutral Pacific did the opposite. In every model, they scored below a forecast built from nothing but the historical odds of one state following another.

Inside a single model, the gap between starting points was larger than the gap between the best and worst models.

“The finding that one-year forecasts starting from La Niña perform well in all nine of the models tested suggests there is something about La Niña conditions that makes the tropical Pacific system more predictable over the following year,” Freund said.

In a recent development, stronger La Niña events were predicted better than weaker ones. For El Niño the pattern was less clear, though badly missed forecasts of strong El Niños were rare.

The team then asked the question a farmer might ask of any forecast: when a model predicts a particular switch, how often does it actually happen?

In one American model, a forecast of El Niño issued during a La Niña came true 82 percent of the time, a year ahead of the event. The same model’s forecast of a La Niña from neutral conditions came true only 9 percent of the time.

In a recent development, three of the nine models were right more than 70 percent of the time when they predicted a La Niña would give way to an El Niño. Eight of the nine were at their worst predicting a La Niña from a neutral year, a switch that is rare in the real ocean.

And when a model called for an El Niño from neutral conditions, not one beat the historical odds. Those calls are the likeliest false alarms.

Across all starts from neutral, the models were right 23 to 43 percent of the time. A forecast built from the historical odds alone would have been right 61 percent of the time.

Sources indicate that freund told Earth.com that the weakness from neutral starts remains an important caveat. “Unfortunately, starting from a neutral Pacific, the physics-based models often make the wrong predictions,” she stated.

“The system can be very sensitive: it is an example of what is known as the ‘butterfly effect’ where very small disturbances can be amplified over time into huge changes in a system’s behavior.”.

Asked by Earth.com what farmers and water managers should take from the result, Freund stated the study is encouraging.

Those are people, she said, who rely on knowing about an El Niño much further ahead than forecasts now allow. When a La Niña is under way, a forecast for the following year can be trusted more.

“This gives farmers, water managers and other decision-makers valuable extra time to prepare, including decisions about which crops and seed varieties to plant or how to manage water resources,” she noted.

The method itself is simple, Freund said, and would not take much for forecasting agencies to consider. “It could provide this extra layer of confidence we can lay on certain predictions of ENSO,” she said.

The researchers also tested two-year forecasts, and for almost every kind of switch those were wrong more often than right.

Industry observers note that the one exception came after an El Niño, when every model did better than the historical odds at saying there would be no El Niño for the next two years. Long stretches without an El Niño have been linked to multi-year droughts across the subtropics.

Why a La Niña makes the following year easier to predict is the open question. The team offered three possibilities.

Sources indicate that A La Niña’s cool water tends to linger into spring instead of fading in February or March the way an El Niño’s warmth does. Earlier studies also found fewer random atmospheric disturbances during a La Niña.

And a La Niña is when the upper tropical Pacific refills with warm water, so the state of that reservoir may carry a lot of information about what comes next.

The authors set aside long-term warming trends, slow decade-scale swings in the Pacific and the differences between one El Niño and another.

They also didn’t test the statistical and machine learning methods they suspect would do better from a neutral start. Those methods work from past patterns instead of from today’s conditions. Whether the La Niña advantage holds in the models agencies actually run each season hasn’t been tested.

The team’s next step is to work out which of the three explanations is doing the work. The confidence check it proposes can be run on any model from the forecasts it has already made.

The full study was published in the journal Science Advances.

#147035. Tech Report: A remote island in Newly introduced Zealand was supposed to be a safe haven for wildlife

📅 26 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (917 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Earth ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: A remote island in Newly introduced Zealand was supposed to be a safe haven for wildlife

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (917 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A remote island off Latest Zealand’s coast reveals the challenges of protecting native birds from invasive predators.
  • Today’s Image of the Day from NASA Earth Observatory features Resolution Island, a remote expanse of wilderness off the southwestern coast of Latest Zealand.
  • Surrounded by deep blue waters and covered in dense vegetation, the island appears to be an ideal sanctuary for wildlife.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A remote island off Latest Zealand’s coast reveals the challenges of protecting native birds from invasive predators.

Today’s Image of the Day from NASA Earth Observatory features Resolution Island, a remote expanse of wilderness off the southwestern coast of Latest Zealand.

Surrounded by deep blue waters and covered in dense vegetation, the island appears to be an ideal sanctuary for wildlife.

Its isolation, however, has not always offered the protection that conservationists envisioned.

For more than a century, Resolution Island has been at the center of an ambitious effort to preserve some of New Zealand’s most extraordinary native birds.

Its history reveals both the potential and the limitations of using islands as natural barriers against invasive species.

The image was captured on December 12, 2025, by the Operational Land Imager aboard the Landsat 9 satellite.

Resolution Island lies within Fiordland National Park, a spectacular region of mountains, forests, waterfalls, and narrow waterways that extend deep into the southwestern coast of New Zealand’s South Island.

During past ice ages, enormous glaciers moved through the region, gradually carving deep valleys into the landscape.

As the glaciers retreated and sea levels rose, ocean water flooded many of these valleys, creating the dramatic fjords visible today.

Resolution Island is the largest island within the national park. Its mountainous terrain reaches an elevation of 3,507 feet at the summit of Mount Clerke.

The island’s varied landscape supports wetlands, ancient evergreen forests, and high-elevation grasslands. These distinct environments provide a range of habitats for native wildlife.

New Zealand’s long geographical isolation allowed wildlife to evolve in remarkable ways.

Before humans arrived, the country had virtually no native land mammals other than bats. Birds occupied many ecological niches that mammals filled elsewhere in the world.

Some species gradually lost the ability to fly, while others developed behaviors that left them particularly vulnerable to ground-dwelling predators.

Among them were kiwi, which forage along the forest floor, and kākāpō, the world’s only flightless parrot.

For millions of years, these birds survived without facing the kinds of mammalian predators found on other continents.

That evolutionary advantage became a liability when people introduced unfamiliar animals into New Zealand’s ecosystems.

Rats, cats, and members of the weasel family brought fresh pressures that native birds were poorly equipped to withstand.

By the nineteenth century, the decline of New Zealand’s native wildlife was becoming increasingly apparent.

In a recent development, european settlers had introduced stoats and other predators in an attempt to control rabbit populations. Instead, these animals created another ecological problem by preying on vulnerable native species.

In 1872, conservationist Thomas Henry Potts suggested that Resolution Island could provide a refuge for birds threatened by introduced predators.

The surrounding ocean appeared to offer a natural protective barrier, allowing native species to survive without the dangers they faced on the mainland.

Resolution Island became a protected reserve in 1891, making it part of a pioneering chapter in Upcoming Zealand’s conservation history.

Long before modern wildlife restoration programs existed, naturalists were experimenting with ideas that would eventually become central to endangered species management.

One of the most dedicated figures in this undertaking was Richard Henry, who became the island’s caretaker.

Henry recognized the urgency of protecting birds that were rapidly disappearing from other parts of the country.

Working in an isolated and physically demanding environment, he transported hundreds of native birds across the waters of Fiordland.

More than 700 birds, primarily kiwi and kākāpō, were relocated to Resolution Island and neighboring islands during his conservation efforts.

Much of the work involved traveling by rowboat through a region known for challenging weather and rugged terrain.

Henry’s efforts represented an early attempt to prevent extinction by establishing wildlife populations in geographically isolated locations.

Unfortunately, the assumption that the surrounding waters would keep predators away proved incorrect.

Industry observers note that by 1900, invasive predators had been detected on Resolution Island. Stoats were capable of swimming across the channels that separated the island from nearby land.

The discovery undermined years of painstaking conservation work and exposed a weakness in the island’s natural defenses.

In a recent development, stoats are highly adaptable hunters. Their ability to exploit different environments makes them particularly problematic in Fresh Zealand, where many native birds nest on or near the ground.

Henry attempted to control the invading predators through trapping but eventually left the island to pursue conservation work elsewhere.

His experience demonstrated that geographical isolation alone was not necessarily enough to protect vulnerable species.

More than a century later, conservationists continue to build on Henry’s original vision.

In 2008, New Zealand’s Department of Conservation launched a predator management program on Resolution Island to improve the prospects of native wildlife.

Maintaining such a program across a large, mountainous island presents considerable challenges.

Dense forests, steep slopes, and remote locations complicate efforts to monitor wildlife and control invasive animals.

Conservation also extends into the surrounding waters, where a marine reserve protects coastal ecosystems near the island’s distinctive Five Fingers Peninsula.

Viewed from space, Resolution Island offers a striking portrait of an apparently untouched wilderness.

Yet beneath its forest canopy lies a complex ecological history shaped by human intervention, invasive species, and generations of conservation work.

The island remains a powerful reminder that protecting nature sometimes requires far more than simply setting it aside.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, this is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .).

Dor Minzer remembers sitting in an undergraduate computation class at Tel Aviv University. He was intrigued by his professor and soon found himself pulled into a latest world: the mystifying intersection of math and computation, first laid out by Alan Turing during World War II. Working with the professor, Minzer became deeply interested in the limitations of what computers can and can’t do.

“My part is actually to prove not only do I not know how to do it, but I can prove that it’s impossible,” Minzer claims. “You have to really be curious.”.

According to recent reports, minzer’s hard work has paid off. In 2018, he proved a theoretical computer science problem called the 2-to-2 games conjecture. It asks whether computers can efficiently distinguish games where almost all rules can be satisfied from those where almost none can be satisfied, when the rules have a strict structure.

According to recent reports, in September, Minzer and his two graduate students at MIT posted a 95-page milestone paper on the unique games conjecture, which builds off the 2-to-2 conjecture. The paper wasn’t quite ready, but they published to get ahead of a press release from OpenAI, describing its proof for the same problem, slated for only days later. It’s a situation that many mathematicians have found themselves in this year as AI companies flood the field with findings at lightning speed.

It has been revealed that minzer indicates it’s critical to remember that math, and all the research and contemplation behind it, is very human. “It’s a human activity,” he says. “Research is sort of a living organism, a living body.”.

Industry observers note that minzer teaches his own students now. Some days, he talks to his class and gets the sense that nobody is paying attention. But other days, he gets a few students that participate. They have ideas, they’re excited, and they remind him of his own days as a graduate student.

Recent findings suggest that “I feel like now I feel like I’m passing the torch,” he notes. “Before you have a Ph.D. adviser, you’re like a latest person in a dark room. There are infinite places to go. Your Ph.D. adviser is the person that holds your hand and says, ‘Okay, let’s walk here.’”.

#147032. What makes a hug truly memorable has a lot to do with empathy and how you handle relationships

📅 26 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1142 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Earth ↗ Open Full Page

What makes a hug truly memorable has a lot to do with empathy and how you handle relationships

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1142 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A survey of 15,049 adults demonstrates most people remember hugs for comfort and support.
  • We tend to think of a hug as a universal source of warmth, yet nearly three in ten adults in a large survey could not recall one that had left a positive mark.
  • When a hug did stick in someone’s memory, it was much more likely to be for comfort, support, or understanding than for romance.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A survey of 15,049 adults demonstrates most people remember hugs for comfort and support. Empathy, attachment patterns, and hugging habits also play a role.

We tend to think of a hug as a universal source of warmth, yet nearly three in ten adults in a large survey could not recall one that had left a positive mark.

When a hug did stick in someone’s memory, it was much more likely to be for comfort, support, or understanding than for romance.

According to recent reports, whether someone could remember a hug at all came down to a few key traits. The top three were how much empathy they felt, how they handled closeness, and whether they usually hugged their friends hello.

Anna Lena Dueren of the University of Bristol‘s School of Psychological Science led the analysis of 15,049 adults in the U.K. Their answers came from the Touch Test, a national survey on touch that BBC Radio 4 promoted in early 2020.

Industry observers note that the study is a snapshot of who remembers what. It can show which traits go together with a hug memory, not what causes one.

Recent findings suggest that in an interview with Earth.com, Dueren put the main finding simply. “Most participants remembered hugs because they conveyed comfort, understanding, or support,” she remarked.

To her knowledge, she added, it’s the first large study to ask people why a hug stayed with them.

It has been revealed that the question was plain: is there a hug you remember because of its positive emotional effect on you? Of the 15,046 people who answered, 10,457 stated yes, or 69.5 percent.

People who mentioned yes then picked the single best reason from a short list. Among the 9,703 who chose a listed reason, about a third picked comfort, 29 percent said the hug conveyed understanding, and 20 percent said support.

In a recent development, comfort, understanding, and support together cover more than four in five of the hugs people kept. Just 147 people, or 1.5 percent of the group, said the hug was memorable because it was physically arousing.

Earlier studies had linked daily hugs to lower stress and better mood, and these answers fit.

Industry observers note that men and women were about equally likely to remember a hug at all. The reasons they gave, though, differed in a small but consistent way.

Among men, 3.9 percent chose arousal as the reason, compared with 0.8 percent of women. Men were also more likely to pick friendliness, 12.3 percent, in comparison to 4.8 percent of women.

Sources indicate that women chose comfort more often, at 34.6 percent to men’s 25.3 percent, and understanding more often too. The team suggested that the nurturing side of a hug may count for more among women.

Dueren’s team noted that only 2,197 men gave a reason, against 7,506 women, so they advise reading the gender differences with caution.

Dueren’s team, which includes researchers at UCL, the University of Sussex, and the University of Greenwich, then checked which traits went with keeping an emotional memory of a hug.

The strongest link was a habit: people who always greet friends and family with a hug were more likely to recall one.

Industry observers note that disliking the feel of being hugged went the other way, and so did finding it hard to know how firmly to hug someone. Asked by Earth.com what someone who dislikes hugging might take from the work, Dueren pointed to the size of the gap.

Recent findings suggest that “In our study, people who disliked the feeling of being hugged were slightly less likely to recall a hug that had a positive emotional effect on them than those who did not dislike it,” she noted. “The findings highlight that hugging experiences are not equally remembered by everyone.”.

Industry observers note that empathy mattered too, whether measured as reading other people’s feelings or as feeling them alongside someone. Higher scores went with higher odds of remembering a hug.

So did attachment style, how a person relates to those closest to them. Insecure attachment comes in two forms.

Recent findings suggest that people who feel distress at separation, the anxious form, were more likely to hold a hug in memory. People who prize independence in relationships, the avoidant form, were less likely to.

All of these effects were small, and together the traits explained only 10 to 14 percent of the variation in who remembered a hug.

According to recent reports, dueren’s team expected that people who are less satisfied with their bodies would be more likely to remember a hug for the comfort or support it gave. That expectation failed.

In a recent development, A person’s satisfaction with their own body did not influence whether they remembered a hug, or why. However, there was a measure that did.

The team built a five-item scale of how much a person’s sense of their body runs through touch. One item asked whether they choose clothes partly for how the fabric feels on the skin.

People who scored higher on it were more likely to remember a hug, and to remember it for understanding or arousal rather than comfort. The scale is new, and the team called those results preliminary.

Industry observers note that being tucked in with a hug and a kiss as a child had no bearing on whether a person remembered a hug. Neither did how often that person gets hugged day to day.

It has been revealed that the people who answered chose to take part and were not paid, so they may care about touch more than average. Three-quarters were women, and all lived in the U.K., where attitudes to touch differ from those elsewhere.

The survey didn’t ask who gave the remembered hug or where it happened, so it can’t say whether comfort from a partner is remembered differently from comfort given by a friend.

Recent findings suggest that answers were collected between January and March 2020, and fewer than 1 percent arrived after the U.K.’s first lockdown began. So this is a record of hugging before the pandemic changed it.

In a recent development, dueren told Earth.com that she wants to pursue why the same hug feels so different to different people. “The same type of touch can feel pleasant for one person and uncomfortable to another,” she said. “I would like to better understand factors that contribute to these differences in experience.”.

Empathetic people may store up hugs, or memorable hugs may make people more empathetic, and this survey can’t tell which. Settling that would mean following the same people over years, and that study has not yet been run.

The full study was published in the journal PLOS One.
