#147031. Millions of Americans use a form of birth control that surveys have overlooked

📅 26 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1449 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Earth ↗ Open Full Page

Millions of Americans use a form of birth control that surveys have overlooked

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1449 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • More Americans use menstrual cycle tracking to avoid pregnancy than surveys suggested, with use rising in some states.
  • Tracking the menstrual cycle to avoid pregnancy may be far more common than scientists once believed.
  • Around 7% to 8% of US birth control users aged 18 to 44 tracked their cycles in 2022 and 2023.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

More Americans use menstrual cycle tracking to avoid pregnancy than surveys suggested, with use rising in some states.

Tracking the menstrual cycle to avoid pregnancy may be far more common than scientists once believed. Based on national surveys conducted over the years, only a small share of Americans were thought to rely on it.

A latest study tells a different story.

Around 7% to 8% of US birth control users aged 18 to 44 tracked their cycles in 2022 and 2023. That share nearly doubled by 2026 in three Western states.

Its popularity has also been underestimated because of the way most surveys count birth control users.

The study was led by Chelsea Polis, a principal research scientist at the Guttmacher Institute.

She worked with Rebecca Simmons, a research associate professor of obstetrics and gynecology at University of Utah Health.

According to recent reports, no newly introduced information was gathered for the project. Data from four large surveys were reanalyzed instead.

Cycle tracking for pregnancy prevention falls under a category of contraception known as fertility awareness-based methods (FABMs).

“I hope that these results are a shock to the family planning community,” Simmons said.

“There’s been a lot more acceptance of FABMs as legitimate methods over time, but most people still aren’t putting them on their radar enough for how important they are in the cultural milieu.”.

“This is a really crucial thing that I’m hoping that people will sit up and pay attention to right now.”.

According to recent reports, pregnancy is possible on only six to nine days of each menstrual cycle. These days fall around ovulation, when an egg is released by an ovary.

Some people count days on a calendar to work out when they are fertile. Others check their temperature every morning, and some watch for changes in cervical mucus. A smartphone app is used by some.

To avoid pregnancy, they skip sex on fertile days or use condoms as a backup. People who are trying to conceive can use the same information.

More than a dozen fertility awareness-based methods exist, but they don’t all work equally well.

“FABMs are a method class,” Simmons said.

Industry observers note that “They’re not a single method. Within that method class, some of those methods, like the rhythm method, are not very effective, and some are actually comparable to the effectiveness of short-acting methods like pills or patches.”.

According to recent reports, two of the surveys covered the whole country. One was the 2022–2023 National Survey of Family Growth. The other was a 2022 survey on access to birth control.

It has been revealed that the other two were limited to six states between them. One was conducted in Arizona, New Jersey and Wisconsin. The Mountain West Sexual and Reproductive Health Survey was carried out in Idaho, Nevada and Utah.

Industry observers note that each survey recruited its participants in its own way. The time frame for current use also varied from the month of the interview to the previous three months.

Despite these differences, the four estimates for 2022 and 2023 fell within a narrow band of 6.6% to 8.3%.

The federal survey alone suggests that more than 2.2 million people in the US use these methods.

“Fertility awareness-based methods are used by a meaningful share of US contraceptive users,” Polis said.

“Although many clinicians do not receive robust training on FABMs, our data show that FABMs are more frequently used than several other contraceptive methods that clinicians are routinely trained to provide.”.

Gaps in knowledge about birth control are nothing newly introduced. Earlier research found that many healthcare providers don’t offer self-injected birth control either.

In a recent development, picture a woman who keeps track of her cycle and relies on condoms during her fertile days. A national survey would most likely record her as a condom user.

According to recent reports, that happens because each person is usually assigned the most effective method they mention. Cycle tracking is ranked low on that scale and is therefore easily missed.

Recent findings suggest that such combined owners made up about a quarter of cycle trackers in three surveys. In the fourth, they were close to half.

When they were added back into the federal survey, the estimate went from 4.3% to 6.6%. The standard approach had overlooked about a third of the people who track their cycles.

Sources indicate that people who paired tracking with the pill, an IUD, an implant or sterilization were not counted. They accounted for about one in five cycle trackers, compared with roughly 9% in a 2013 to 2015 analysis.

According to recent reports, several of those methods prevent ovulation entirely. In that case tracking offers almost no extra protection, and the researchers suggested that some owners may not realize it.

Cycle tracking appears to be gaining ground, at least in some parts of the country.

Between 2019–2020 and 2022–2023, its use in Arizona, Fresh Jersey and Wisconsin increased from 5% to 6.9%.

A sharper rise was recorded in Idaho, Nevada and Utah. There, the share of birth control owners who tracked their cycles stood at 7.5% in December 2022. It had grown to 12.5% by June 2024 and then to 14.5% by January 2026.

Most of this growth came in the first 18 months. The later increase was small enough that it could have been due to chance.

Is the same trend playing out nationwide? That question can’t be answered yet. Because the federal survey has since been redesigned, its latest results cannot be compared reliably with earlier rounds.

According to recent reports, several factors could be involved, according to Simmons. Concerns about hormonal birth control may be one.

The popularity of tracking apps and difficulty getting other contraceptives may be others. None of these reasons was examined in the study.

Industry observers note that social media could be adding to the trend as well. Earlier studies of popular TikTok videos about birth control found cycle tracking was discussed more than any other method.

Among cycle trackers in the federal survey, 63% were married. Only 45% of people using other methods were.

The gap in Arizona, Fresh Jersey and Wisconsin looked much the same, at 60% versus 43%.

Cycle tracking only works when both partners cooperate. Couples in steady relationships may find it easier to decide together when sex should be avoided or a condom used.

A link between relationship commitment and the birth control choices of young adults has been reported before as well.

In a recent development, some surveys pointed to a role for education too. In Arizona, New Jersey and Wisconsin, 55% of cycle trackers had a college degree. Among other birth control users, the figure was 42%.

According to recent reports, no consistent link with religion was found. Cycle tracking therefore cannot be explained simply as a religious practice.

Adults aged 25 to 34 were the most likely to track their cycles in three of the four surveys.

It has been revealed that why more people are turning to cycle tracking is still unclear. Some people might just like it better. For others, getting hold of their preferred contraceptive may have become harder.

“Are people choosing these methods because they’re their preferred method, or are they choosing these methods because they’re out of options?” Simmons said.

“It might be that people are choosing these because they no longer have access to a doctor and they can’t afford the method that they need.”.

Sources indicate that how people track their cycles is another open question. In the surveys, scientifically tested methods could not be told apart from more casual ones.

Recent findings suggest that many period tracking apps were never designed to prevent pregnancy. Two apps have been cleared for birth control by the US Food and Drug Administration. Only one of them, Natural Cycles, is still on the US market.

It has been revealed that the findings have some limits. All birth control habits were self-reported. Other factors that might explain the differences between groups were not accounted for.

The Idaho, Nevada and Utah survey was also carried out online and in English. Some groups in it were small, so the results may not reflect the rest of the country.

Future research could ask cycle trackers directly what led them to choose the method.

New national data expected in 2027 could reveal whether the growing popularity of cycle tracking reflects a regional trend or a fundamental shift in how Americans approach birth control.

The full study was published in the journal The Lancet Regional Health – Americas.

#147029. Industry News: Scientists find a upcoming way to study some of the ocean’s most elusive microbes

📅 26 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1040 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Earth ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: Scientists find a upcoming way to study some of the ocean’s most elusive microbes

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1040 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A fresh study sheds light on the largely unexplored microbial world beneath the ocean and its potential ecological significance.
  • It has been revealed that most of the microbes living on the deep seafloor have never grown in a lab dish.
  • The sudden change can kill the microbes before anyone gets to study them.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A fresh study sheds light on the largely unexplored microbial world beneath the ocean and its potential ecological significance.

It has been revealed that most of the microbes living on the deep seafloor have never grown in a lab dish. On the way to the surface, a sample loses the high pressure and steady cold its microbes are adapted to.

The sudden change can kill the microbes before anyone gets to study them.

According to recent reports, A robotic system called DISCUSS keeps both conditions in place, from the seafloor all the way to the lab bench where single microbes are picked out. With it, a team grew a bacterium that barely grows at ordinary air pressure.

Sources indicate that the work was led by Jing-Chun Feng of Guangdong University of Technology in China. Zhengguang Liu, a researcher in the University of Manchester Department of Chemical Engineering, was one of the paper’s corresponding authors.

“Scientists have long struggled to grow many microorganisms found in nature under laboratory conditions, limiting our understanding of how they live and function,” stated Liu.

The deep sea is home to a vast diversity of microbes, many of which have adapted to extreme pressure and near-freezing temperatures.

Some deep-sea microbes even produce enzymes and other molecules.

The molecules that deep-sea microbes create can be useful for medicines, latest materials, food and energy.

Scientists say that less than one percent of deep-sea microbes can be grown with normal lab techniques.

“Deep-sea microbes are particularly fascinating because they have evolved to survive extreme pressure, cold and unusual chemical conditions,” Liu stated.

The testing of this technology was carried out in the South China Sea at a depth of 4,300 feet (1,300 meters) in a cold seep location.

Cold seeps are areas of the seafloor where methane and other compounds emerge at temperatures similar to those of the surrounding water.

At this depth, the water pressure would be 1,900 pounds per square inch (13 megapascals), which is about 130 times the atmospheric pressure at sea level, and water temperature would be 39°F (4°C).

Before carrying out any sampling procedure, sensors detected the levels of methane, carbon dioxide, oxygen, acidity, temperature, and pressure on the seafloor.

After evaluation by the software, only those locations with scores related to methanotrophic microbes were sampled.

The sealed samplers kept more than 98% of the seafloor pressure on the way up.

In a recent development, in the lab, the system built a virtual copy of the seafloor conditions from the sensor readings. Researchers call that kind of copy a digital twin, and the machine used it as the target to hold.

Industry observers note that when a sample moved from one chamber to the next, one pump pushed while another pulled at a matched rate. That kept the pressure from jumping during the handoff.

Industry observers note that to grow one kind of microbe on its own, a microbiologist spreads cells thinly across a soft gel. Each cell that survives grows into a small dot called a colony.

DISCUSS performs this task inside a sealed, high‑pressure chamber. A robot arm spreads the cells with a needle, and a camera watches through a sapphire window.

Sources indicate that A force sensor in the arm lets it press lightly enough not to tear the gel. In tests, the camera software recognized colonies with 94.6% accuracy.

The needle hit its target within 0.002 inches of the intended spot. Between tasks, the system sterilized the needle using light, keeping the pressure seal intact.

“From an engineering perspective, what excites me most is how intelligent sensing, modeling and automation can help us explore biological systems that were previously difficult to study,” said Liu.

The team recovered 34 microbes and grew each one on its own.

In 11 of them, a gene that scientists use to tell microbes apart differed enough from known reference strains that they may belong to groups not yet described.

It has been revealed that the team took a close look at two of the 34. Both turned out to be strains of known species.

One belongs to Pseudomonas songnenensis, and the other, named HP_SR10, belongs to Bacillus cereus.

To test how much each strain depended on pressure, the researchers grew both for 11 days at five pressures, from ordinary air pressure to a little above the seafloor’s.

The Pseudomonas strain grew about as well at ordinary air pressure as it did at seafloor pressure. HP_SR10 didn’t. It grew best at the same pressure as the seep it came from, and poorly at ordinary air pressure.

The authors wrote that this strain can’t be recovered with conventional methods, which grow microbes at surface pressure.

The system also kept a whole community of microbes alive and working for 180 days.

At its center was a partnership between methane-eating archaea, single-celled microbes distinct from bacteria, and bacteria that use sulfate from seawater.

Pumps fed the community methane and nutrients and flushed out waste. That kept sulfide, a byproduct that holds these microbes back at high levels, below 4 millimoles per liter.

Around day 110, both partners became noticeably more common.

The authors wrote that communities like this one typically collapse in closed lab containers with no fresh supply.

Carbon made near the ocean surface can sink to the deep ocean, and scientists still don’t fully understand how deep-sea microbes change it.

Growing a wider range of these microbes under conditions close to home could help scientists study that process.

In a recent development, only two of the 34 microbes were studied in detail. The study doesn’t describe what the 11 possibly new microbes do, or whether any make useful molecules.

All of the samples also came from a single seep. The authors noted that the design could be adapted for deeper water and for very hot places such as hydrothermal vents.

Next, the team plans to run many plates at once under different conditions and to track dissolved chemicals more closely as they change.

The researchers also plan to automate growing microbes in liquid instead of on gel.

The full study was published in the journal Nature Sensors.

Sources indicate that rep. Gabe Evans, here arriving at the Capitol in July for a House Republican Conference meeting, lost his bid for a second term representing Colorado's 8th District. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call) (Bill Clark CQ Roll Call).

According to recent reports, colorado Rep. Gabe Evans, who lost reelection earlier this month, announced Monday a 2028 run from the neighboring district of fellow defeated Republican Rep. Lauren Boebert.

“Now more than ever, Colorado needs conservatives in Congress who will fight to keep our border secure, cut taxes for working families, keep boys from dominating girls' sports and locker rooms, protect our water, and make energy affordable,” Evans mentioned in a statement.

His announcement comes less than two weeks after he lost his bid for a second term representing the battleground 8th District in the Denver area. While the race had been considered one of the most competitive in the country, Democratic former state Rep. Manny Rutinel secured victory by 15 points.

According to recent reports, as part of House Democrats’ massive midterm gains, they flipped three seats in Colorado. Boebert narrowly lost her reelection bid in the 4th District to Democrat Eileen Laubacher, while Republican Rep. Jeff Crank lost in the 5th District.

Evans’ statement cited his ties to the 4th District, which encompasses the eastern part of the state and extends into the Denver metro area.

“From Loveland to Lamar, I’m ready to keep fighting in the 4th District, where I grew up, and where my family has lived since 1976,” he remarked.

The district has a deep history of voting Republican. Boebert won by 11 points in 2024 while Donald Trump carried the district by 18 points.

Evans is far from the first member of Congress to switch to a district seen as more favorable to his party. Boebert herself shifted from Colorado's more competitive 3rd District to run for the heavily conservative 4th in 2024.

The 4th District will likely be a top target for Republicans in 2028, and Evans’ campaign sought to portray him as a clear front-runner in what could become a crowded GOP primary.

Sources indicate that “Gabe Evans will enter 2027 and the race for Colorado’s 4th Congressional District with $300,000 in campaign funds and name recognition that no first-time candidate in the district could match,” his campaign noted in the statement. “Combined with his record as an Army aviator, police officer, rancher, and member of Congress, that gives him a head start in money, name recognition, and credibility before the field takes shape.”.

A former state legislator and Denver-area police officer, Evans also served 12 years in the Army. He was first elected to the House in 2024, unseating Democrat Yadira Caraveo, and currently sits on the Energy and Commerce and Homeland Security committees.

In a recent development, laubacher, a Navy veteran who will take office on Jan. 3, is the first Democrat elected to represent the 4th District since Betsy Markey won her lone term in 2008. In response to Evans’ announcement, Laubacher’s campaign remarked she would be “focused on making Washington deliver” for district residents.

“There’s real work to do: ending the war in Iran that Gabe Evans voted six times to continue, lowering the cost of groceries and fertilizer that his eight votes for the tariffs helped drive up, and protecting the rural hospitals across the 4th district he voted to gut,” Laubacher spokesperson Taylor Gillespie said in a statement.

Industry observers note that isabel Angelo spends her days searching the cosmos for exoplanets and signs of extraterrestrial intelligence. But Angelo’s head isn’t in the stars. It’s buried under mountains of 0s and 1s — data from space telescopes old and new.

In a recent development, to piece together a fuller picture of what’s out there (alien megastructures around nearby stars, perhaps?), Angelo and her colleagues at the SETI Institute in Mountain View, Calif., are turning to machine learning models. These tools are analyzing the troves of telescope data for anomalies — things that look “weird” in space that we don’t know how to explain yet.

Most of the space weirdos will probably turn out to be total normies — a comet, a newborn star or a star surrounded by lots of gas and dust. “These are things that I would expect [the models] to find,” Angelo says. “But the goal is to find something that’s not even in any of these categories.”.

Sources indicate that in the meantime, Angelo keeps her whimsy and wonder for space alive by remembering historic moments, like the reveal of the first portrait of a black hole in 2019. The scientists “put all of these telescopes all over the Earth. They wait for the Earth to rotate. They do all this math to construct this one image,” Angelo notes. “I can’t believe how creative and innovative we have to be to learn about space. It’s such a specific and really fun challenge.”.

Tech Report: In a 1996 study, researchers reviewed 22,793 poinsettia cases reported to U.S. poison centers and found no deaths, but the plant can still upset pets

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (754 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, poison Control indicates the deadly reputation rests on a child's death over 100 years ago.
  • Every holiday season, poinsettias go up on tables and windowsills, and so does an old warning: keep them away from children, because they are deadly.
  • It has been revealed that researchers led by the Pittsburgh Poison Center checked that idea against hard numbers.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, poison Control indicates the deadly reputation rests on a child's death over 100 years ago. Tests of about 500 to 600 leaves found no poisonous dose.

Every holiday season, poinsettias go up on tables and windowsills, and so does an old warning: keep them away from children, because they are deadly.

It has been revealed that researchers led by the Pittsburgh Poison Center checked that idea against hard numbers. In a study published in 1996 in the American Journal of Emergency Medicine, they analyzed 849,575 plant exposures reported to the American Association of Poison Control Centers (HRSA).

Sources indicate that poinsettias accounted for 22,793 of those cases. There were no deaths among them.

The researchers wrote that the poinsettia “is a much-maligned plant which is thought by the public and some health professionals to be extremely toxic.”.

Sources indicate that their data told a different story. Almost all of the poinsettia exposures, 98.9%, were accidental, and 93.3% involved children.

Most of the people involved, 96.1%, were not treated in a health care facility. And 92.4% did not develop any toxicity related to the poinsettia at all.

“Most patients do not require any type of therapy and can be treated without referral to a health care facility,” the authors concluded.

The study is 30 years old, but the current advice from Poison Control, run by the National Capital Poison Center, notes the same thing.

Industry observers note that “The poinsettia plant is often considered deadly. That’s wrong,” its guidance states. “Poinsettia can be irritating but it is not fatal if eaten.”.

Industry observers note that poison Control claims some stories “just won’t go away.” “Over a hundred years ago, a child was found next to a wild poinsettia plant. He died and people blamed the plant. This hasn’t happened since,” it says.

Sources indicate that researchers have even tried to find a poisonous dose. They “just couldn’t, even after reaching experimental doses of about 1.25 pounds (500-600 leaves),” according to Poison Control.

That does not mean the plant is a snack. If children or pets eat it, Poison Control says, they can develop mouth irritation and stomach upset, such as nausea, vomiting or diarrhea.

The sap can cause a skin rash, and Poison Control notes reports of gardeners who work with the plant frequently developing one.

In a recent development, poison Control describes one real case. On Christmas Day, a 10-month-old put a small piece of a poinsettia leaf in his mouth, and his mother called a poison center.

The specialist told her no problems were expected and advised her to wipe the child’s mouth and give him something to drink.

The plant can also be a choking hazard, so Poison Control recommends placing poinsettias, and other houseplants, where children and pets cannot reach them.

The ASPCA lists the poinsettia as toxic to dogs, cats and horses, and it names the plant’s irritant sap as the toxic principle.

Under clinical signs, the ASPCA describes the plant as “irritating to the mouth and stomach, sometimes causing vomiting, but generally over-rated in toxicity.”.

Recent findings suggest that poinsettias are only one of the season’s concerns for pet owners. Earth.com has looked at how to keep cats safe at Christmas, from toxic trees to dangling decorations, and at festive plants that may be less safe than they look.

The poinsettia is the most popular flowering plant sold in the United States, with more than 70 million sold each year, according to a Clemson Cooperative Extension factsheet last revised in 2015.

It is named after Joel R. Poinsett, the first U.S. ambassador to Mexico. He brought the plant to the Bartram Botanical Garden in Philadelphia in 1828, and a Philadelphia nurseryman, Robert Buist, named it after him, the factsheet states.

The wild plants in Mexico grew 12 to 15 feet tall. The red parts that people think of as flowers are actually bracts, a kind of modified leaf. The true flowers are the small yellow clusters in the center.

If someone does swallow part of a poinsettia, Poison Control’s advice is to call a poison center at 1-800-222-1222, which is free, confidential and available 24 hours a day.

The information was obtained from the study Poinsettia exposures have good outcomes…just as we thought (American Journal of Emergency Medicine, 1996), Poison Control’s page Are poinsettias poisonous?, the ASPCA’s poinsettia entry, and Clemson Cooperative Extension’s poinsettia factsheet.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

An experimental mRNA treatment helped mouse heart cells divide after a heart attack, improving pumping function, but human trials are still needed.

An experimental treatment pushed adult heart muscle cells in mice to divide again after a heart attack, something those cells normally cannot do.

Researchers at the University of Cambridge delivered a modified messenger RNA that briefly switches on two proteins inside heart cells, Myc and Cyclin T1.

Treated mice pumped around 10 percent more blood with each heartbeat than mice given a mock treatment, the university reported.

Sources indicate that the gain held when the animals were reassessed at 12 weeks. The work was done in mice, and the treatment has not been tested in people.

It has been revealed that an adult human heart can lose up to one billion heart muscle cells in a heart attack. Those cells are never replaced, which weakens the pump and leaves scar tissue behind.

An estimated 920,000 people in the U.K. are living with heart failure, and a transplant is the only cure, according to the British Heart Foundation (BHF).

“Getting the human heart to repair itself is the holy grail for cardiologists,” said Professor Bryan Williams, chief scientific and medical officer at the BHF.

Myc is better known as a cancer gene. Switching it on makes liver cells multiply within days, yet in the heart it does almost nothing.

A 2020 mouse study explained why. Myc protein binds DNA in heart muscle cells but cannot turn genes on, because the heart is short of a partner protein, Cyclin T1.

Recent findings suggest that “When the Ccnt1 and Myc genes were expressed together, the heart switched into a regenerative state,” said Dr. Megan Bywater, a senior research officer at QIMR Berghofer Medical Research Institute and first author of that work.

The new experiment turns that finding into something closer to a therapy. Instead of altering genes, it uses mRNA, the kind of instruction a cell reads and then breaks down.

The team injected 100 micrograms of modified mRNA straight into the heart muscle during surgery. Injections guided by ultrasound did not work efficiently.

Myc and Cyclin T1 protein demonstrated up in heart tissue one hour and four hours after the injection, and had gone by 24 hours.

A fluorescent version of the molecule, used to track where it travelled, was still visible around damaged heart cells 24 hours after the injection.

The university notes the brief, localized signal is not expected to cause any permanent modification, which is meant to limit the risk of overgrowth.

Ultrasound scans tracked each animal on days three, six and 28 after treatment.

Ejection fraction, the share of blood the left ventricle pushes out with each beat, dropped by 26 percent in treated mice by day 28. In untreated animals it fell by 37 percent.

At 12 weeks the decline was 7.1 percent in the treated group, against 16.1 percent in controls.

Markers of cell division rose in the treated hearts, and the number of heart muscle cells had climbed by day five.

Tagging cells and their descendants showed 41.5 percent of labeled heart muscle cells sitting in adjacent pairs after treatment, compared with 5.5 percent in control hearts.

A genetically engineered version of the same approach did even better, holding the day-28 decline to 9 percent against 23 percent in controls.

Scar tissue told a different story. By day 28 the scar was no smaller in treated mice, although the volume of working muscle in the left ventricle had grown.

Recent findings suggest that waiting did not ruin the effect. In the transgenic model, switching the two proteins on seven to eight days later held the ejection fraction drop to 14 percent by day 36, against 30 percent in untreated animals.

No tumors were found in the treated animals at either checkpoint, and laboratory tests found no added capacity to transform cells.

Switching Myc on across the whole heart, by contrast, killed seven of eight mice in the transgenic version of the experiment, which is why the team confined the signal to the injured area.

Among the animals that received the mRNA, survival across 12 weeks did not differ significantly from controls.

Human heart muscle cells grown from stem cells in a dish also highlighted more signs of division after treatment.

The Cambridge group is now refining the treatment with BHF funding.

Larger animal studies, and then human trials, are needed to establish safety and effectiveness before the approach could help a human heart heal after a heart attack.

Industry observers note that “These are really exciting results,” said Dr. Catherine Wilson, an associate professor of pharmacology at the University of Cambridge and co-senior author of the study.

“We’re not just treating the symptoms of heart failure – this approach could help the heart to repair itself,” Wilson added.

“That makes it exciting when studies like this are able to reignite regeneration in heart muscle cells,” Williams said.

The study was published in the journal Nature Cardiovascular Research.

  • Challenger Deep is the deepest valley in the deepest trench in the ocean, plunging to roughly 11,000 meters below sea level.
  • Now, scientists have a fresh clue about how it got to be so … well, deep.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .).

Challenger Deep is the deepest valley in the deepest trench in the ocean, plunging to roughly 11,000 meters below sea level.

Now, scientists have a fresh clue about how it got to be so … well, deep.

Recent findings suggest that challenger Deep is found within the Mariana Trench, a crescent-shaped gouge in the seafloor east of the Philippines in the Pacific Ocean. The trench is the scene of a slo-mo tectonic collision called a subduction zone: The Pacific plate is diving beneath the Mariana plate, bending downward as it sinks into the mantle, forming a steep trench on the ocean floor.

All subduction zones are deep, but “it’s interesting why this is the deepest spot in the Earth’s ocean,” says geoscientist Robert Stern, an emeritus professor at the University of Texas at Dallas and a visiting researcher at the University of California, Los Angeles.

Industry observers note that he and colleagues employed a remotely operated robot called ROV Jason/Medea to descend to more than 6,000 meters and explore the Mariana Trench seafloor around the edges of Challenger Deep. The rocks turned out to contain pyroclastic deposits, evidence of an erstwhile explosive volcanic eruption. Those deposits included platelike blocks that could indicate eruption pulses, and lobe-shaped rocks where the volcanic flows ended and rapidly cooled.

These are the deepest pyroclastic deposits found on Earth, the scientists report November 23 in Frontiers in Earth Science.

How explosive an eruption is at Earth’s surface depends on the chemical makeup of the magma. When the molten rock contains a high proportion of volatile gases, including water vapor, those gases suddenly expand when the magma reaches the surface, producing a violent explosion.

Such explosive volcanism shouldn’t be possible in the deep sea; the pressure is too high for any escaping gases to expand, Stern indicates. Along with that mystery, the volcanic deposits were found unusually close to the trench, compared with what would be expected for a subduction zone.

Stern and his colleagues developed a hypothesis that incorporates these disparate pieces of evidence: The extreme depth of Challenger Deep, they say, may be at least partially due to an especially sharp bend in the Pacific Plate as it sinks into the mantle.

That tighter bend would explain why volcanism is happening closer to the subduction zone than usual. The classic subduction zone scenario is that the sinking plate heats up and melts partially as it descends; the magma rises through the overhanging plate and erupts, forming volcanic island arcs several hundred kilometers from the collision zone. Here, the volcanic deposits were just a hundred kilometers or so from the trench — which makes sense if the plate is dipping more steeply.

Recent findings suggest that as for the pyroclastics, “we can’t answer if the eruptions were really explosive,” Stern notes. But at those pressures, any gases such as water vapor contained in the magma wouldn’t be able to explosively expand as they would at the surface.

It has been revealed that instead, the pyroclastic rocks might have formed through a upcoming version of deep-sea eruption, one in which water emerging from the magma is initially in a supercritical fluid state. That would minimize any explosive expansion during the eruption and could also produce fragmented, dense deposits like those seen by Jason/Medea.

The discovery of deep-sea pyroclastics is “surprising and unprecedented,” indicates William Chadwick, a geologist at Oregon State University in Newport. Challenger Deep may be the only place on Earth “with the ingredients to produce explosive volcanism in the super-deep ocean,” he says. “Imagining this happening is … pretty mind-boggling.”.

According to recent reports, A lot more work remains to be done to evaluate all of these fresh ideas, Stern claims. “But a lot of things are now coming together.”.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • India baked under a stubborn heat dome while southern China lurched from flooding into dangerous, humid heat.
  • A new analysis links the May 2026 extremes to the same sprawling high-pressure system.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A new analysis reveals how atmospheric circulation connected extreme heat in India with a rapid shift from flooding to humid heat in southern China.

India baked under a stubborn heat dome while southern China lurched from flooding into dangerous, humid heat.

A new analysis links the May 2026 extremes to the same sprawling high-pressure system.

Meng Gao from Hong Kong Baptist University led the analysis, with collaborators from the Chinese Academy of Meteorological Sciences and Nanjing University of Information Science and Technology.

For much of early May, temperatures across the Indian region studied had been below normal.

Starting on May 17, that changed sharply, with temperatures staying over 1°C above the recent May average.

The researchers combined weather observations, atmospheric reanalysis, and climate simulations to trace the change.

Their maps highlighted daily average temperatures exceeding 40°C in some locations.

Sources indicate that may 20 stood out. Across the region studied, it was the hottest May 20 in the record stretching back to 1979.

Industry observers note that humidity added to the strain. The wet-bulb temperature, which reflects the combined effects of heat and moisture, ranked third-highest for that date.

For people working outside, particularly in northern India, the combination made an already difficult season more dangerous.

It has been revealed that the developing El Niño offered part of the explanation. By May, the central and eastern equatorial Pacific had entered El Niño conditions.

Atmospheric circulation shifted far beyond its shores.

The researchers linked this developing El Niño to a stronger western Pacific subtropical high. This broad area of high pressure also stretched farther west than usual.

Meanwhile, a persistent wave pattern in the upper atmosphere strengthened another high-pressure system over the Iranian Plateau. That system moved eastward.

Over India, the two highs joined, creating a stable “heat dome.” Air sank beneath it, warming as it descended and helping keep skies clear.

With more sunshine reaching the ground, temperatures continued rising. Warm waters in the northern Indian Ocean also helped strengthen the Pacific high, further supporting the persistent heat.

In southern China, the same Pacific high helped produce a different sequence of hazards.

Guangdong had endured repeated downpours since early May.

Particularly heavy rain between May 19 and 23 brought widespread flooding, followed almost immediately by humid heat from May 24–29.

Recent findings suggest that the abrupt switch followed the high-pressure system’s movement northwestward. Rain eased, sunshine increased, and descending air warmed the region.

The atmosphere, however, remained laden with moisture after the downpours. The result was a “rainfall-to-deadly humid heat” sequence, with little time between the two emergencies.

The paper reports dozens of heatstroke ambulance calls in Shenzhen and thousands of livestock deaths in Maoming.

Such dangerous combinations of heat and humidity arrived one to two months earlier than usual.

Air temperatures alone did not explain what happened in Guangdong. Readings were near the top of the historical range, but comparable heat had occurred before.

The difference was the moisture accompanying them. Relative humidity during the dangerous hours averaged about 60%, compared with roughly 50% during similarly hot hours in earlier years.

Humid air makes it harder for sweat to evaporate, limiting the body’s ability to shed heat. That means familiar thermometer readings can conceal much greater physical strain.

For several hours, conditions exceeded a modeled threshold for safe, sustained activity among healthy adults aged 65 or older. That applied even to sitting quietly or standing with minimal movement.

That threshold describes a particular group under specified conditions. Heat tolerance varies with age, activity, and exposure to sunlight.

The timing was exceptional too: these conditions appeared earlier than in any year of the available 2011–2025 comparison record.

The team also asked how human influence had changed the likelihood of India’s heat.

Using 11 climate models, the researchers compared simulations including human influences with a preindustrial climate.

Their central estimate suggested human influences had made a similarly intense Indian heatwave roughly 27 times more likely.

The estimated range was wide: about 16 to 52 times, at a 90% confidence level. The authors caution that differences between models and limitations in correcting their biases affect the result.

Recent findings suggest that the authors describe the finding as evidence of a likely human contribution, with the precise scale still uncertain. The estimate applies to the Indian event, not to the entire sequence across both countries.

Sources indicate that A common atmospheric influence helps explain why distant places suffered heat at nearly the same time. Whether those heatwaves also reinforced each other remains unresolved.

According to recent reports, for southern China, the order of events matters. Flooding can damage electricity supplies and other infrastructure, leaving residents without reliable cooling when the heat follows.

Warnings therefore need to account for what happened in the preceding days.

A heat forecast issued during flood recovery may reach people whose homes, workplaces, and access to electricity are already disrupted.

The researchers call for stronger infrastructure and better preparation in vulnerable regions.

In places facing rapid weather reversals, flood response and heat preparation may need to happen at the same time.

The study is published in the journal Advances in Atmospheric Sciences.

Sources indicate that gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Garages and unfinished basements are often poorly insulated, making them prone to extreme cold in fall and winter. A garage heater can turn this typically frigid space into a warm, practical area for woodworking projects, vehicle maintenance, and more. If you plan to spend time in your garage this winter tackling projects at your workbench, raising the ambient air temperature is a must.

Sources indicate that garage heaters come in various styles, though the most popular models are electric and propane. Electric heaters are convenient and easy to install if a power outlet is nearby. Propane heaters are more portable and can cover more surface area. Natural gas garage heaters are also powerful options for larger garages and can offer long-term heating solutions.

Heaters can benefit not only comfort but also safety. Cold temps can cause condensation to collect on tools and stored items, which may lead to rust and other damage. Wintry environments can also cause car engines and batteries to wear out faster. A well-heated garage protects your investments and provides a warmer, safer place to work.

If you're ready to prep for winter weather, read on for our in-depth reviews of the best garage heaters, followed by the most notable things to know before buying.

Although we haven’t tested the models below ourselves, we applied our experience testing space heaters and patio heaters to supplement our search for the best garage heaters. We spent a lot of time vetting features and specs, checking manufacturer websites, gauging prices, and consulting user reviews before deciding which ones made the cut. We spoke with mechanical and electrical engineering experts to understand what makes a great garage heater, and we considered heat types (electric, propane, or kerosene), as well as whether the heaters are permanent or portable.

This 240-volt compact garage heater is the best all-around choice for most spaces, with 7,500 watts of heating power and the option to mount it on the wall or ceiling.

According to the manufacturer, it warms a typical garage or unheated building to between 50 and 85 degrees Fahrenheit and should be installed with a foot of clearance from combustible surfaces.

The garage heater’s adjustable louvers let you direct air where you need it most, and a remote-controlled thermostat is built into the front of the heater. A wall-mounted thermostat is available for the unit as well, but it’s sold separately.

It has been revealed that thanks to its Wi-Fi capability, you can operate this heater from virtually anywhere to ensure your garage is warm when you get home, or to heat the space before you spend time at your workbench. You can turn the unit on and off and set recurring schedules through the app.

Industry observers note that the garage heater is rated to warm a 1,000-square-foot area, with an adjustable output of up to 20,000 BTUs. It can be mounted to the wall or ceiling, and its large digital temperature display is easy to read, even from across the room.

But for the price, it’s disappointing that the garage heater doesn’t include wiring.

For a powerful 5,600-watt portable garage heater, we recommend this NewAir model. It’s designed to warm spaces up to 600 square feet, and it includes a 6-foot cord that neatly coils on top of the unit, with brackets to hold it down.

The fan has two settings: automatic (which turns on when the heating element activates) and continuous. You can switch between the two manually.

Use continuous mode to keep air moving in spaces with high ceilings or when you’re operating an air-cleaning appliance, like a bench-top air filter, as it helps push dusty air through to speed up the process.

Recent findings suggest that designed for outdoor areas like patios, this Briza heater still works well in a garage thanks to its dust-resistant properties. It comes with an adjustable tripod that you can set between 44 and 84 inches tall. Selecting between its three heat settings—900, 1,200, or 1,500 watts—is easy with the unit’s remote control.

In a recent development, the heater has a built-in safety sensor that automatically shuts the appliance off if it tips over. A timer provides additional safety (and energy savings) by automatically shutting the heater off after 1 to 9 hours of operation.

According to recent reports, for a compact, affordable garage heater ideal for targeted heating, this propane-fueled unit from Mr. Heater is a great choice. It delivers 4,000 to 9,000 BTUs from a single 1-pound liquid propane canister and can heat up to 250 square feet. It works great on the floor by your workbench or desk.

Sources indicate that the heater can run for up to three hours on high, or you can upgrade to a 20-pound tank with a separately sold adapter. The heater’s size and weight make it easy to reposition, and it’s easy to bring with you to a shed, campsite, or other workspace.

This heavy-duty, 240-volt garage heater is ideal for climates with major temperature swings, featuring a two-stage high-and-low heating system.

Recent findings suggest that its lower heat output suits mildly cool days, while the higher stage can warm garages in single-digit temperatures. It also has a fan mode ideal for increasing airflow in a potentially stuffy garage, plus an energy-saving setting that defaults to the lowest wattage to maintain the desired temperature.

It has been revealed that A universal bracket is included for easy mounting to a ceiling or wall, and this heater has a remote-controlled thermostat. The only drawback is that it doesn’t offer much coverage for the price.

If you have an uninsulated wood garage or another minimally insulated space, this large, ceiling-mounted garage heater is worth a look.

It has been revealed that it runs on natural gas (a propane conversion kit is included) and, with a built-in electric fan, can warm areas up to 2,000 square feet thanks to its impressive 80,000-BTU output. It also has a powered exhaust that allows for vertical or horizontal venting.

Note that the Big Maxx does not come ready to install; you’ll have to purchase a thermostat, gas hose, fittings, and regulator separately. For most people, it’s best to have a licensed heating-cooling contractor install this garage heater.

There’s a lot to consider when using a heater to keep your garage safe and comfortable. So we picked the brain of Pat Porzio, a mechanical engineer and multi-licensed tradesman (electrical, plumbing, HVAC). He’s also the HVAC manager for Russo Brothers in East Hanover, New Jersey. We also spoke with David Shapiro, an electrician, author, and expert on old house wiring who contributes to electrical product and installation standards.

Both agree on one thing: Your overarching concern in heating a garage is safety. The first words out of both their mouths were identical: “Pull a permit.” That is, if you plan to use a permanently installed electric or gas-fired garage heater, you need to file a building permit for the work—whether you do the work yourself or hire a contractor. Permitted installations are inspected by the town or other authority with jurisdiction over this work where you live, which increases the likelihood of a safe installation.

Industry observers note that aside from pulling a building permit for the electrical work, Shapiro steers homeowners away from any heater without a UL (or other safety-related U.S. testing agency) listing.

Using a 120-volt space heater is simpler; same goes for small propane-fired and kerosene heaters. You don’t need a building permit to use one of these in a garage. Still, there are safe and unsafe ways to use these heaters. For more on that topic, check out our garage heater safety tips below.

As we mentioned earlier, there are a couple of different types of garage heaters. Electric heaters are easier to install, don't require a vent, and are generally safer. But depending on your local electricity rates, they can be more expensive to run. Gas heaters use natural gas or propane, and they can be a more cost-effective option for heating larger garages. They require ventilation, which can be a pain if you don't already have the right setup.

Infrared heaters heat objects rather than the air, so they can be a good companion for localized projects at your workbench. Forced-air heaters use a fan to distribute heat swiftly and work well for large spaces, but they require good insulation to run efficiently and may kick up dust around your workshop.

Sources indicate that for most garages, an electric heater is often the most viable option because it's easy to install, safe, and effective. But if you have a larger or poorly insulated garage, a gas heater might be the way to go.

According to recent reports, “A bigger heater is not necessarily better,” Porzio claims. “An oversized heater will short cycle. That is, it will turn on and off too frequently. It satisfies heating demand very rapidly and abruptly turns off. A heater that is too small will do just the opposite. It will run and run and never fulfill the heating demand, eventually wearing itself out.”.

Before contractors install a boiler or furnace, they perform a series of calculations, called a Manual J, to determine the correct size. While homeowners can get a rough estimate by multiplying the area's square footage by 50 to get the required BTUs, Porzio recommends using simplified Manual J forms online or a sizing tool like those on King-Electric.com and Newair.com.

For reference, a two-car garage will need a heater ranging from 30,000-50,000 BTUs to reach a consistent, comfortable temperature.

Industry observers note that whether you attempt the electrical work or hire it out, Shapiro has two more recommendations. First, don’t install the heater so that a power cord leading to a machine or tool could be draped directly in front of it. The heat can damage the cord.

Sources indicate that second, consider installing a CO alarm in the garage. A CO alarm can make the garage a safer place to work, especially if you’re heating it with gas, and it can also protect the occupants of the house.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Eric Ueland, No. 2 official at the White House Office of Management and Budget, arrives for his confirmation hearing in the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee on April 3, 2025. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call).

President Donald Trump on Monday nominated Eric Ueland, deputy director for management in the White House budget office, to be the next comptroller general to lead the Government Accountability Office.

The nomination fills in the blanks after Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Chairman Rand Paul, R-Ky., had scheduled a Nov. 19 hearing to examine more than a dozen of Trump’s nominees for executive and judicial positions but without identifying who the comptroller general candidate would be. Ueland's name has since been added to the hearing agenda.

The move sets up an unprecedented scenario where a top official of the Office of Management and Budget, a White House office that has tangled with the Government Accountability Office since Trump’s first term, is put forward as the next head of the legislative agency.

It has been revealed that the GAO, a congressional watchdog with some 3,000 employees, has repeatedly accused the administration of violating the 1974 budget law by withholding or "impounding" enacted, appropriated funds. In September, for example, the GAO said Trump’s cancellation of $810 million in spending without the approval of Congress through a so-called pocket rescission was illegal.

White House Budget Director Russ Vought was quick to respond on X, writing that GAO “has become hyper partisan and ... they make their legal assessments based on whether Democrats are in the White House.” The administration has dismissed GAO opinions, arguing the agency has no authority over the executive branch because it is part of the legislative branch.

Democrats immediately denounced Ueland's nomination, saying it promised to further inflame tensions between the executive and legislative branches over the power of the purse.

“It would be lunacy for the Senate to hand a 15-year term leading Congress’ nonpartisan watchdog to a Russ Vought acolyte who spends his days plotting newly introduced ways for this administration to defy Congress," stated Senate Appropriations ranking member Patty Murray, D-Wash., who is likely to chair the panel next year.

"Ueland orchestrated the president’s destructive mass firing campaign, is presiding over the razing of USAID, and is the last person who should be leading GAO," Murray said in a statement.

It has been revealed that sen. Gary Peters, D-Mich., ranking member of the Homeland Security committee, urged all senators to oppose the Ueland nomination, saying it would provide “further power to the Executive Branch at a time when independent oversight from Congress is needed more than ever.”.

Peters also reiterated his previous criticism of Republicans for skipping bipartisan deliberations by a special 10-member legislative commission that is charged under statute with recommending candidates to the president for nomination.

“All three times the Commission process has occurred in the past, the president has selected a nominee with bipartisan support,” Peters mentioned.

In a sign of potential trouble for the nomination, a few Republicans expressed qualms about Ueland and what critics described as a rushed process for picking a GAO chief.

Recent findings suggest that "I'm not a fan," stated retiring Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., who faulted Ueland's boss for not providing proof of the cost savings claimed by Trump's Department of Government Efficiency, known as DOGE.

"To me, there's a lack of discipline or business experience in there to answer that simple question, or the reason they don't answer it is they don't have an answer," Tillis remarked. "Both are bad.".

While Tillis stopped short of promising to oppose Ueland, he said the nomination "deserves individual consideration" instead of being taken up in a group with several other nominees.

Sources indicate that and Sen. John Curtis, R-Utah, "has concerns that the nomination is too partisan, particularly given how independent and long-term the appointment of the Comptroller General is," a spokesman said in a statement.

Industry observers note that ueland has served as deputy director for management at the White House budget office since last year following his confirmation by the Senate on a party line 52-45 vote. He also has been performing the duties of the OMB controller since September 2025, according to his LinkedIn profile.

An expert on legislative procedure and strategy, Ueland has worked in a wide range of administrative and policy-oriented positions in the executive branch — including at OMB, the State Department and White House — and before that in the Senate.

He served as director of legislative affairs for Trump in his first term, as well as the State Department undersecretary for civilian security, democracy and human rights, and director of the department’s Office of U.S. Foreign Assistance, among other positions.

In a recent development, before that, he was the Senate Budget Committee’s GOP staff director under then-Chairman Michael B. Enzi, R-Wyo., for four years through the end of 2017.

Earlier, he worked as chief of staff to then-Senate GOP Whip Don Nickles of Oklahoma and then-Senate Majority Leader Bill Frist of Tennessee.

Ueland, who has a bachelor’s degree in history from the University of San Francisco, lacks the financial background of recent past comptrollers. He has, however, gone deep in the weeds with numbers at OMB and the Senate Budget Committee, and has extensive experience as an administrator.

Former comptroller Charles A. Bowsher was a CPA, a partner at Arthur Anderson and assistant secretary of the Navy for financial management before President Ronald Reagan tapped him to lead the GAO in 1981.

Recent findings suggest that david M. Walker, his successor, was a CPA, a partner at Arthur Anderson, assistant secretary of labor in the Employee Benefits Security Administration, and deputy executive director of the Pension Benefit Guaranty Corporation before his nomination by President Bill Clinton.

Gene L. Dodaro, whose 15-year term ended last year, had a bachelor’s degree in accounting and had worked at GAO for some 35 years before President Barack Obama nominated him to succeed Walker.

When Dodaro left, he designated Orice Williams Brown, who was GAO’s chief operating officer, as acting comptroller.

Recent findings suggest that before Trump nominated Ueland, the six Republican members of the legislative commission sent a letter to the White House last week recommending three candidates for the position — Ueland, Brian C. DeBusk and Roland Foster, according to sources.

DeBusk is president and CEO of DeRoyal Industries, a privately held medical equipment manufacturer. He served on the Medicare Payment Advisory Commission from 2016 to 2022 after being appointed by Dodaro. Foster is a longtime GOP aide at the moment serving as senior adviser to retiring Sen. Joni Ernst, R-Iowa.
